TITLE: Active Label Refinement with Semi-Supervised Learning
PROPOSAL: Inspired by self-training approaches, we incorporate semi-supervised training into active label refinement, allowing the model to harness its predictions to correct label noise online. Semi-supervised objectives are judiciously employed alongside standard cross-entropy loss for data that initially tags unclear label structures. We hypothesize this combination enhances learning from noisy labels through the active correction of potential label errors.
CONTROLS: This research will be evaluated with performance comparisons with our uncertainty-aware sample-weighting, Novorob loss, and standard semi-supervised learning on chosen benchmarks.
COST: 27000
PREDICTION: This combination may offer helpful uncertainty reduction; however, adapting semi-supervised training to incorporate label refinement properly could involve complex algorithm updates that weaken the cooperative synergy in the considered schemes.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Instance-Level Label Correction with Unsupervised Data Validation
PROPOSAL: Implement the AdaLabel method, a recently proposed data-driven approach that actively selects and corrects noisy labels, using a variety of real-world datasets (e.g., Clothing1M, WebVision, CIFAR-10) with simulated label noise, and quantifies its performance using metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and robustness to different types of noise.
CONTROLS: Compare AdaLabel to other state-of-the-art algorithms in the literature (e.g., Co-teaching, Mentornet), including a no-label-correction baseline where models are trained on noisy data without any correction mechanisms, and three ablations of AdaLabel: 1) without the unsupervised data validation step, 2) without the correction calculator based on loss and confidence levels, and 3) without the iterative selection and correction refinement.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: We expect AdaLabel to surpass state-of-the-art methods in correcting noisy labels, especially on datasets with significant instance-dependent noise (e.g., Clothing1M), and the ablations to demonstrate the importance of each component in maintaining high robustness. This method may fail on datasets with mostly class-conditional noise (e.g., CIFAR-10) where the correction calculator may over-correct clean labels.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Exploring Adversarial Training Regimens for Label Corruption Resistance
PROPOSAL: Investigate novel adversarial training regimens, such as mini-max approaches and regularization based on conditional entropy, to enhance label corruption resistance in neural networks, and evaluate their effectiveness on challenging instance-dependent noisy datasets (e.g., Clothing1M, WebVision) with real-world noise (not simulated).
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed methods to traditional adversarial training, as well as other concurrent label correction methods (e.g., AdaLabel), and analyze the impact of hyperparameters and noise levels on the learned models.
COST: 20250
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the novel adversarial training regimens will improve label corruption resistance and achieve state-of-the-art performance on the mentioned datasets, particularly under high noise levels, but may be less effective when the noise is mostly class-conditional or extremely instance-dependent. Additionally, we hypothesize that a higher number of iterations may lead to overfitting and decreased performance on noisy validation sets.

CONTROLS: Use the new metric to compare label noise in the analyzed datasets, and then investigate how well the label correction methods from previous experiments can resist this type of noise.

PREDICTION: We expect the analysis to provide valuable insights into the characteristics of real-world label noise and to demonstrate that our proposed metric is effective in capturing its nuances. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporal Event RNN for Causal RGB-Event Fusion
PROPOSAL: Train an encoder-decoder architecture, leveraging a temporal Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) module as the core for event-driven representation. Integrate with an RGB feature extractor for spatial information, forming a unified flow that can process event streams continuously in time. The causal aspect ensures that predictions only rely on information up to the last observed RGB frame, meeting the first constraint. The decoder is tasked with generating dense semantic segmentations for any arbitrary time Δt after the last observed frame, satisfying the anytime requirement.
CONTROLS: Baseline: a state-of-the-art multi-modal fusion network without causal, anytime constraints; ablations: removing the RNN module and evaluating the impact of spatiotemporal feature fusion on perceptual performance.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: This method will show a consistent improvement over state-of-the-art multi-modal fusion networks; it will struggle in scenarios with complex event distributions due to the lack of context beyond the RNN step size.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-modal Fusion Network with Attention for High-Frame-Rate Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Implement a deep neural network architecture that fuses the initial RGB frame $I_t$ and the event stream $\mathcal{E}_{t-\Delta t \to t+\delta t}$ using a multi-modal fusion module and an attention mechanism. The fusion module will employ late fusion, early fusion, or hybrid fusion techniques to combine spatial and temporal features from both data modalities. The attention mechanism will focus on the most informative regions and frames, such as areas with high motion or object appearance/disappearance events. The network will be trained end-to-end on a dataset of autonomous driving scenes, drone navigation videos, and quadruped robot navigation scenarios, using a sliding window paradigm to generate target semantic maps for all possible timestamps $\delta t \in (0, \Delta t]$.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard RGB-based semantic segmentation models (e.g., PSPNet, DeepLabV3+) and with existing multi-modal fusion methods (e.g., RGBD-Fusion, EvNet) applied in the same context.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: The proposed network will achieve improved segmentation performance compared to purely RGB-based models, with a moderate increase in accuracy due to the incorporation of event-based information. However, its performance might suffer from the challenges of handling high-dynamic scenes and sparse event data, potentially leading to failure in cases with extreme motion or object occlusion.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Event-based Feature Enhancement for RGB-based Models
PROPOSAL: Develop an event-enhanced version of the ResNet-50 (or similar RGB-based semantic segmentation model) that leverages the high-temporal-resolution information from the event stream to improve its feature learning. Specifically, the enhanced model will take an RGB frame $I_t$ and pass it through the standard ResNet-50 convolutional features, followed by the mean event values and standard deviations computed from $\mathcal{E}_{t-\Delta t \to t+\delta t}$, which will be used to modulate the learned features. This can help compensate for the RGB camera's low frame rate by injecting the temporal coherence information obtained from events.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the event-enhanced model with its RGB-only baseline on the same dataset and with the multi-modal fusion network proposed in the previous experiment.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: The event-enhanced model can improve the RGB-only model's accuracy, particularly in areas with temporal coherence, such as pedestrian motion or moving vehicles. However, its effectiveness may be limited when dealing with scenes containing many occlusions, rapid changes, or inaccurate event data, resulting in suboptimal performance.

TITLE: Transfer Learning for Event Cameras in Dynamic Scenes
PROPOSAL: Develop a transfer learning framework that adapts pre-trained models for RGB-based semantic segmentation to the event camera domain, leveraging the shared semantic knowledge between RGB and event data to reduce the need for extensive retraining on event-based data. This will involve fine-tuning a pre-trained RGB model on a small dataset of event-based data, which can serve as a more efficient and scalable solution for adapting to the unique characteristics of event cameras.

However, the effectiveness of transfer learning may be limited by the degree of similarity between RGB and event data, which could result in decreased performance when transferred to scenarios with significant domain shifts or novel event patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-modal Fusion Network with Attention for High-Frame-Rate Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: Implement a deep neural network architecture that fuses the initial RGB frame $I_t$ and the event stream $\mathcal{E}_{t-\Delta t \to t+\delta t}$ using a multi-modal fusion module and an attention mechanism. The fusion module will employ late fusion, early fusion, or hybrid fusion techniques to combine spatial and temporal features from both data modalities. The attention mechanism will focus on the most informative regions and frames, such as areas with high motion or object appearance/disappearance events. The network will be trained end-to-end on a dataset of autonomous driving scenes, drone navigation videos, and quadruped robot navigation scenarios, using a sliding window paradigm to generate target semantic maps for all possible timestamps $\delta t \in (0, \Delta t]$.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard RGB-based semantic segmentation models (e.g., PSPNet, DeepLabV3+) and with existing multi-modal fusion methods (e.g., RGBD-Fusion, EvNet) applied in the same context.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: The proposed network will achieve improved segmentation performance compared to purely RGB-based models, with a moderate increase in accuracy due to the incorporation of event-based information. However, its performance might suffer from the challenges of handling high-dynamic scenes and sparse event data, potentially leading to failure in cases with extreme motion or object occlusion.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Event-based Feature Enhancement for RGB-based Models
PROPOSAL: Develop an event-enhanced version of the ResNet-50 (or similar RGB-based semantic segmentation model) that leverages the high-temporal-resolution information from the event stream to improve its feature learning. Specifically, the enhanced model will take an RGB frame $I_t$ and pass it through the standard ResNet-50 convolutional features, followed by the mean event values and standard deviations computed from $\mathcal{E}_{t-\Delta t \to t+\delta t}$, which will be used to modulate the learned features. This can help compensate for the RGB camera's low frame rate by injecting the temporal coherence information obtained from events.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the event-enhanced model with its RGB-only baseline on the same dataset and with the multi-modal fusion network proposed in the previous experiment.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: The event-enhanced model can improve the RGB-only model's accuracy, particularly in areas with temporal coherence, such as pedestrian motion or moving vehicles. However, its effectiveness may be limited when dealing with scenes containing many occlusions, rapid changes, or inaccurate event data, resulting in suboptimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sparse Event Regularization for Dense Semantic Maps
PROPOSAL: Modify the loss functions used in the multi-modal fusion network and event-enhanced model to incorporate a regularization term that utilizes the characteristics of sparse event data. This term will be designed to enforce consistency between the predicted semantic maps and the event stream, encouraging the model to predict objects and regions that are consistent with the observed events. The regularization can be achieved through an L1 or L2 penalty term combined with an event-driven loss function.
CONTROLS: Compare the results of the sparse event regularization method with the baseline multi-modal fusion network and event-enhanced model on synthetic and real-world datasets, also with different levels of occlusions and event noise.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: The sparse event regularization can improve the model's robustness to noise and occlusions and help exploit the informative content of event data. However, it may exacerbate existing errors when the model mistakenly "fills in" missing data or introduces fictitious events, which could lead to decreased accuracy in certain situations.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Sparse Event Regularization for Dense Semantic Maps
PROPOSAL: Modify the loss functions used in the multi-modal fusion network and event-enhanced model to incorporate a regularization term that utilizes the characteristics of sparse event data with a scene flow-based approach. This term will be designed to enforce consistency between the predicted semantic maps and the event stream, encouraging the model to predict objects and regions that are consistent with the observed events, taking also into account the spatial layout of objects in the scene.
CONTROLS: Compare the results of the revised sparse event regularization method with the baseline multi-modal fusion network and event-enhanced model on synthetic and real-world datasets, also with different levels of occlusions and event noise.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: The modified regularization can lead to more accurate density estimates and scene understanding due to its improved fusion of semantic and spatial layouts. However, as before, the potential for over-smoothing may arise when lacking accurate flow and scene geometry, especially with low-resolution event streams or relatively small model capacity, resulting in decreased accuracy.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Sparse Event Regularization for Dense Semantic Maps (3)
PROPOSAL: Develop a more sophisticated scene flow estimation module that leverages the asynchronous nature of event data and its high temporal resolution to accurately predict the motion between events and optimize the event-driven loss function for better alignment with the dense semantic map. This will be achieved by using a GAN-based architecture that takes event data as input and generates pseudo-depth images for training and validation stages.
CONTROLS: Compare the results of the revised scene flow module with different variants of the multi-modal fusion network, event-enhanced model, and standard RGB-based models on real-world autonomous driving and quad-rotor datasets, as well as on synthetic datasets to validate the reliability of the model.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: The improved scene flow estimation should help to accurately model the movement of objects in the scene and lead to better segmentation accuracy in dynamic scenes. However, deriving accurate scene flow estimates might be challenging when dealing with high-velocity motion or complex scene geometry, potentially resulting in decreased model accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Active Temporal Pooling for Event Data
PROPOSAL: Implement an active temporal pooling strategy for event data, which can adaptively select relevant events across time to improve the modeling of object trajectories, motion patterns, and other relevant temporal cues in the scene. This will be achieved by introducing a learnable temporal attention mechanism that dynamically weighs the contributions of events to the overall representation of the scene, allowing the model to effectively focus on the most informative events.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the proposed active temporal pooling against standard pooling schemes (e.g., uniform, Gaussian) and other temporal attention-based approaches on different datasets and scenarios, such as dynamic scenes with frequent occlusions, high-speed motion, or transient events.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: The active temporal pooling strategy should lead to improved segmentation accuracy and robustness in dynamic scenes, by effectively incorporating the temporal structure of event data into the semantic representation. However, it may face difficulties when dealing with scenes containing many irrelevant or redundant events, which could result in decreased model performance if not properly addressed.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Active Temporal Pooling for Event Data (4)
PROPOSAL: Incorporate an uncertainty estimation component into the active temporal pooling framework to account for the reliability of individual events and their spatial correspondences in the scene. This will involve learning an uncertainty map for the event representation and integrating it with the temporal attention mechanism to output a temporally and spatially weighted event representation, which can be used to augment the RGB feature representation in the multi-modal fusion network or event-enhanced model.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the revised active temporal pooling with uncertainty estimation against the baseline active temporal pooling and other methods that incorporate uncertainty or reliability representations, such as probabilistic or mixture of distributions-based models, on dynamic scene segmentation tasks.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: The incorporation of uncertainty estimation should improve the robustness and reliability of the active temporal pooling approach, particularly in scenarios with noisy or uncertain event data, leading to better segmentation performance and reduced variability in model predictions. However, deriving accurate uncertainty estimates might be challenging when events are highly correlated or contain high-frequency fluctuations, potentially resulting in decreased model accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Event Cameras in Dynamic Scenes
PROPOSAL: Develop a transfer learning framework that adapts pre-trained models for RGB-based semantic segmentation to the event camera domain, leveraging the shared semantic knowledge between RGB and event data to reduce the need for extensive retraining on event-based data. This will involve fine-tuning a pre-trained RGB model on a small dataset of event-based data, which can serve as a more efficient and scalable solution for adapting to the unique characteristics of event cameras.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the transfer learning approach with end-to-end training of an event-driven model on large-scale event-based datasets, as well as with other transfer learning techniques that rely on different forms of adaptation or data augmentation, on dynamic scene segmentation tasks.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: The proposed transfer learning framework should facilitate the adaptation of existing RGB-based models to event cameras in dynamic scenes, leading to improved efficiency and reduced compute requirements for training and deployment. However, the effectiveness of transfer learning may be limited by the degree of similarity between RGB and event data, which could result in decreased performance when transferred to scenarios with significant domain shifts or novel event patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Multi-Modal LSTM-Like Fusion for Anytime RGB-Event Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: We propose a deep neural network that combines a 2D LSTM-like architecture to process RGB frames, a 1D LSTM-like architecture to process event streams, and a spatial-temporal fusion gate to integrate the features from both modalities. This model will be trained on the KITTI-360 dataset, a large-scale real-world autonomous driving dataset with RGB videos and corresponding event camera data, to learn to predict dense semantic maps at any arbitrary timestamp given the initial RGB frame and event stream.
CONTROLS: A baseline model will be the state-of-the-art video semantic segmentation method, TVS, applied to a synthesized high-frame-rate version of the KITTI-360 RGB videos to test for framerate independence. Ablations will include removing the LSTM-like architecture for event processing or the spatial-temporal fusion gate to investigate their relative contributions.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: This approach should outperform the baseline on.semantic segmentation metrics due to its ability to effectively leverage the temporal information from event camera data. However, it may struggle with cases of fast object appearance or disappearance due to the limitations of the LSTM architecture in capturing high-speed motion.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Event-Informed Feature Transfer for Enhancing RGB Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: We propose an event-informed feature transfer approach that adapts the static semantic context from a single past RGB frame to the dynamic scene captured by an event stream. The idea is to utilize a neural network to compute event-informed representations of the static semantic features, and then transfer these representations to densely reconstruct frames between low-frame-rate time-steps, enabling high-frame-rate semantic perception. This approach will be evaluated on the EventCam dataset, which contains real-world event camera data paired with corresponding RGB videos from various scenes.
CONTROLS: We will implement and compare our event-informed feature transfer method to a variant that uses a random dot product for feature transfer to investigate the importance of the learned transfer mechanism. Additionally, we will train a baseline model that uses the static RGB features without event-informed transfer to assess the impact of the proposed method on semantic segmentation accuracy.
COST: 7340
PREDICTION: This approach should significantly improve the accuracy of semantic segmentation within the perceptual gap enabled by event-informed feature transfer, showing its potential as a practical method for high-frame-rate perception in real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Feature Fusion with Temporal Context for Dense Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: To capture both short-term and long-term temporal relationships within the event stream and between the event and RGB frames, we propose a hierarchical feature fusion architecture that integrates features from multiple temporal scales. This framework will incorporate a hierarchical event-based feature extraction mechanism to capture subtle changes in the event stream and an attention-based fusion module to selectively weigh features from different temporal scales. We will evaluate this method on the KITTI-360 dataset.
CONTROLS: Compared to the revised event-informed feature transfer method, the hierarchical feature fusion approach will be augmented with three ablation studies to investigate its sensitivity to different temporal scales, the effect of attention-based fusion, and the contribution of event-based feature extraction. Furthermore, we will implement a baseline using a standard RGB semantic segmentation model without incorporating event-based information.
COST: 14000
PREDICTION: By leveraging hierarchical temporal relationships between the event and RGB frames, this method should enhance the accuracy of dense semantic segmentation within the perceptual gap, while also generalizing better to diverse dynamic scenarios.

TITLE:  Revision of Hierarchical Feature Fusion with Temporal Context for Dense Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: We expand our hierarchical feature fusion architecture with an additional, bottom-up processing module that leverages event-driven attention to adaptively select informative event snippets and their corresponding RGB representations, effectively bridging the event-based information gap. This revised approach will emphasize learning robust and multimodal representations that capture dynamic scene patterns under variable temporal scales, without substantive changes to the top-down processing and fusion architecture. Our experiments will use the same dataset, and we will introduce additional publicly available autonomous driving datasets to increase the variety of environments tested.
CONTROLS: We will simulate the effect of removing the event-driven attention component, reducing the number of selected event snippets, and comparing our revised method to the baseline without event-based information. Additionally, we will evaluate the robustness of the event-driven attention mechanism against synthetically occluded or corrupted event data.
COST: 14000
PREDICTION: By incorporating event-driven attention, we expect a significant improvement in accuracy and robustness under dynamic, real-world driving scenarios, including reductions in erroneous segmentation due to event data corruption.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Efficient Online Learning for Dynamic Event-RGB Fusion Modalities
PROPOSAL: To further improve the adaptability and efficiency of our event-RGB fusion models, we propose a dynamic online learning approach that learns to incorporate incoming event data to refine the fusion strategy as the scene changes over time. This will enable the model to maintain high accuracy even under rapidly changing environments, where outdated fusion strategies may lead to suboptimal performance. Our experiments will use a combination of autonomous driving and drone navigation datasets.
CONTROLS: We will compare our dynamic online learning approach to two baseline methods: a traditional offline learning framework and a fixed online learning framework. We will also evaluate the impact of different learning rates and query sampling strategies on the performance of our dynamic online learning approach.
COST: 16560
PREDICTION: By adapting the fusion strategy to the changing scene, our online learning approach should lead to a significant reduction in performance drift, resulting in more robust and accurate event-RGB fusion modalities for dynamic scenes.

TITLE:  Event-Informed Feature Transfer for Enhancing RGB Semantic Segmentation
PROPOSAL: We propose an event-informed feature transfer approach that adapts the static semantic context from a single past RGB frame to the dynamic scene captured by an event stream. The idea is to utilize a neural network to compute event-informed representations of the static semantic features, and then transfer these representations to densely reconstruct frames between low-frame-rate time-steps, enabling high-frame-rate semantic perception. This approach will be evaluated on the EventCam dataset, which contains real-world event camera data paired with corresponding RGB videos from various scenes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improved Knowledge Distillation for Point Cloud Personalization
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel knowledge distillation method to distill the identity-preserving knowledge from a large-scale 3D model to a smaller, subject-driven 3D model. This is achieved by training a student model on a set of intermediate views between the input view and the unobserved view, conditioned on a subject-specific prompt. We utilize a recently proposed text-to-point-cloud diffusion model (Diffusion-Accelerated Imperialist Competitive Algorithm, DIA-ICA), and fine-tune it on a small number of example images from the subject, providing better encoding of subject-specific features.
CONTROLS: We compare with different number of fine-tuning iterations, different subject prompts, and different student model sizes. Direct comparison is made with a query-based solution that iteratively refines an initial asset by one view, applying the DIA-ICA model to optimize the novel view, and also with a principal component analysis (PCA) approach that captures subject-specific variations in training data.
COST: 2681.63
PREDICTION: Our knowledge distillation method is expected to reduce both the time required to generate novel views and the hallucination in colors, and bring significant reductions in hallucination colors and improvements in identity preservation when compared to the baseline models. Failure could occur if there is insufficient fine-tuning data for the subject and the network captures noise over true features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Conditional Volumetric Rendering for Identity-Preserving 4D Generation
PROPOSAL: We leverage recent advances in conditional generative models (CGMs) for volumetric rendering, and propose a CGM-based approach for 4D generation. This involves learning a scene-specific prior through conditioning on a subject-specific video prompt, and then using a Volumetric Image Transformer (VIT) to hallucinate novel views. The video prompt is used to provide cues for the VIT to capture the subject's appearance in different lighting conditions and viewpoints, thus preserving identity across views. We utilizeTpl2020)style transformer architecture and fine-tune on a subset of videos from the same domain as the target subject.
CONTROLS: We compare with different architectures (StyleGAN2, DCGAN, etc.) in the volumetric rendering and student model sizes, and different velocity prompts, incorporating findings from 2D knowledge transfer to evaluate the merits of the approach.
COST: 4147.2
PREDICTION: Our method should be able to generate novel views with similar colors and appearance as the input video, but failure may occur if the scene-specific prior is not well-learned or when the subject-specific video prompt does not cover all necessary viewpoints or lighting conditions.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of a diffusion-based model (e.g., StyleGAN-ADA) for 3D generation with an identity-aware loss function that encourages the model to preserve the appearance of the given subject across viewpoints. PROPOSAL: Design a multi-view diffusion model (MVD) that utilizes convolutional autoencoders (CAEs) to learn a subject-specific representation of the identity from multiple views. The CAEs will be trained to preserve the appearance and structure of the subject, while the MVD will learn to expand this representation into the unobserved views. This approach will enable the model to capture more detailed and accurate identity information from the input image/video.

The loss function will be a weighted combination of the reconstruction loss, adversarial loss, and identity loss, which measures the similarity between the generated 3D asset and the input image/video.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Design a multi-view diffusion model (MVD) that utilizes convolutional autoencoders (CAEs) to learn a subject-specific representation of the identity from multiple views. The CAEs will be trained to preserve the appearance and structure of the subject, while the MVD will learn to expand this representation into the unobserved views. This approach will enable the model to capture more detailed and accurate identity information from the input image/video.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Reusing Lookahead Decoding for Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We modify the existing Lookahead decoding method to not only reuse the target model's hidden states but also to cache the draft tokens it proposes during the Lookahead iterations. Then, at each cascade round, we use the cached draft tokens as input to the next draft model, thus creating a cascade of Lookahead decodings. We expect this to be faster than standard speculative decoding with Lookahead decoding and to have comparable quality.
CONTROLS: We compare this approach to standard Lookahead decoding, standard speculative decoding, and a retrieval-based statistical drafter at the bottom of the hierarchy.
COST: 330
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a 20% reduction in inference time while maintaining 95% of the quality compared to standard Lookahead decoding. However, the results might fail to generalize to more complex tasks due to the caching mechanism's limitations in capturing long-range dependencies.

We consider various scheduling choices such as the number of cascade rounds, the draft length at each level, and the number of tokens to draft for each self-speculative technique. Our goal is to identify the optimal configuration for each self-speculative technique to accelerate the inference time of a target LLM model.
CONTROLS: We evaluate the top-performing configurations for each self-speculative technique against standard speculative decoding and retrieve-based statistical drafting.

TITLE: Reusing Lookahead Decoding for Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We modify the existing Lookahead decoding method to not only reuse the target model's hidden states but also to cache the draft tokens it proposes during the Lookahead iterations. Then, at each cascade round, we use the cached draft tokens as input to the next draft model, thus creating a cascade of Lookahead decodings. We expect this to be faster than standard speculative decoding with Lookahead decoding and to have comparable quality.
CONTROLS: We compare this approach to standard Lookahead decoding, standard speculative decoding, and a retrieval-based statistical drafter at the bottom of the hierarchy.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve a 20% reduction in inference time while maintaining 95% of the quality compared to standard Lookahead decoding. However, the results might fail to generalize to more complex tasks due to the caching mechanism's limitations in capturing long-range dependencies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adapting Self-Speculative Decoding for Cascade Configurations
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with adapting self-speculative techniques such as Lookahead decoding and SWIFT to create a cascade configuration with a cheap retrieval-based drafter at the bottom. We will implement two main variants: a pre-defined fixed schedule where the intermediate draft models use pre-determined parameters, and a dynamic schedule where the intermediate models are chosen based on their predicted acceptance rates and costs. We will experiment with four real-world models (including Llama, Mixtral, and Qwen) on five tasks (two from multi-turn conversation, one from machine translation, one from summarization, and one from question answering).
CONTROLS: Comparing the two variants to each other and to a baseline of standard speculative decoding with no retrieval-based drafter, as well as a separate ablation study to see the effect of each variant individually.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: We expect the dynamic schedule to significantly outperform the fixed schedule, achieving moderate speedups over standard speculative decoding while being on par with a dedicated retrieval-based drafter. However, the adaptive choice of draft model may lead to lower acceptance rates at some points of the cascade.

textes:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adapting Self-Speculative Decoding for Cascade Configurations
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with adapting self-speculative techniques such as Lookahead decoding and SWIFT to create a cascade configuration with a cheap retrieval-based drafter at the bottom. We will implement two main variants: a pre-defined fixed schedule where the intermediate draft models use pre-determined parameters, and a dynamic schedule where the intermediate models are chosen based on their predicted acceptance rates and costs. We will experiment with four real-world models (including Llama, Mixtral, and Qwen) on five tasks (two from multi-turn conversation, one from machine translation, one from summarization, and one from question answering).
CONTROLS: Comparing the two variants to each other and to a baseline of standard speculative decoding with no retrieval-based drafter, as well as a separate ablation study to see the effect of each variant individually.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: We expect the dynamic schedule to significantly outperform the fixed schedule, achieving moderate speedups over standard speculative decoding while being on par with a dedicated retrieval-based drafter. However, the adaptive choice of draft model may lead to lower acceptance rates at some points of the cascade.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Benefits and Bottlenecks of Adaptive Cascade Scheduling
PROPOSAL: We will carry out an in-depth analysis of the adaptive cascade scheduling approach to understand the key factors that affect its performance, including the impact of task characteristics, the choice of draft model, and the number of cascade rounds. We will conduct an exhaustive hyperparameter search to explore the sensitivity of the adaptive approach to different scheduling parameters, and compare its performance to that of the pre-defined fixed schedule and standard speculative decoding.
CONTROLS: Experimenting with a wide range of tasks from different domains, including mathematical reasoning and retrieval-augmented generation, to identify the situations where the adaptive approach excels and where it falls short. 
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: We expect the adaptive approach to outperform the fixed schedule on tasks with a high degree of variability, such as multi-turn conversation and question answering, but to struggle on tasks with a fixed input-output structure, such as machine translation and summarization. However, the optimal scheduling parameters may vary significantly between tasks and models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Pretraining Self-Optimized Draft Models for Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We will explore the idea of pretraining self-optimized draft models that are specifically designed to work well in a cascade configuration, without access to any information about the target model. We will train two types of pretrianed models: a variant that is optimized for speedup over the original target model, and a variant that is optimized for robustness to different scheduling parameters.
CONTROLS: Ablation study to measure the benefits of pretraining, compared to training draft models on the fly. 
COST: 40000
PREDICTION: We expect the pretrained models to achieve moderate speedups over the original target model, with optimal performance achieved when combined with adaptive scheduling. However, the benefits of pretraining may be limited if the cascade configuration changes significantly from the training scenario.

ACTION: REVISE
 TITLE: Adapting Self-Speculative Decoding for Cascade Configurations
 PROPOSAL: We will experiment with using pretrianed self-optimized draft models in conjunction with the adaptable cascade scheduling approach from proposal 2, instead of training draft models on the fly as previously mentioned. This will allow us to take greater advantage of the benefits of pretraining while still benefiting from the adaptability of the scheduling approach.
CONTROLS: All the same as before, as well as an additional ablation study to determine the relative importance of pretraining vs adaptive scheduling.
COST: 50000
PREDICTION: We expect the use of pretrained self-optimized draft models to significantly improve the performance of the adaptable cascade scheduling approach, especially in scenarios with high variability.

ACTION: REVISE 3
 TITLE: Pretraining Self-Optimized Draft Models for Cascade Speculative Decoding
 PROPOSAL: We will experiment with adding an additional loss term to the pretraining process, which incentivizes the draft models to occupy specific regions of the latent space that are beneficial for the adaptive cascade scheduling approach. This will allow the pretrained draft models to be more effective when used in conjunction with the adaptable scheduling approach.
CONTROLS: A new ablation study to measure the benefits of the additional loss term, as well as the same controls mentioned in proposal 3.
COST: 60000
PREDICTION: We expect the additional loss term to improve the performance of the pretrained draft models when used in conjunction with the adaptable scheduling approach, resulting in overall speedups of the adaptive cascade scheduling approach.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Use of Efficient Alternating Models in Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with using alternating models in the cascade configuration, which can be efficiently pre-trained and fine-tuned using domain-specific data. This will allow us to take advantage of the benefits of domain-specific pre-training while still using pre-trained models.
CONTROLS: An ablation study to measure the benefits of using alternating models, as well as comparing them to pre-trained self-optimized draft models and the adaptable cascade scheduling approach.
COST: 90000
PREDICTION: We expect the use of alternating models to offer competitive performance to the pre-trained self-optimized draft models and adaptive scheduling approach, with the added benefit of being more accessible to researchers with less resources due to the efficient pre-training process.

ACTION: ADD

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Lookahead Decoding for Recursive Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of Lookahead decoding as a layer-parallelism-based self-speculative method for accelerating the draft models in a recursive cascade, including a retrieval-based initial drafter, on a set of benchmarks from diverse experimental domains such as multi-turn conversation, machine translation, and summarization. We will compare the walltime improvement, speedup in terms of GFLOPS, and accuracy of the generated text using Lookahead decoding and standard speculative decoding with a retrieval-based drafter, using the entire PyTorch  Sphinx family of benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Standard speculative decoding with Loc grafting and retrieval-based prompt lookup decoding
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: Lookahead decoding should achieve a significant speedup over standard speculative decoding in terms of walltime and GFLOPS, and can outperform or match the performance of standard speculative decoding with Loc grafting and prompt lookup decoding on several benchmarks, particularly under scenarios with long sequences and parallel decoding efforts failing through slower accuracy expectations after low thresholds  P

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Feasibility of Using Early Exit for Layer Parallelism in Recursive Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the effectiveness of combining early exit with layer-parallel self-speculative methods like EAGLE and Loc grafting for accelerating the draft models in a recursive cascade, using a set of machine translation benchmarks from WMT. We will measure the speedup, walltime improvement, and accuracy of the generated text when using early exit with different layer-skipping patterns and compare the results to the performance of Lookahead decoding and other state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: Standard speculative decoding with early exit, Loc grafting, EAGLE
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: Early exit with layer parallelism can significantly accelerate the draft models in the recursive cascade, particularly when combined with high-quality self-speculative methods like EAGLE, and show better results than using early exit alone. However, it may trade off accuracy due to early termination.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating the Feasibility of Using Early Exit for Layer Parallelism in Recursive Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: In addition to evaluating the performance of combining early exit with layer-parallel self-speculative methods like EAGLE and Loc grafting for accelerating the draft models in a recursive cascade, we will also investigate the impact of using different early exit policies, such as exit after a fixed number of layers, top-k exit (using k most confident layers), and adaptive exit (learning to exit based on attention weights), on the overall performance of the recursive cascade. This will be evaluated using a set of large-scale summarization and question answering benchmarks from the Deep Learning for Question Answering (QuAC) and Natural Language for Conversational Question Answering (QuAC-top) datasets.
CONTROLS: Standard speculative decoding with early exit, Loc grafting, EAGLE
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: The results will show that adaptive exit policies outperform fixed and top-k exit policies, and combining early exit with high-quality self-speculative methods like EAGLE can further improve the overall performance of the recursive cascade.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Configuration of Recursive Cascade Speculative Decoding for Multi-Turn Conversation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the possibility of adaptively configuring the recursive cascade for multi-turn conversation based on the conversation history, by using a combination of attention-based routing and reinforcement learning to select the most appropriate draft model and adjust the skipping patterns for each turn. We will compare the performance of this adaptive configuration to a fixed configuration using the WMT and multi-turn conversation benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Standard speculative decoding, Lookahead decoding with fixed configuration, Early Exit with adaptive configuration
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: The results will show that the adaptive configuration of the recursive cascade can significantly improve the performance of multi-turn conversation, particularly in terms of coherence and relevance, but may require more training data and may be more computationally expensive than fixing the configuration.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Implicit Caching in Recursive Cascade Speculative Decoding for LLM Inference Acceleration
PROPOSAL: Explore the possibility of using implicit caching to reuse the intermediate results of the recursive cascade for different parts of the input sequence, by using a combination ofadem multiplication and h-transforms to partition the input sequence into smaller chunks that can be processed independently. We will compare the performance of this implicit caching approach to the standard recursive cascade approach on large-scale summarization and question answering benchmarks from the QuAC and QuAC-top datasets.
CONTROLS: Standard speculative decoding, Lookahead decoding, Early Exit with adaptive configuration
COST: 6930
PREDICTION: The results will show that implicit caching can significantly improve the performance of the recursive cascade by reducing the number of forward passes and increasing the cache hits, but may require careful tuning of the caching policy and may add significant memory overhead.

We will measure the speedup, walltime improvement, and accuracy of the generated text when using early exit with different layer-skipping patterns and compare the results to the performance of Lookahead decoding and other state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: Standard speculative decoding with early exit, Loc grafting, EAGLE
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: Early exit with layer parallelism can significantly accelerate the draft models in the recursive cascade, particularly when combined with high-quality self-speculative methods like EAGLE, and show better results than using early exit alone. However, it may trade off accuracy due to early termination.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating the Feasibility of Using Early Exit for Layer Parallelism in Recursive Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: In addition to evaluating the performance of combining early exit with layer-parallel self-speculative methods like EAGLE and Loc grafting for accelerating the draft models in a recursive cascade, we will also investigate the impact of using different early exit policies, such as exit after a fixed number of layers, top-k exit (using k most confident layers), and adaptive exit (learning to exit based on attention weights), on the overall performance of the recursive cascade. This will be evaluated using a set of large-scale summarization and question answering benchmarks from the Deep Learning for Question Answering (QuAC) and Natural Language for Conversational Question Answering (QuAC-top) datasets.
CONTROLS: Standard speculative decoding with early exit, Loc grafting, EAGLE
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: The results will show that adaptive exit policies outperform fixed and top-k exit policies, and combining early exit with high-quality self-speculative methods like EAGLE can further improve the overall performance of the recursive cascade.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Configuration of Recursive Cascade Speculative Decoding for Multi-Turn Conversation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the possibility of adaptively configuring the recursive cascade for multi-turn conversation based on the conversation history, by using a combination of attention-based routing and reinforcement learning to select the most appropriate draft model and adjust the skipping patterns for each turn. We will compare the performance of this adaptive configuration to a fixed configuration using the WMT and multi-turn conversation benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Standard speculative decoding, Lookahead decoding with fixed configuration, Early Exit with adaptive configuration
COST: 16200
PREDICTION: The results will show that the adaptive configuration of the recursive cascade can significantly improve the performance of multi-turn conversation, particularly in terms of coherence and relevance, but may require more training data and may be more computationally expensive than fixing the configuration.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Implicit Caching in Recursive Cascade Speculative Decoding for LLM Inference Acceleration
PROPOSAL: Explore the possibility of using implicit caching to reuse the intermediate results of the recursive cascade for different parts of the input sequence, by using a combination ofadem multiplication and h-transforms to partition the input sequence into smaller chunks that can be processed independently. We will compare the performance of this implicit caching approach to the standard recursive cascade approach on large-scale summarization and question answering benchmarks from the QuAC and QuAC-top datasets.
CONTROLS: Standard speculative decoding, Lookahead decoding, Early Exit with adaptive configuration
COST: 20700
PREDICTION: The results will show that implicit caching can significantly improve the performance of the recursive cascade by reducing the number of forward passes and increasing the cache hits, but may require careful tuning of the caching policy and may add significant memory overhead.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-Aware Cascade Scheduling for LLM Inference Acceleration
PROPOSAL: Investigate the possibility of using task-aware scheduling to adjust the number of cascade levels and the draft model configurations for different tasks, by using a combination of feature extraction and clustering to identify the commonalities and differences between tasks and allocate the resources accordingly. We will compare the performance of this task-aware scheduling approach to the standard recursive cascade approach on a set of multi-task benchmarks from the GLUE dataset.
CONTROLS: Standard speculative decoding, Lookahead decoding, Early Exit with adaptive configuration, Implicit caching
COST: 27000
PREDICTION: The results will show that task-aware scheduling can significantly improve the performance of the recursive cascade by allocating the resources more efficiently and adapting to the specific needs of each task, but may require careful tuning of the scheduling policy and may add significant model complexity.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Adaptive Configuration of Recursive Cascade Speculative Decoding for Multi-Turn Conversation
PROPOSAL: Expand the adaptive configuration approach to include reinforcement learning objectives for the draft model configuration and the skipping patterns, allowing the model to learn the optimal strategy for the specific conversation context. We will evaluate the impact of this more advanced approach on the performance of the recursive cascade and compare it to task-aware scheduling and other standard methods using a set of multi-turn conversation benchmarks, including the WMT and MultiWOZ datasets.
CONTROLS: Standard speculative decoding, Lookahead decoding, Early Exit with adaptive configuration, Implicit caching
COST: 27000
PREDICTION: The results will show that adding reinforcement learning objectives can significantly improve the performance of the adaptive configuration and make it more competitive with task-aware scheduling and other advanced methods.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the possibility of using a horizontal cascade architecture, where the draft models are ordered in terms of increasing latency, to accelerate large-scale LLM inference tasks. We will compare the performance of this horizontal cascade approach to the standard recursive cascade approach on a set of large-scale machine translation and summarization benchmarks, using the multi-scale attention architecture of the MM-Transformers.
CONTROLS: Standard speculative decoding, Lookahead decoding, Early Exit with adaptive configuration, Implicit caching, Task-Aware Cascade Scheduling
COST: 40500
PREDICTION: The results will show that the horizontal cascade approach can achieve significant speedup and parallelism, particularly for large-scale LLM inference tasks, but may require careful tuning of the draft model configurations and the latency-weighting strategy.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the possibility of adaptively selecting the self-speculative methods (e.g., lookahead decoding, early exit, implicit caching, and task-aware scheduling) for the recursive cascade on-the-fly during inference, based on the characteristics of the input sequence and the available resources. We will propose a neural network-based approach to predict the most suitable self-speculative method for each part of the input sequence and compare the performance of this adaptive selection approach to the standard use of each self-speculative method individually on a set of large-scale machine translation and summarization benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Standard speculative decoding, Lookahead decoding, Early Exit with adaptive configuration, Implicit caching, Task-Aware Cascade Scheduling, Horizontal Cascade Speculative Decoding

TITLE: A Unified Framework for Recursive Cascade Speculative Decoding: Theory and Practice
PROPOSAL: Develop a unified theoretical framework to analyze and optimize the performance of the recursive cascade speculative decoding, incorporating the various self-speculative methods and adaptive selection strategies explored in the previous proposals. We will provide a general framework for designing and tuning the recursive cascade architecture, including draft model configurations, self-speculative methods, and adaptive selection strategies, and demonstrate its effectiveness on a set of large-scale machine translation and summarization benchmarks.
CONTROLS: All previous methods and experiments
COST: 94500
PREDICTION: The results will show that the unified framework can achieve state-of-the-art performance in terms of speedup, accuracy, and robustness, and provide valuable insights for designing and optimizing the recursive cascade architecture for large-scale LLM inference tasks.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating the efficacy of Lookahead decoding in a cascade setup
PROPOSAL: Train Lookahead decoding on top of Qwen, Llama, and Mixtral using different cascade configurations (layers to skip, number of tokens to draft). Compare the effects on walltime, accuracy, and F1 score with baseline self-speculative decoding results from EAGLE, Medusa, and BiTA, along with a simple retrieval-based drafter (prompt lookup decoding).
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard self-speculative decoding; ablation study: disabling Lookahead decoding at different levels of the cascade; controls: adding a separate retrieval-based drafter at each level of the cascade (as presented in prior analysis of cascade speculative decoding)
COST: 165.6
PREDICTION: On par or slightly worse than state-of-the-art for multi-turn conversations and question answering, but showing consistent gains in mathematical reasoning and summarization tasks due to Lookahead's optimization of hidden states; Lookahead's limited speedup may make it difficult to surpass the drafter-only baseline.

TITLE: Adaptive Scheduling of Cascade Layers with Learned Weights
PROPOSAL: Implement a neural architecture search module that adapts the weights of Lookahead layers based on the input sequence and optimizes for walltime reduction while maintaining output quality. This module would dynamically choose between skipping, pruning, or modifying Lookahead layers based on learned weights to adjust the lossless acceleration ratio with respect to F1 scores on the target task upon cascaded training data and in validation and training time.
CONTROLS: Baselines: look like normal look-ahead setup; ablation study: disabling the adaptation module; simple case: additional fixed scheduling for comparison with the approach proposed

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Jointly Optimizing Multi-Branch Weights for Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: Train a joint neural network to generate and optimize the branch weights for Lookahead decoding in the cascade setup. This optimizer takes the input sequence and target model weights as inputs and outputs the branch weights. The best weights are used to compute the prediction, and then both the prediction and branch weights are fed back into the network to further optimize the weights in a feedback loop.
CONTROLS: Baselines: training each branch separately and then combining their outputs; ablation study: disabling the feedback loop; controls: adding an to OUTSIDE mechanism that backpropes to the multi- branches based on OUTSIDE rewrite evaluation
COST: 1170
PREDICTION: Jointly optimizing multi-branch weights leads to significant improvements in all LLM inference tasks while reducing walltime, as the network finds more optimal and balanced combination of branch weights.

TITLE: Attention-Weighted Cascade Speculative Decoding with Pruned Architectures
PROPOSAL: Introduce an attention mechanism that selectively prunes the weighs of intermediate layers of the cascade based on their relative importance for the output. This is done by computing attention weights for each layer and only keeping a subset of the layers with the highest weights until the desired output is reached. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Shot Reward Learning via Constrained Confidence Intervals
PROPOSAL: Design a constrained optimization framework to derive a new score that approximates the absolute reward value, while explicitly incorporating the uncertainty inherent in human preference judgments. This framework leverages the confidence intervals of the ranking probabilities output by the discriminative reward model, thus enabling zero-shot learning in novel domains. Specifically:
a) Represent the ranking probabilities as a set of confidence intervals for each response and its neighboring responses.
b) Regularize these intervals using a quadratic penalty, encapsulating a degree of confidence uncertainty and annotator disagreement.
c) Select the optimal confidence multiplier that best balances the ranking accuracy with the absolute score obtainability across novel domains.

CONTROLS: Compare against the vanilla discriminative reward model with extended hyperparameters, in addition to the calibration baseline that leverages limited quality annotations for a particular domain as ground-truth reference.

COST: 1200
PREDICTION: This method will exhibit competitive performance in scoring absolute quality across novel domains compared to traditional discriminative reward models that rely on complex pretraining frameworks for calibration, given the constraints added to quantitatively capture uncertainty.

PROPOSAL: Introduce an auxiliary adversarial critic to assist in calibrating the discriminative reward model when a small set of quality-annotated data is available in a domain. This critic is trained to distinguish between real and synthesized absolute reward values. By incorporating auxiliary feedback from the critic, the discriminative reward model learns to constrain its output within a more plausible range in the target domain. Specifically:
a) Train the auxiliary adversarial critic using GAN losses combined with the ranking accuracy of the discriminative model.

c) Regularize the discriminative reward output by incorporating predictions from the auxiliary critic as confidence bounds.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Active Reward Learning for Efficient Exploration
PROPOSAL: Design an active learning protocol for the discriminative reward model, in which the selection of candidate responses for human evaluation is guided by a probabilistic uncertainty estimation of the model's output. By focusing on the most uncertain regions of the output distribution, the model efficiently accumulates high-quality annotations in a target domain, scaling up to larger product spaces where exhaustive labeling is impractical. Specifically:
a) Represent user preferences as latent variables with Gaussian mixtures over multiple synthetic candidate ratings.
b) Perform a trial-and-error clarification loop between the model and a human proxy, selecting the least confident output samples as the topic of preference elicitation.
c) Periodically incorporate newly collected annotations into the model training pipeline through incremental re-calibration.

CONTROLS: Compare against passive learning schemes with equal resources.

COST: 2520
PREDICTION: The proposed active learning approach will provide better generalization performance and effective efficiency of annotator input compared to the random sampling baseline.

PROPOSAL: Design a novel reward shaping framework, dubbed Aequilibrium, that aligns the reward function with the model's output distribution to improve the quality of the generated responses. PROPOSAL: This theoretical work establishes probabilistic bounds on the scores of discriminative reward models, thereby providing a calibrated and uncertainty-aware measure of confidence. We analyze the behavior of Bradley-Terry models under a probabilistic interpretation, leveraging concentration inequalities and the regret of the base model to derive a lower and upper bound on the probability of choosing a suboptimal response.
CONTROLS: Compare to naive (deterministic) scoring and propose a new baseline trained with log-loss objective to regress to the mean, instead of ranking, aiming for calibration-ignorant ordinal ranking to minimize bias.

TITLE: Reward Model Calibration with Anchor Points
PROPOSAL: This experiment investigates the use of anchor points for calibrating the scores of a reward model trained on relative preference data. Inspired by distractor-anchored and behavior-anchored techniques from evaluation metrics, we identify instances with clear “good” or “bad” responses as anchors and propose scoring them first; optimal rewards are pre-defined, either from experts or learned ML models, and assigned to anchor instances during annotation time. Post-hoc anchor-injection involves adjusting the reward scores of responses using a cached mapping between anchors, increasing the overall calibration of the reward function.

TITLE: Transfer Learning for Reward Models in Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Scenarios
PROPOSAL: This experiment investigates the use of transfer learning for reward models in zero-shot and few-shot scenarios. We train a reward model on a large dataset and then fine-tune it on a new, unseen dataset with limited annotation. We propose a new transfer learning method, dubbed "RLTF", which uses a recursive fine-tuning framework to adapt the reward model to the new dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare to traditional fine-tuning and baseline models that are trained from scratch.
COST:  14000
PREDICTION: RLTF shows improved performance in zero-shot and few-shot scenarios, but may require careful selection of the initial dataset and fine-tuning hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Reward Models to Adversarial Perturbations
PROPOSAL: This experiment investigates the robustness of reward models to adversarial perturbations, which can occur when the input data is manipulated to deceive the model. We propose a new attack method, dubbed "RewardPerturb", which generates adversarial examples that aim to maximize the reward or minimize the quality of the response. We evaluate the robustness of several state-of-the-art reward models, including the ones proposed in this paper.
CONTROLS: Compare to traditional adversarial attacks and baseline models that are not trained with adversarial examples.
COST:  21000
PREDICTION: RewardPerturb shows that existing reward models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, which can degrade their performance. However, the impact of adversarial attacks can be mitigated by incorporating adversarial training into the reward model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Calibration of Discriminative Reward Models
PROPOSAL: We develop a new regularization technique for discriminative reward models, dubbed Adversarial Calibration (AC), to constrain their outputs to a calibrated interval with a well-defined upper and lower bound. This is achieved by introducing a secondary adversary model that attempts to minimize or maximize the reward model's output across a batch of paired responses. The reward model is then optimized to maximize the margin between its chosen response and the adversary's optimal output within the constrained interval. We test AC on the standard HelpSteer2-Preference and InternLM2-Reward datasets, and compare its performance against calibration-loss variants of Skywork-Reward and ArmoRM, as well as the dummy baseline of an uncalibrated discriminative model.
CONTROLS: HelpSteer2-Preference and InternLM2-Reward datasets, dummy baseline of uncalibrated discriminative model, calibration-loss variants of Skywork-Reward and ArmoRM
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: AC should substantially improve discriminative model performance on tasks requiring high-quality, probabilistically-interpretable scores, and reduce scores' variance on response quality, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance adversarial regularization and LLM alignment.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Relaxed Supervision for Generative Reward Models
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel method for training generative reward models with relaxed supervision, where a fraction of the supervision is provided as a probabilistic confidence measure over a response's quality, rather than a deterministic quality score. Our approach, dubbed RelaxGen, leverages this "probabilistic supervision" to learn a more robust response generator, and infuses this uncertainty into the final preference judgment. We compare RelaxGen to state-of-the-art generative models on HelpSteer2-Preference, InternLM2-Reward, and Chatbot-SA datasets, and demonstrate its ability to improve ranking accuracy and quality while reducing annotator burden.
CONTROLS: HelpSteer2-Preference, InternLM2-Reward, Chatbot-SA datasets, state-of-the-art generative models
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: RelaxGen is expected to achieve near-state-of-the-art performance on ranking accuracy and response quality, while reducing annotation burden significantly in scenarios where high-confidence judgments are available. Its ability to tackle the annotator disagreement present in preference data remains a methodological unknown.

TITLE: Integrating Value Functions into Generative Reward Models for Better Confidence Estimation
PROPOSAL: We explore the integration of value functions into generative reward models to enhance confidence estimation in preference judgments. Our approach, dubbed VGerm, combines generative model critiques with value functions, learned from labeled quality annotations, to produce not only a preference score but also an estimate of confidence in that judgment. We compare VGerm with state-of-the-art generative models and discriminative models on HelpSteer2-Preference, InternLM2-Reward, and Chatbot-SA datasets, assessing its performance and comparing confidence estimates against ground truth annotation reliability.
CONTROLS: HelpSteer2-Preference, InternLM2-Reward, Chatbot-SA datasets, state-of-the-art generative models, discriminative models
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: VGerm should exhibit improved confidence estimation in response to judgments of moderate uncertainty, as infusing conditional value functions into generative models reduces their sensitivity to annotation variability. However, VGerm's better confidence results might compromise the model's overall ranking accuracy due to the untuned trade-off between estimating confidence based on reliability of current annotations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Calibration of Discriminative Reward Models
PROPOSAL: We develop a new regularization technique for discriminative reward models, dubbed Adversarial Calibration (AC), to constrain their outputs to a calibrated interval with a well-defined upper and lower bound. This is achieved by introducing a secondary adversary model that attempts to minimize or maximize the reward model's output across a batch of paired responses. The reward model is then optimized to maximize the margin between its chosen response and the adversary's optimal output within the constrained interval. We test AC on the standard HelpSteer2-Preference and InternLM2-Reward datasets, and compare its performance against calibration-loss variants of Skywork-Reward and ArmoRM, as well as the dummy baseline of an uncalibrated discriminative model.
CONTROLS: HelpSteer2-Preference and InternLM2-Reward datasets, dummy baseline of uncalibrated discriminative model, calibration-loss variants of Skywork-Reward and ArmoRM
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: AC should substantially improve discriminative model performance on tasks requiring high-quality, probabilistically-interpretable scores, and reduce scores' variance on response quality, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance adversarial regularization and LLM alignment.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Enhanced Generative Reward Models with Bayesian Feedback Networks
PROPOSAL: We incorporate Bayesian feedback networks (BFNs) into generative reward models to capture the uncertainty and annotator disagreement inherent in human preference data. Our approach, dubbed BFN+, adds a Bayesian network to the model's existing critique generation process, such that the network's predictive uncertainty is infused into the final preference judgment. This allows the model to provide probabilistic, calibrated scores that naturally encapsulate both response quality and confidence. We evaluate BFN+ on suite of real-world datasets for LLM reward modeling, including HelpSteer2-Preference, InternLM2-Reward, and Chatbot-SA, comparing its performance against baseline generative models, discriminative models with calibration, and the frontiers of state-of-the-art generative models.
CONTROLS: HelpSteer2-Preference, InternLM2-Reward, Chatbot-SA datasets, baseline generative models, discriminative models with calibration, state-of-the-art generative models
COST: 4200
PREDICTION: BFN+ is expected to significantly outperform baseline generative models in terms of both ranking accuracy and absolute response quality, while also providing interpretable, probabilistically-calibrated scores that quantify the model's confidence in its judgments. However, it remains to be seen whether BFN+ can match the efficiency and accuracy of state-of-the-art generative models on computationally-constrained settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Input Preprocessing on Hallucination Detection in RAG
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with different input preprocessing techniques (e.g., stopping removal, stemming, lemmatization, and named entity recognition) on a standard RAG model (e.g., T5-large) across a variety of real-world benchmarks (e.g., CNN/Daily Mail, NewsQA, and TriviaQA) to investigate their effects on hallucination detection. To measure the impact of each preprocessing method, we will compute traditional metrics such as accuracy and F1-score, as well as a task-specific metric tailored to hallucination detection, e.g., F1-score on the hallucinated instances.
CONTROLS: We will explore the effect of various preprocessing techniques, and compare against the results with no preprocessing, and also investigate if the improvements are achieved through retraining the RAG model or if they are due to the better representation of the input data.
COST: 81
PREDICTION: We expect that some input preprocessing techniques will have a positive impact on hallucination detection accuracy, although the results may vary across different datasets and preprocessing methods. We anticipate potential pitfalls in the performance comparison when different preprocessing techniques require retuning the RAG model, and might encounter difficulty in generalizing the results to the same high accuracy across all datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Introducing Retrieval-Augmentation Complexity (RAC) as a Hallucination Detection Metric
PROPOSAL: We propose a new metric, Retrieval-Augmentation Complexity (RAC), which assesses the complexity of the retriever-augmented generation process by measuring the ratio of external context usage to internal knowledge usage. RAC is computed by comparing the similarity between the generated response and the retrieved documents, as well as the similarity between the generated response and the model's internal knowledge (measured through the weighted sum of the attention weights and output probabilities). We hypothesize that lower RAC values will be associated with higher hallucination rates.
CONTROLS: We will compare RAC with existing metrics (e.g., BLEU score, ROUGE score) and evaluate its effectiveness on the same benchmarks as in proposal 1.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: Our results may indicate that RAC is a promising metric for detecting hallucinations, especially when used in conjunction with existing methods. However, calculating RAC may be computationally expensive, and its design might require fine-tuning to account for variations in_different domains or tasks.

TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Knowledge Graph Augmentation on RAG Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We explore whether augmenting the external context with knowledge graphs, similar to approaches like Knowledge Graph-Augmented Transformers (KGAT), can improve hallucination detection in RAG systems. We hypothesize that integrating knowledge graphs into the external context will allow the model to rely less on internal knowledge and more on the factual information provided by the graphs, thereby reducing the likelihood of hallucinations.
CONTROLS: We will investigate the impact of different knowledge graph representations (e.g., RDF triples, ConceptNet) and incorporation methods (e.g., indirect attention, explicit prediction) on hallucination detection.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: By incorporating knowledge graphs into RAG, we anticipate a reduction in hallucination rates and an improvement in detectors' accuracy, potentially achieving more robust and reliable results, especially in domains such as news summarization. However, successful retrieval and use of these knowledge graph nodes may present challenges, as we could see worse rank-multiplication when inadequate, both denoted and replicable facts might emerge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Partition-Based Framework for Analyzing and Detecting Hallucinations in RAG
PROPOSAL: We design a partition-based framework to analyze and detect hallucinations in RAG systems by partitioning the generated text into sections based on their factual support from the external context. We use sequential sparse models to identify and segment constructed sentences, then label these segments as supported or unsupported. Detection of divergent segments can identify fragmented occasions for RAG hallucination taking place across both the internally used contextual and the given retrievable external dialogue prompts.
CONTROLS: We evaluate the effectiveness of the partition-based framework by comparing its performance with previous approaches (e.g., RAC, Knowledge Graph Augmentation) and explore the impact of different partitioning methods (e.g., word-level, sentence-level) and evaluation metrics on hallucination detection.
COST: 1620
PREDICTION: The partition-based framework is expected to improve hallucination detection accuracy and robustness by identifying and segmenting unsupported sections of the generated text, potentially mitigating the effects of internal knowledge over-reliance. However, accurate segmentation may be challenging, and potential misclassifications may reduce the overall precision of the method.

However, implementing and integrating feedback mechanisms may increase computational complexity and require additional resources.
