ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Input Preprocessing on Hallucination Detection in RAG
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with different input preprocessing techniques (e.g., stopping removal, stemming, lemmatization, and named entity recognition) on a standard RAG model (e.g., T5-large) across a variety of real-world benchmarks (e.g., CNN/Daily Mail, NewsQA, and TriviaQA) to investigate their effects on hallucination detection. To measure the impact of each preprocessing method, we will compute traditional metrics such as accuracy and F1-score, as well as a task-specific metric tailored to hallucination detection, e.g., F1-score on the hallucinated instances.
CONTROLS: We will explore the effect of various preprocessing techniques, and compare against the results with no preprocessing, and also investigate if the improvements are achieved through retraining the RAG model or if they are due to the better representation of the input data.
COST: 243
PREDICTION: We expect that some input preprocessing techniques will have a positive impact on hallucination detection accuracy, although the results may vary across different datasets and preprocessing methods. We anticipate potential pitfalls in the performance comparison when different preprocessing techniques require retuning the RAG model, and might encounter difficulty in generalizing the results to the same high accuracy across all datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Introducing Retrieval-Augmentation Complexity (RAC) as a Hallucination Detection Metric
PROPOSAL: We propose a new metric, Retrieval-Augmentation Complexity (RAC), which assesses the complexity of the retriever-augmented generation process by measuring the ratio of external context usage to internal knowledge usage. RAC is computed by comparing the similarity between the generated response and the retrieved documents, as well as the similarity between the generated response and the model's internal knowledge (measured through the weighted sum of the attention weights and output probabilities). We hypothesize that lower RAC values will be associated with higher hallucination rates.
CONTROLS: We will compare RAC with existing metrics (e.g., BLEU score, ROUGE score) and evaluate its effectiveness on the same benchmarks as in proposal 1.
COST: 720
PREDICTION: Our results may indicate that RAC is a promising metric for detecting hallucinations, especially when used in conjunction with existing methods. However, calculating RAC may be computationally expensive, and its design might require fine-tuning to account for variations in_different domains or tasks.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: (Introducing Retrieval-Augmentation Complexity (RAC) as a Hallucination Detection Metric)
PROPOSAL: REVISED RAC metric is a hybrid measure combining the similarity ideas of the previous version with sequence-to-sequence alignment metrics, focusing on how well the internal knowledge relates to the external context in the generated output. This will be achieved by measuring token-to-token similarities (e.g., cosine similarity) between the generated output, the retrieved documents, and the internal knowledge states of the model (normalized dot products). Different alignment methods, such as the widely used alignment-metrics samples based on the Hungarian algorithm, will also be explored and analyzed with ablations.
CONTROLS: We compare this variants of the proposed metric against both BLEU-post and TF-IDF-based markers for hallucinations, to determine if improvements assign to our approach, on real-world benchmarks. This also allows us to examine whether different components contribute more to objectively determining externally supported or internally grounded responses
COST: 1080
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the revised RAC metric will lead to better detection of hallucinations and improved performance on various benchmarks compared to the baseline metrics and previous versions of RAC, potentially gaining better evaluation in scenarios when factualness information is not readily available

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: (Introducing Retrieval-Augmentation Complexity (RAC) as a Hallucination Detection Metric)
PROPOSAL: We expand the capacity of the proposed revised RAC metric by incorporating multimodal elements. For example, we analyze the alignment between the audio waveform or visual features of the generated text versus the supporting documents. By comparing distances between these different forms of entities (AC and slow distance attenuation along the sentence tokens offered through permutations), it's possible for the model to achieve improved summary veracities, Figuring these modalities via slowed posterior recognition could allow better discrimination between hallucinations and devised inputs.
CONTROLS: 
COST: 1440
PREDICTION: Multimodal integration may improve RAC's ability to distinguish between hallucinations and supported responses, given potential gains stemming from augmented information presented to the RAG algorithm due to its integration of richer input data. However, developments must still adhere to incremental increases in noise or competing situated inputs exhibiting predictable confused misreflection and contextual challenges

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Knowledge Graph Augmentation on RAG Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We explore whether augmenting the external context with knowledge graphs, similar to approaches like Knowledge Graph-Augmented Transformers (KGAT), can improve hallucination detection in RAG systems. We hypothesize that integrating knowledge graphs into the external context will allow the model to rely less on internal knowledge and more on the factual information provided by the graphs, thereby reducing the likelihood of hallucinations.
CONTROLS: We will investigate the impact of different knowledge graph representations (e.g., RDF triples, ConceptNet) and incorporation methods (e.g., indirect attention, explicit prediction) on hallucination detection.
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: By incorporating knowledge graphs into RAG, we anticipate a reduction in hallucination rates and an improvement in detectors' accuracy, potentially achieving more robust and reliable results, especially in domains such as news summarization. However, successful retrieval and use of these knowledge graph nodes may present challenges, as we could see worse rank-multiplication when inadequate, both denoted and replicable facts might emerge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Partition-Based Framework for Analyzing and Detecting Hallucinations in RAG
PROPOSAL: We design a partition-based framework to analyze and detect hallucinations in RAG systems by partitioning the generated text into sections based on their factual support from the external context. We use sequential sparse models to identify and segment constructed sentences, then label these segments as supported or unsupported. Detection of divergent segments can identify fragmented occasions for RAG hallucination taking place across both the internally used contextual and the given retrievable external dialogue prompts.
CONTROLS: We evaluate the effectiveness of the partition-based framework by comparing its performance with previous approaches (e.g., RAC, Knowledge Graph Augmentation) and explore the impact of different partitioning methods (e.g., word-level, sentence-level) and evaluation metrics on hallucination detection.
COST: 4860
PREDICTION: The partition-based framework is expected to improve hallucination detection accuracy and robustness by identifying and segmenting unsupported sections of the generated text, potentially mitigating the effects of internal knowledge over-reliance. However, accurate segmentation may be challenging, and potential misclassifications may reduce the overall precision of the method.

TITLE: Evaluating Language Models' Utilization of External Context and Internal Knowledge via Textual Similarity Metrics
PROPOSAL: We propose using a set of pre-defined textual similarity metrics, such as paraphrase, semantic similarity, and word embedding-based similarity, to quantify an LLM's utilization of external context and internal knowledge. For each generated response, we will compute the similarity between the response and the retrieved document, and between the response and a masked version of the response filled in using only the model's internal knowledge. We will then compare these similarity scores to determine when the model is relying too heavily on its internal knowledge, indicating a potential hallucination.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to the current state-of-the-art methods, including ReDeEP and its variants, and evaluate our performance on standard benchmarks for retrieval-augmented question answering (RAQA) and news summarization.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to outperform existing methods in detecting hallucinations, particularly in scenarios where the retrieved document is highly relevant and sufficient, as the textual similarity metrics should capture the agreement between the model's output and the context. However, we anticipate that our approach may struggle in situations where the model's internal knowledge is highly confident and inconsistent with the external context, as this could lead to high textual similarity scores for hallucinated responses.

ACTION: REVISE (3)
TITLE: Utility-Tolerating Pseudo-Relevance Feedback Enhanced (UTPREF)
PROPOSAL: We revise UTPRF to incorporate ranking-based self-consistency: we add an iterative fine-tuning step, post-UTPRF, where the retriever uses the learned query weights to re-rank a subset of its own results from the original set of retrieved documents. The goal is to filter out unreliable noisy retrievals, reduce over-reliance on internal knowledge, and stabilize the LLM's predictions. We hypothesize UTPREF will improve external context utilization (ECU) and reduce hallucination rates.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD (6)
TITLE: Joint Decomposition Modeling (JDM)
PROPOSAL: We introduce JDM, a model that jointly learns to decompose the generated response into a retrieved context component and an internal knowledge component. JDM is based on a variant of the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) framework, where the context and internal knowledge latent variables are jointly learned from the generated response, and the retrieved context and internal knowledge are used to constrain the generator.
CONTROLS: Evaluation on SQuAD, TREC, and NewsSum datasets, comparing JDM with BERT, RoBERTa, and other popular LLMs.
COST: 9360
PREDICTION: JDM offers a clear separation between the model's internal knowledge and external context, allowing for better understanding of the role of each component in generating responses. However, it may require a large amount of training data to effectively learn the jointly decomposed representations.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD (7)
TITLE: Evaluation of Context Consistency via SchemaMatching
PROPOSAL: We propose SchemaMatching, a framework to evaluate the consistency of the external context with the internal knowledge representation of the LLM. SchemaMatching analyzes the schema-compatibility between the retrieved documents and the generated response, allowing us to assess whether the model correctly incorporates the external context.
CONTROLS: Evaluation on SQuAD, TREC, and NewsSum datasets, comparing SchemaMatching with existing evaluation metrics and contextualized embedding models such as UTPREF, CASL, and RAKE.
COST: 12600
PREDICTION: SchemaMatching provides a valuable tool to assess the quality of retrieval-augmented generation, and its use will lead to more reliable and robust models by ensuring that the LLM correctly incorporates the external context. However, the method's performance may degrade for cases with noisy or incorrect external context.

ACTION: ADD (1)
TITLE: No-Free-Lunch in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose a theoretical framework that rigorously characterizes the relationship between the utilization of external context and the likelihood of hallucination in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. Specifically, we derive a lower bound on the probability of a response a being a hallucination given its internal knowledge utilization I and external context utilization E, as a function of the model's internal prior P and the external context density p_d. The bound is negatively dependent on E, thereby strengthening the conjecture that over-reliance on internal knowledge is a key source of hallucinations.
CONTROLS: N/A (theoretical framework without baselines)
COST: 100
PREDICTION: The framework is theoretically sound and provides valuable insights into the fundamental limits of RAG systems. However, its practical implications might be limited due to the complexity of estimating the model's internal prior P and external context density p_d.

ACTION: ADD (2)
TITLE: Retrieval-Augmented Contrafactual Analysis (RACA)
PROPOSAL: Building on the theoretical framework (1), we design an experiment that leverages Contrafactual Analysis to measure actual utilization of external context E and internal knowledge I during retrieval-augmented generation. We collect a set of "causal" samples {(q, d, a)} where changing the external context d induces a change in the generated response a, indicating actual usage of E. We then analyze how the model's behavior (I, E) changes when retaining or removing the original d while keeping q fixed.
CONTROLS: Comparison with BERT, RoBERTa, and other popular LLMs on CNN/Daily Mail and NewsSum datasets
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: RACA provides a fine-grained understanding of how LLMs actually use external context, which should help identify the alleged causes of hallucination. However, we expect a lack of clear relationships between retrieved documents and generated responses, making substantial variation across different LLMs.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Utility-based Evaluation Framework for RAG
PROPOSAL: We develop a utility-based evaluation framework for RAG systems that directly measures the utilization of external context and internal knowledge. The framework consists of two utility functions: (1) Context Utility (CU) measures the relevance and sufficiency of the retrieved documents to the response, and (2) Knowledge Utility (KU) measures the reliance on the LLM's internal knowledge. We propose using Information-theoretic (IT) metrics, such as Mutual Information (MI), to compute CU and KU. Specifically, for a given response a generated for query q and retrieved documents d, we compute CU(d | a, q) and KU(a | d, q) as follows: CU = MI(a, d) / MI(d, q) and KU = MI(a, d) / MI(a, q). We argue that the ratio of KU to CU should serve as a signal for detecting hallucinations.
CONTROLS: tSNE and UMAP visulzations for the complete generated output and other models on benchmarking research halluagitations comparison with baselines and previous ReDeEP methods detecting factual hallucinations in RAG at distances of more than $\frac{1.5}{sqrt(n)}$.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: This framework should robustly detect hallucinations with a false positive ratio (FNR) of +5% ±2% and improve over previous ReDeEP methods by correctly rejecting 22% more hallucinatory responses.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Utility-based Evaluation Framework for RAG
PROPOSAL: We revise the utility-based evaluation framework for RAG by incorporating an additional IT metric to better estimate internal knowledge utilization: I-model. We use the LLM's encoding of the query and its generation of a response as proxies for its internal knowledge, and measure the similarity between the LLM's internal states using the Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) metric. We compute the JSD between the LLM's encoding of the query and its encoding of the response, I-model. We then modify the KU metric to be a combination of I-model and MI(a, d). The updated KU metric: KU = (1-α) * MI(a, d) / MI(d, q) + α * I-model, where α ∈ [0, 1] controls the trade-off between I-model and MI. This revised framework can better detect instances where the model relies too heavily on its internal knowledge.

TITLE: Adversarial Attack on RAG Hallucination Detectors
PROPOSAL: We propose an adversarial attack approach to test the robustness of our proposed utility-based evaluation framework, attention analysis methods, and existing ReDeEP methods against intentional hallucinations. We generate adversarial examples by modifying the input text to induce hallucinations in the RAG model while attempting to evade detection by the hallucination detectors. We then evaluate the performance of the detectors on these adversarial examples.
CONTROLS: We control for the degree of adversarial perturbation by varying the frequency and type of modifications made to the input text, and also evaluate the detectability of the adversarial examples by human annotators.

PREDICTION: Our adversarial attack study should reveal the vulnerabilities of the existing ReDeEP methods, but demonstrate that our proposed utility-based framework is more robust, with an average of 50% reduction in detection accuracy when faced with adversarial examples.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Long-form Hallucination Detection using Named Entity Recognition and Coreference Resolution
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to hallucination detection that incorporates long-form contextual information from named entity recognition (NER) and coreference resolution. We leverage a state-of-the-art NER model to identify entities in the input text and a coreference resolution model to determine the relationships between them. We then use this information to inform our proposed utility-based evaluation framework and attention analysis methods for hallucination detection.
CONTROLS: We control for the effectiveness of our approach by comparing its performance to existing hallucination detection methods on a range of long-form text datasets, including but not limited to, the LAMPAD and SnEDD.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: Our long-form hallucination detection approach should demonstrate an average improvement of 12% in detection accuracy over existing methods, with a particular improvement in detecting hallucinations related to entities and their relationships.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Fourier Neural Networks for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose using Fourier Neural Networks (FNNs) to model channel-dependent temporal relationships in multivariate time-series data. Specifically, we will introduce a novel variant of the FNN, which integrates multiple Fourier transformations with gated mechanisms to effectively capture periodic patterns and interactions across different variates.
CONTROLS: We will ablate FNNs with existing channel-independent and channel-dependent architectures, such as convolutional neural networks and state space models, and carefully compare their performance on the proposed variants. For real-world data, comparisons with a simple linear projection-based decoding mechanism will also be examined.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By employing FNNs to model the interactions between variates and exploiting the periodic nature of these patterns, we expect to achieve state-of-the-art performance in a variety of multivariate forecasting tasks. However, we may encounter fundamental limitations of FNNs in capturing non-periodic cross-channel dependencies.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Hybrid Temporal Decomposition for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose introducing a novel temporal decomposition method that combines the strengths of both state space models and neural networks to improve the representation of temporal dependencies and cross-variable interactions in multivariate time-series data. Specifically, we will pre-process the data using a state space model to extract component-wise features and then use a neural network encoder to model the interactions among these features.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed hybrid approach with existing state space models and neural network architectures on various multivariate forecasting tasks. As a baseline, we will also consider a simple state space model without neural network assistance. 
COST: 2250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By incorporating insights from both state space models and neural networks, our hybrid approach is expected to achieve significant improvements in forecasting accuracy and robustness over state-of-the-art methods. However, the increased complexity of the approach may introduce new challenges in model selection and hyperparameter tuning, especially for longer forecasting horizons.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Dynamic Masking Objectives for Pretraining Encoders in Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose introducing a novel self-supervised masking objective for pretraining encoders in multivariate time-series forecasting tasks. In contrast to existing masking objectives, our method adaptively masks both temporal and channel-dependent segments of the data, allowing the encoder to dynamically learn to recover missing information in both space and time.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed masking objective with existing BERT-inspired masking objectives, specifically considering the impact on encoder performance and overall forecasting accuracy when fine-tuned on real-world forecasting tasks.
COST: 3064 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By tailoring the pretraining objective to the complexities of multivariate time-series forecasting, our dynamic masking method is expected to yield consistent improvements in encoder performance and, consequently, better overall forecasting results. However, this improvement may be limited to a specific set of forecasting tasks and horizon lengths.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Fourier Neural Networks for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We initiate an in-depth analysis of the Fourier Neural Networks (FNNs) variant proposed earlier, which integrates multiple Fourier transformations with gated mechanisms. In this revised proposal, we explore the impact of different frequency resolution, gating strategies, and pre-processing techniques on the overall performance of FNNs. We hypothesize that FNNs will yield the most benefits when applied to tasks with prominent periodic patterns, whereas less effective performance may be expected for tasks lacking distinct periodicities.
CONTROLS: We will examine the empirical sensitivity of FNNs to varying frequency resolution, compare different popular gating strategies, and evaluate the effect of pre-processing techniques such as band-pass filtering on FNN's overall forecasting accuracy.
COST: 2100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By refining the understanding and application of FNNs, we will identify potential use cases where the model excels and areas for focus to mitigate its limitations, thus improving the model's strengths and addressing potential overfitting for a specific subset of tasks and frequencies.

TITLE: Neural Co-Surfing: A Decoding Framework for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose Neural Co-Surfing, a new decoding framework for multivariate time-series forecasting that integrates insights from both temporal and channel-dependent correlations. Our method employs a neural network to learn a shared temporal representation across multiple variates and then utilizes this shared representation to produce predictions for individual variates.
CONTROLS: We will compare Neural Co-Surfing with existing linear projection-based decoding methods and state-of-the-art channel-dependent encoders, focusing on both multiple forecasting horizons and channels.
COST: 3500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging the shared temporal information across variates and utilizing this representation for individual prediction, Neural Co-Surfing is expected to yield significant improvements in forecasting accuracy, particularly for tasks involving complex temporal dynamics and cross-variable interactions. However, the added complexity may hinder model interpretability and may struggle to capture disjoint temporal structures among variates.

TITLE: Investigating Fourier Neural Networks for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose using Fourier Neural Networks (FNNs) to model channel-dependent temporal relationships in multivariate time-series data. Specifically, we will introduce a novel variant of the FNN, which integrates multiple Fourier transformations with gated mechanisms to effectively capture periodic patterns and interactions across different variates.
CONTROLS: We will ablate FNNs with existing channel-independent and channel-dependent architectures, such as convolutional neural networks and state space models, and carefully compare their performance on the proposed variants. For real-world data, comparisons with a simple linear projection-based decoding mechanism will also be examined.
COST: 4500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By employing FNNs to model the interactions between variates and exploiting the periodic nature of these patterns, we expect to achieve state-of-the-art performance in a variety of multivariate forecasting tasks. However, we may encounter fundamental limitations of FNNs in capturing non-periodic cross-channel dependencies.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Hybrid Temporal Decomposition for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose introducing a novel temporal decomposition method that combines the strengths of both state space models and neural networks to improve the representation of temporal dependencies and cross-variable interactions in multivariate time-series data. Specifically, we will pre-process the data using a state space model to extract component-wise features and then use a neural network encoder to model the interactions among these features.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed hybrid approach with existing state space models and neural network architectures on various multivariate forecasting tasks. As a baseline, we will also consider a simple state space model without neural network assistance. 
COST: 6800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By incorporating insights from both state space models and neural networks, our hybrid approach is expected to achieve significant improvements in forecasting accuracy and robustness over state-of-the-art methods. However, the increased complexity of the approach may introduce new challenges in model selection and hyperparameter tuning, especially for longer forecasting horizons.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Dynamic Masking Objectives for Pretraining Encoders in Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose introducing a novel self-supervised masking objective for pretraining encoders in multivariate time-series forecasting tasks. In contrast to existing masking objectives, our method adaptively masks both temporal and channel-dependent segments of the data, allowing the encoder to dynamically learn to recover missing information in both space and time.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed masking objective with existing BERT-inspired masking objectives, specifically considering the impact on encoder performance and overall forecasting accuracy when fine-tuned on real-world forecasting tasks.
COST: 9200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By tailoring the pretraining objective to the complexities of multivariate time-series forecasting, our dynamic masking method is expected to yield consistent improvements in encoder performance and, consequently, better overall forecasting results. However, this improvement may be limited to a specific set of forecasting tasks and horizon lengths.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Catalyzing Cross-Channel Dependencies in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a new neural network architecture, called ADOFlex, which combines an adversarial disentanglement-based encoder (ADO) with a flexible decoder. The ADO encoder separately captures the variational and invariant features of the input signals, allowing the decoder to selectively focus on specific features and preserve the channel-dependent correlations. The decoder is implemented as a treeStructured fully convolutional network (TS-FCN), enabling it to learn efficient hierarchical representations of the encoded features. We will experiment with ADOFlex on publicly available multivariate time-series datasets from weather, electricity consumption, traffic flow, solar power generation, and electricity transformer temperature forecasting domains.
CONTROLS: ADOFlex will be compared against channel-independent baselines (ResNet-1D, CNN), channel-dependent baselines (ARNN, STFN), and prior state-of-the-art methods (TSSM, DCRNN).
COST: 420 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ADOFlex will outperform the channel-independent baselines by at least 10% inroot mean squared percentage error (RMSPE), and improve upon state-of-the-art models by 2.5% in selected benchmarks, showcasing the effectiveness of ADOFlex in capturing and leveraging cross-channel dependencies. However, its application might fail for datasets in domains with strong distribution shifts or domain-specific non-linearities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Optimal Training Objective for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasts
PROPOSAL: We investigate the optimal training objective for multivariate time-series forecasting models, considering two orthogonal components: reconstruction and synthesis. We propose an empirically grounded theoretical framework that discovers the trade-off between reconstructive and synthetic targets, leading to the derivation of a new training objective, denoted as ReSyn. ReSyn encourages the model to effectively recover masked past observations and to predict future values based on both the past label information and contextual patterns. Empirical evaluations will be performed on publicly available benchmarks from the listed domains, and we will analyze the reconstruction and synthesis capacities of ReSyn and compare it with state-of-the-art pretraining-and-finetuning schemes, as well as simple linear reconstruction objectives.
CONTROLS: We will compare ReSyn with standard pretraining-and-finetuning objectives (e.g.,  BERT-inspired masking-and-reconstruction), simple linear reconstruction objectives (e.g., mean squared error), state-of-the-art pretraining methods (e.g., T4S-B, etc.).
COST: 630 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ReSyn will demonstrate better performance on moderate to long-term forecasting tasks and reveal improved capacity to detect non-linear dynamics, offering a theoretical foundation for the optimal training objective.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Supervised Learning for Time-Series Anomaly Detection using Multivariate Time-Series Data
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel self-supervised learning framework, Anomaly Detection using Auxiliary Tasks (ADAT), to identify anomalies in multivariate time-series data. ADAT relies on three auxiliary tasks: reconstruction, prediction, and noise injection for learning robust and discriminative representations of normal and anomalous data. We train a deep neural network, incorporating a specialized anomaly detection module, using a masked reconstruction loss function. The proposed framework conducts anomaly detection without requiring explicit labels or domain knowledge.
CONTROLS: We will compare ADAT with existing self-supervised anomaly detection methods, and traditional supervised methods on MVTec AD dataset and real-world multivariate time-series data.
COST: 1012 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ADAT demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in detecting anomalies and outperforms supervised methods on anomaly detection benchmarks and real-world datasets.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revision of 2. Revision of 2. Revision of 2. Optimal Training Objective for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasts
PROPOSAL: We modify the ReSyn training objective to incorporate a novel regularizer, Temporal Periodic Normalization (TPN), that encourages the model to learn periodic patterns and dependencies within the data. This regularizer, combined with the original reconstruction loss, results in a hierarchical training objective. The objective is learned without using auxiliary tasks or explicit period inference and can handle varying periodicity across tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the modified ReSyn with existing models, and empirically characterize the effectiveness of TPN in capturing periodic patterns.
COST: 5721 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: TPN improves the robustness and generalization of ReSyn, enabling it to effectively capture periodic patterns and extend its applicability to a broader range of forecasting tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revision of 2. Revision of 2. Revision of 2. Optimal Training Objective for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasts
PROPOSAL: We further refine the hierarchical training objective by incorporating a novel module, called Periodic Signal Decomposition (PSD), to directly learn the periodic patterns and dependencies within the data. PSD decomposes the input signal into multiple periodic components, and the model learns to predict the future values based on these components. By minimizing the reconstruction loss and the decomposition loss, the model is encouraged to capture both periodic and non-periodic patterns in the data.
CONTROLS: We will compare the revised ReSyn with existing models, and empirically evaluate the effectiveness of PSD in capturing periodic patterns and dependencies.
COST: 2409.6 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: PSD improves the accuracy and robustness of ReSyn, enabling it to effectively capture both periodic and non-periodic patterns in the data, and resulting in superior performance on a wide range of forecasting tasks.

TITLE: Bayesian Optimization for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting Model Selection
PROPOSAL: We propose a Bayesian optimization framework, ModelSelector, to select the best combination of hyperparameters for multivariate time-series forecasting models. ModelSelector uses a probabilistic model to represent the posterior distribution of the hyperparameters, and it iteratively samples the hyperparameters using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm. By selecting the optimal combination of hyperparameters, ModelSelector improves the forecasting performance and robustness of the models.
CONTROLS: We will compare ModelSelector with existing hyperparameter optimization methods, such as random search and grid search, and evaluate its performance on multiple datasets.
COST: 4103 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ModelSelector demonstrates significant improvements in forecasting performance and robustness, outperforming existing hyperparameter optimization methods on multiple datasets.

TITLE: Catalyzing Cross-Channel Dependencies in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a new neural network architecture, called ADOFlex, which combines an adversarial disentanglement-based encoder (ADO) with a flexible decoder. The ADO encoder separately captures the variational and invariant features of the input signals, allowing the decoder to selectively focus on specific features and preserve the channel-dependent correlations. The decoder is implemented as a treeStructured fully convolutional network (TS-FCN), enabling it to learn efficient hierarchical representations of the encoded features. We will experiment with ADOFlex on publicly available multivariate time-series datasets from weather, electricity consumption, traffic flow, solar power generation, and electricity transformer temperature forecasting domains.
CONTROLS: ADOFlex will be compared against channel-independent baselines (ResNet-1D, CNN), channel-dependent baselines (ARNN, STFN), and prior state-of-the-art methods (TSSM, DCRNN).

However, its application might fail for datasets in domains with strong distribution shifts or domain-specific non-linearities.

PROPOSAL: We refine the ADOFlex architecture by incorporating the self-supervised learning framework ADAT for anomaly detection. We modify the encoder to produce an additional output representing the anomaly score for each data point, while keeping the original output for forecasting. We evaluate the effectiveness of ADAT-ADOFlex in identifying anomalies and anomaly detection performance on various datasets.
CONTROLS: We compare ADAT-ADOFlex with existing anomaly detection methods, ADOFlex without ADAT, and other state-of-the-art models on anomaly detection benchmarks.

PROPOSAL: We modify the ADAT framework to employ a novel self-supervised objective, SIAMESE, that encourages the model to learn a similarity measure between normal and anomalous data points. COST: 6503 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: SIAMESE-ADAT enhances the anomaly detection performance of ADAT, producing a more robust and accurate detector that effectively identifies anomalies even in the presence of noise and data corruption.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Enhancing Cross-Channel Interactions in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel hybrid encoder that combines the strengths of channel-independent and channel-dependent encoders. The proposed encoder, named CHIE (Channel-Hierarchial Interaction Encoder), consists of a channel-independent Transformer for variate-wise feature extraction, followed by a channel-dependent graph neural network (GNN) to model cross-variable interactions. This hybrid approach aims to capture both temporal dependencies within each variate and cross-channel relationships, while reducing computational overhead.
CONTROLS: Compare CHIE against a state-of-the-art channel-independent encoder (Transformer) and channel-dependent encoder (Graph Transformer).
COST: 10.68322GPU--hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvements in forecasting accuracy over baseline models, particularly for tasks involving complex cross-variable interactions (e.g., traffic flow forecasting, solar power generation forecasting). Potential limitations include increased training complexity and potential overfitting to specific domains.

TITLE: Enhancing Cross-Channel Interactions in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel hybrid encoder that combines the strengths of channel-independent and channel-dependent encoders. The proposed encoder, named CHIE (Channel-Hierarchial Interaction Encoder), consists of a channel-independent Transformer for variate-wise feature extraction, followed by a channel-dependent graph neural network (GNN) to model cross-variable interactions. This hybrid approach aims to capture both temporal dependencies within each variate and cross-channel relationships, while reducing computational overhead.
CONTROLS: Compare CHIE against a state-of-the-art channel-independent encoder (Transformer) and channel-dependent encoder (Graph Transformer).
COST: 32GPU--hours
PREDICTION: Expected improvements in forecasting accuracy over baseline models, particularly for tasks involving complex cross-variable interactions (e.g., traffic flow forecasting, solar power generation forecasting). Potential limitations include increased training complexity and potential overfitting to specific domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting with Hierarchical Attention
PROPOSAL: Introduce a hierarchical attention mechanism within the encoder of an already established model (e.g., Transformer or CHIE). This mechanism allows the model to focus on relevant features and variables at multiple levels of abstraction, effectively capturing both high-level temporal dependencies and low-level cross-variable interactions. To evaluate this approach, design an experimental workflow to compare hierarchical attention with existing models using various forecasting metrics.
CONTROLS: Implement hierarchical attention within the Transformer and CHIE architectures, and compare their performance against standard Transformer and CHIE models, as well as a simple linear attention mechanism.
COST: 40GPU- hours
PREDICTION: Exploiting hierarchical attention may lead to betterinferencing and performance gains for time-series forecasting tasks with diverse temporal and cross-channel characteristics (e.g., water and traffic forecasting across urban areas.) Weaknesses of the approach could arise in noise-heavy datasets, failing to introduce any performance changes.

CONTROLS: Retain ablation studies to assess the impact of the self-attentive mechanism.
COST: 60GPU- hours
PREDICTION: Improved forecasting performance over base versions of CHIE, potentially at the cost of higher computational complexity in certain scenarios, and more challenging interpretability due to added attentions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Augmentation via View-Dependent Mutual Information Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel adaptation mechanism that dynamically adjusts the augmentation pipeline for each instance based on a view-dependent mutual information estimation. Specifically, we introduce a new objective that encourages the model to learn a mapping from individual instances to a distribution over possible augmentations, allowing for a data-driven selection of augmentations that are specifically tailored to each instance. We will implement this using an extension of the InfoNCE loss function that incorporates a view-dependent KL-divergence term, and experiment on a variety of real-world datasets using a scaled-down version of SimCLR as a baseline.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed method to a baseline of standard SimCLR using fixed augmentations, as well as an ablation study where we remove the view-dependent KL-divergence term from our objective.
COST: 330
PREDICTION: Our method should show significant improvement over the baseline on tasks that require fine-grained representation of individual instances (e.g. image classification), but may struggle in settings where large-batch sampling is possible (e.g. large-scale object detection).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Representational Divergence in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment that directly measures the representational divergence between different instances in the latent space learned by contrastive learning models, using a newly-introduced spectral analysis technique that combines ideas from spectral clustering and Laplacian smoothing. This technique allows us to visualize and quantify the extent to which different instances are embedded in distinct neighborhoods of the latent space, providing a new lens through which to evaluate the semantic consistency of contrastive learning representations.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to the spectral clustering approach of Fortuin and Kasteleyn (1969) and to a standard 2D UMAP embedding, to establish a baseline for contrasting representational architectures.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Our method should highlight regions of the latent space that correspond to coherent semantic categories, and show that these regions are well-separated from one another in high-quality contrastive learning models, while also highlighting the limitations of contrastive learning when it comes to representing intra-instance variation.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Adaptive Augmentation via View-Dependent Mutual Information Estimation
PROPOSAL: We modify our previous proposal to incorporate a hierarchical augmentation scheme, where the augmentation pipeline is adapted not only at the instance level, but also at the category level. Specifically, we introduce a new attention mechanism that selects augmentations that are specifically tailored to the category of the instance, as well as to the instance itself. This allows for a more nuanced and context-dependent augmentation of the input data.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed hierarchical augmentation scheme to our previous view-dependent adaptation mechanism, as well as to a standard SimCLR model with fixed augmentations.
COST: 831
PREDICTION: Our modified method should yield even better performance on tasks that require fine-grained representation of individual instances, as well as better semantic consistency across instances within the same category.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: On the Robustness of Contrastive Learning to Augmentation Variability
PROPOSAL: We investigate the robustness of contrastive learning to variability in augmentation pipelines, with a focus on understanding how changes in augmentation strength and type affect the quality of the learned representations. We will conduct a thorough sensitivity analysis of different contrastive learning models to various augmentation schemes, using a range of real-world datasets and metrics.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to a standard SimCLR model with a fixed augmentation scheme, as well as to a simple interpolation between different augmentation schemes.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: Our analysis should provide valuable insights into the robustness of contrastive learning to real-world variability in data quality and quantity, helping to identify key factors that impact performance in different scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating Representational Divergence in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We modify our previous proposal to incorporate a new metric for evaluating representational divergence, which takes into account the distribution of nearest neighbors in the latent space. Specifically, we define a metric based on the KL-divergence between the true category distribution and the predicted category distribution, using the softmax outputs of the contrastive learning model as the predicted distribution. This allows us to quantify the representational capacity of the model and evaluate its ability to distinguish between different semantic categories.
CONTROLS: We will compare our new metric to the standard spectral clustering approach, as well as to a standard 2D UMAP embedding.
COST: 1170
PREDICTION: Our new metric should provide a more nuanced understanding of representational divergence, highlighting cases where the contrastive learning model is able to capture complex semantic relationships and patterns in the data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Suppressing View Similarity in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel mechanism for suppressing view similarity in contrastive learning, by introducing a new type of loss function that encourages the model to maximize the mutual information between the positive and negative pairs, but with a twist: the negative pairs are drawn from a distribution that is specifically tailored to reduce view similarity. This allows us to decouple the objectives of view similarity and semantic consistency, leading to improved representation quality and reduced overfitting.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed loss function to standard InfoNCE, as well as to a standard InfoNCE variant with an added regularization term.
COST: 4500
PREDICTION: Our approach should lead to improved performance on downstream tasks, as well as better robustness to overfitting and view similarity, but may require careful tuning to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Augmentation via View-Dependent Mutual Information Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel adaptation mechanism that dynamically adjusts the augmentation pipeline for each instance based on a view-dependent mutual information estimation. Specifically, we introduce a new objective that encourages the model to learn a mapping from individual instances to a distribution over possible augmentations, allowing for a data-driven selection of augmentations that are specifically tailored to each instance. We will implement this using an extension of the InfoNCE loss function that incorporates a view-dependent KL-divergence term, and experiment on a variety of real-world datasets using a scaled-down version of SimCLR as a baseline.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed method to a baseline of standard SimCLR using fixed augmentations, as well as an ablation study where we remove the view-dependent KL-divergence term from our objective.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Our method should show significant improvement over the baseline on tasks that require fine-grained representation of individual instances (e.g. image classification), but may struggle in settings where large-batch sampling is possible (e.g. large-scale object detection).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Representational Divergence in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment that directly measures the representational divergence between different instances in the latent space learned by contrastive learning models, using a newly-introduced spectral analysis technique that combines ideas from spectral clustering and Laplacian smoothing. This technique allows us to visualize and quantify the extent to which different instances are embedded in distinct neighborhoods of the latent space, providing a new lens through which to evaluate the semantic consistency of contrastive learning representations.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to the spectral clustering approach of Fortuin and Kasteleyn (1969) and to a standard 2D UMAP embedding, to establish a baseline for contrasting representational architectures.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: Our method should highlight regions of the latent space that correspond to coherent semantic categories, and show that these regions are well-separated from one another in high-quality contrastive learning models, while also highlighting the limitations of contrastive learning when it comes to representing intra-instance variation.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Adaptive Augmentation via View-Dependent Mutual Information Estimation
PROPOSAL: We modify our previous proposal to incorporate a hierarchical augmentation scheme, where the augmentation pipeline is adapted not only at the instance level, but also at the category level. Specifically, we introduce a new attention mechanism that selects augmentations that are specifically tailored to the category of the instance, as well as to the instance itself. This allows for a more nuanced and context-dependent augmentation of the input data.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed hierarchical augmentation scheme to our previous view-dependent adaptation mechanism, as well as to a standard SimCLR model with fixed augmentations.
COST: 2500 ( original cost was 1000; we added more complexity )
PREDICTION: Our modified method should yield even better performance on tasks that require fine-grained representation of individual instances, as well as better semantic consistency across instances within the same category.

This allows us to quantify the representational capacity of the model and evaluate its ability to distinguish between different semantic categories.
CONTROLS: We will compare our new metric to the standard spectral clustering approach, as well as to a standard 2D UMAP embedding.

TITLE: Suppressing View Similarity in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel mechanism for suppressing view similarity in contrastive learning, by introducing a new type of loss function that encourages the model to maximize the mutual information between the positive and negative pairs, but with a twist: the negative pairs are drawn from a distribution that is specifically tailored to reduce view similarity. This allows us to decouple the objectives of view similarity and semantic consistency, leading to improved representation quality and reduced overfitting.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed loss function to standard InfoNCE, as well as to a standard InfoNCE variant with an added regularization term.
COST: 4500
PREDICTION: Our approach should lead to improved performance on downstream tasks, as well as better robustness to overfitting and view similarity, but may require careful tuning to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Analyzing Contrastive Learning Dynamics for Semantic Invariance
PROPOSAL: We aim to study the interaction between augmentations, the information collected through views, and the update dynamics of self-supervised contrastive learning in a principled, information-theoretic framework. Specifically, we focus on operationalizing a lower bound on the information about an instance that can be extracted from its augmented views, using tools from Shannon information theory.
CONTROLS: SimCLR and MoCo as baselines with static augmentations and large-batch sampling; ablation on augmentation schemes with varying transformational complexity
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: The lower bound will indicate, in a probabilistic manner, whether a set of augmentations overpays or underpays on information extraction per instance, likely showing that state-of-the-art methods underpay but providing insight into the minimum information gain attainable; the results will validate long-standing intuitions about augmentation design but could fail to uncover meaningful bounds if the existing methods overpay and overpay not-so-meaningfully.

TITLE: Balanced View Expansion through Transfer Entropy
PROPOSAL: We explore an experiment that expands the diversity of augmented views while maintaining semantic consistency for each instance. TITLE: Unified Framework for Contrastive Learning and Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: Introduce a unified framework, CARE (Contrastive Adversarial Representation), which jointly performs contrastive learning and adversarial training. CARE combines the strengths of both paradigms by leveraging local mutual information and adaptive view expansion to guide the adversarial training process, effectively enhancing the robustness and generalizability of the instance representation.
CONTROLS: Compare CARE against state-of-the-art methods (SimCLR and F-CL) for contrastive learning, and state-of-the-art defense methods (TPE and AEG) for adversarial robustness, on various evaluation metrics (representation robustness and generalizability).
COST: 43200
PREDICTION: CARE effectively improves the robustness and generalizability of the instance representation, outperforming existing methods on both contrastive learning and adversarial robustness tasks.

TITLE: Revising the Analyzing the Role of Local Mutual Information Proposal
PROPOSAL: Introduce a computationally efficient method, Local-MI, to analyze the local mutual information between instances and their augmented views in the representation space, providing insights into the feature relevance and redundancy. Local-MI calculates the mutual information between the instance representation and its individual features, allowing for a detailed understanding of the features' contribution to the instance's overall representation.
CONTROLS: Compare Local-MI against existing methods (PFMI and MPI) on various evaluation metrics (per-instance MI and feature importance) and assess its ability to identify relevant features in the representation space.
COST: 108000
PREDICTION: Local-MI provides a more fine-grained and efficient understanding of the instance representation, effectively highlighting the most informative features and enabling better augmentation strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive View Expansion for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel approach, Adaptive View Expansion (AVE), to adaptively select and combine a subset of augmentation views for each instance, based on the local mutual information and the instance's representation. AVE aims to mitigate the redundancy of views and focus on the most informative ones, effectively increasing the diversified semantic information in the representation space.
CONTROLS: Compare AVE against state-of-the-art methods (SimCLR and MoCo) on various evaluation metrics (representation diversity and semantic consistency) and measure its ability to improve the instance representation with fewer views.
COST: 93600
PREDICTION: AVE effectively increases the representation diversity while maintaining semantic consistency, and outperforms existing methods under various augmentations and view count conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Framework for Contrastive Learning and Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: Introduce a unified framework, CARE (Contrastive Adversarial Representation), which jointly performs contrastive learning and adversarial training. CARE combines the strengths of both paradigms by leveraging local mutual information and adaptive view expansion to guide the adversarial training process, effectively enhancing the robustness and generalizability of the instance representation.
CONTROLS: Compare CARE against state-of-the-art methods (SimCLR and F-CL) for contrastive learning, and state-of-the-art defense methods (TPE and AEG) for adversarial robustness, on various evaluation metrics (representation robustness and generalizability).
COST: 129600
PREDICTION: CARE effectively improves the robustness and generalizability of the instance representation, outperforming existing methods on both contrastive learning and adversarial robustness tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Redefining the Information Theoretic Objectives for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new information-theoretic framework, ITI (Information-Theoretic Insight), that redefines the objectives of contrastive learning by maximizing the inter-instance diversity while minimizing the intra-instance redundancy. ITI aims to tackle the underlying tension between contrastive objectives and the explosion of redundant information in the latent space.
CONTROLS: Compare ITI against existing information-theoretic frameworks (MINE and A InfoGAN) on various evaluation metrics (representation redundancy and generalization to novel instances).
COST: 162000
PREDICTION: ITI effectively encourages the discovery of diverse and non-redundant features in the latent space, leading to improved generalization and robustness of the instance representation, especially in the presence of noisy or corrupted inputs.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Perform a theoretical analysis of the proposed Local-MI method, providing a rigorous derivation of its relationships to existing information-theoretic objectives and providing a lower bound on the representation's expressive power. The goal is to provide a solid theoretical foundation for the Local-MI method, allowing for further optimization and generalization.
CONTROLS: Provide a detailed derivation of the Local-MI objective, comparing and contrasting it to existing information-theoretic objectives, and validate the theoretical results using experimental evaluation.
COST: 196800
PREDICTION: The theoretical analysis provides a novel insight into the relationships between Local-MI and existing information-theoretic objectives, offering a possible way to effectively balance specificity and generality in contrastive learning, and provides a benchmark to evaluate the effectiveness of other information-theoretic methods.

PROPOSAL: We design a family of experiments to quantify the mutual information gained by the model between different views of an instance during self-supervised contrastive learning. We will use the popular ResNet50 model and compute the mutual information between different views of the same instance and different views of different instances on a range of real-world datasets (e.g. ImageNet, CIFAR-10, STL-10). We will compare the information gain through different augmentations (e.g. random cropping, color jittering, flipping) and batch sizes. Our experiments will be controlled by the following baselines: (i) random initialization of the model, (ii) supervised learning with labels, (iii) non-contrastive learning objectives (e.g. predicting the class of the input). PREDICTION: We expect to find that certain augmentations and batch sizes lead to higher information gain, while others do not, and that the information gain is a non-monotonic function of batch size. This may reveal that current augmentation design heuristics are suboptimal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-theoretic Analysis of Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We provide a theoretical framework to understand the information-theoretic foundations of contrastive learning. We derive a novel relationship between the mutual information gain through different views and the capacity of the model to represent semantic information. We show that the mutual information gain is lower-bounded by the semantic capacity of the model, and provide an analytical expression for this lower bound. We also identify the optimal view configurations that achieve the lower bound. Our analysis is based on the alignment principle and uniformity principle of contrastive learning. COST: 32400
CONTROLS: We will compare our theoretical results to the experiments proposed in Measuring Mutual Information Gain Through Contrastive Learning, and to the performance of state-of-the-art contrastive learning methods (e.g. SimCLR, MoCo) on benchmark datasets.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Information Gain in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate how to quantify the information gained by each instance through the views presented to the model using the Mutual Information (MI) framework. Specifically, we will develop a new metric that estimates the mutual information between a given instance and its corresponding augmented views, using either the estimate via MI lower bound with a neural network, or relying on a novel synthetic baseline assuming Gaussian distributions.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1. Original SimCLR on standard train/val/test split and pooled MI estimate by InfoNCE; Baseline 2. Using 12 hand-crafted augmentations (similar to classical baseline architectures)
COST: 160
PREDICTION: We expect the new MI-based metric to track the instance-level feature separation better and outperform both baselines in capturing the information density of each instance. This may fail if successful performance is due merely to converging instances in view space, even when instance-level information gain decreases.

PROPOSAL: Introduce a new penalty term based on the adversarial Lipshitz regularization, in the direction of improving the autoencoder which generates augmentations. Our experiment will test how this regularization impacts model performance when added to training objectives of SimCLR variant.

COST: 474
PREDICTION: We expect to see that by incorporating adversarial Lipshitz regularization into SimCLR and its variant, there is noticeable boost to contrastive gain in dense data distributions. ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Enhanced Contrastive Augmentation
PROPOSAL: Revise the previous proposal, Contrastive Augmentation via Adversarial Lipshitz Regularization, by using a more sophisticated neural network architecture and an adaptive version of the adversarial Lipshitz regularization that depend on batch size and the allocated number of augmentations. The goal is to create a more flexible and self-adaptive augmentation strategy that can adjust to different data distributions.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1. Original SimCLR with standard augmentations and batch size; Baseline 2. SimCLR with merely larger batches; Baseline 3. Enhanced SimCLR without Lipshitz regularization
COST: 700
PREDICTION: We expect that the adaptive version of the adversarial Lipshitz regularization and the more advanced neural network architecture will improve the contrastive augmentation and lead to better performance on a wider range of tasks. If the results are not as expected, further investigation is needed to understand why the adaptive regularization and the advanced architecture did not improve the performance as anticipated.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Batch and Augmentation Scheduling
PROPOSAL: Investigate an adaptive batch and augmentation scheduling framework that dynamically adjusts the batch size and augmentation strategy based on the model's performance and the data distributions. This will allow the model to learn at different rates and adapt to changing data distributions, potentially improving sample efficiency and enabling training on smaller batches.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1. Original SimCLR with standard batch size and augmentations; Baseline 2. SimCLR with dynamic batch size and fixed augmentations; Baseline 3. Enhanced SimCLR with adaptive batch size and augmentation scheduling
COST: 1631.23
PREDICTION: We expect that the adaptive batch and augmentation scheduling framework will improve the sample efficiency of contrastive learning and enable training on smaller batches. However, the scheduling framework may introduce additional computational complexity, and the performance improvements may not be consistent across all datasets and tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-Theoretic Analysis of View Diversity
PROPOSAL: Develop a new theoretical framework to analyze the information-theoretic properties of view diversity in contrastive learning. Specifically, we will investigate how the diversity of augmented views affects the mutual information between the view spaces and the underlying data distribution. This will provide insight into how to optimize the view diversity for better representation learning.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1. Existing literature on information-theoretic properties of contrastive learning; Baseline 2. Empirical analysis of view diversity on a variety of datasets
COST: 2168
PREDICTION: We expect that the new framework will provide a deeper understanding of the information-theoretic properties of view diversity and lead to improved strategies for view diversity optimization. However, the theoretical analysis may not directly translate to practical optimization algorithms, and the empirical analysis may require significant computational resources.

PROPOSAL: Develop a new theoretical framework to analyze the information-theoretic properties of view diversity in contrastive learning. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Consistent Evaluation Framework for Episodic and Online Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Set up a consistent evaluation framework that includes the reproduction of reported baseline results using CLIP as the pre-trained VLM, along with the use of a standardized text prompt and evaluation protocol. Compare the performance of various existing episodic and online TTA methods under this framework, examining their gains over the unadapted model, as well as variations due to pre-trained model checkpoints and text prompts.
CONTROLS: Results will be compared to the original CLIP implementation without adaptation, and variations will be evaluated using ablations of different pre-trained model checkpoints and text prompts.
COST: 1704 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This evaluation framework will reveal discrepancies in the reported performance of existing TTA methods and help to identify areas where more consistent experimental conditions are needed. However, due to the existing diversity in pre-trained model checkpoints and text prompts, some variations in performance may remain inconclusive.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Interplay between Training-Time Fine-Tuning and Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the interplay between training-time fine-tuning and test-time adaptation for VQgan-CLIP, by examining how batch schedules and training epochs of fine-tuning impact the effectiveness of different TTA methods. Our goal is to determine whether and when combining fine-tuning with TTA will lead to performance gains.
CONTROLS: Baselines will include no adaptation, fine-tuning only, TTA only, fine-tuning with different hyperparameters. We will investigate how different adaptation methods (online and episodic) scale with varying fine-tuning schedules.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect that a combination of fine-tuning and TTA can result in improved adaptation performance in specific tasks, where fine-tuning provides a strong initial point for subsequent adaptation. However, our expectation is that TTA is more likely to assist under highly specific, harder tasks to perform.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Consistency Across TTA Implementations
PROPOSAL: To ensure that performance gains of TTA methods can be conclusively attributed to the TTA algorithm itself, we conduct a controlled experiment to reproduce baseline results for six popular episodic and online TTA methods on the standard.music21k dataset using the ViT-B/16 model. We use the official implementation and parameters, and compare our results with the authors' claims using the accuracy metric. If consistent results are replicated, we then fine-tune these models on a held-out test set to evaluate their robustness and stability under practical deployment conditions.
CONTROLS: Compare results with five TTA methods in an ablated version where the TTA module is removed.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: We expect significant performance differences among these TTA methods, and robust replication of previously reported results should demonstrate the consistency of the underlying algorithmic improvements. However, the practical deployment results may reveal a more nuanced relationship between adaptation and robustness.

TITLE: Bias Analysis of Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: To assess potential biases in TTA methods that may affect performance on certain groups of samples or tasks, we design a bias analysis experiment by training a VLM on a dataset with controlled biases (e.g., ImageCLEF) and applying six popular TTA methods to identify whether any of these methods alleviates or exacerbates biases. This will inform best practices for using TTA to ensure fairness and equity.
CONTROLS: Compare TTA methods with and without modifications to tackle the bias (e.g., debiasing).

PREDICTION: We expect to find evidence of bias in some TTA methods that can lead to improved performance on certain types of samples at the expense of reduced performance on others, suggesting that some adaptation strategies might be unfair or biased. Effective modifications can then be developed to mitigate these biases and improve model fairness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Consistent Reproduction of Baselines for Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: We will replicate the implementations of various state-of-the-art episodic and online TTA methods on the CLIP model using a fixed pre-trained checkpoint (ViT-B/32) and a standard evaluation protocol across ImageNet classification and natural language-based test data. Specifically, we will reproduce the results of recent papers, such as "Improving CLIP" and "Episodic Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models". We will also validate the quality of the reproduced baselines by running the same methods on a set of synthetic test data.
CONTROLS: The unadapted baseline, original code and checkpoints of recent papers, ablation of various hyperparameters and components of the TTA methods.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: We expect the reproduced baselines to match or closely approximate the reported results in the original papers. However, potential discrepancies may arise due to variations in computational environments and hardware.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Consistent Reproduction of Baselines for Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: We will replicate the implementations of various state-of-the-art episodic and online TTA methods on the CLIP model using a fixed pre-trained checkpoint (ViT-B/32) and a standard evaluation protocol across ImageNet classification and natural language-based test data. Specifically, we will reproduce the results of recent papers, such as "Improving CLIP" and "Episodic Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models". We will also validate the quality of the reproduced baselines by running the same methods on a set of synthetic test data.
CONTROLS: The unadapted baseline, original code and checkpoints of recent papers, ablation of various hyperparameters and components of the TTA methods.
COST: 54000
PREDICTION: We expect the reproduced baselines to match or closely approximate the reported results in the original papers. However, potential discrepancies may arise due to variations in computational environments and hardware.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Evaluation of Test-Time Adaptation Methods on Diverse VLM Architectures
PROPOSAL: We will extend the reproduction setup from proposal 1 to various other pre-trained VLM models beyond CLIP, including LLaMA-Vision and DALL-E, on the ImageNet classification and COCO captioning tasks. This will allow us to assess the transferability and generalizability of TTA methods across different VLM architectures and application domains.
CONTROLS: The additional VLM models, same evaluation protocol and baselines as in proposal 1, ablation of TTA methods on each VLM model.
COST: 108000
PREDICTION: We expect to see variations in the effectiveness of TTA methods across different VLM architectures, with some methods performing better on certain models or tasks. However, we may also find that certain TTA methods are more robust and generalize better across multiple VLMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Robustness of Test-Time Adaptation Methods to Adversarial Attacks
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the robustness of TTA methods to adversarial attacks on the CLIP model and the other pre-trained VLM models used in proposal 2. Specifically, we will apply various types of adversarial attacks, such as FGSM and PGD, to the models before and after TTA adaptation, and measure the effect on classification accuracy and stability.
CONTROLS: The same TTA methods and VLM models as before, various types of adversarial attacks, ablation of TTA methods in the presence of adversarial attacks.
COST: 162000
PREDICTION: We expect TTA methods to be more vulnerable to adversarial attacks than the unadapted models, as they update the model during inference and potentially amplify the effect of small perturbations. However, certain TTA methods may be more robust to some types of attacks than others.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Systematic Evaluation of Alternative Evaluation Metrics for Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the impact of using alternative evaluation metrics, such as calibration error, F1-score, and edit distance, in addition to accuracy, on the assessment of TTA methods. We will evaluate these metrics on the CLIP model and other pre-trained VLM models used in proposal 2, and compare the results across different TTA methods and evaluation metrics.
CONTROLS: Same TTA methods and VLM models as before, various evaluation metrics, ablation of individual metrics and their combinations.
COST: 270000
PREDICTION: We expect that using alternative evaluation metrics will provide a more nuanced understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of TTA methods, and may reveal that some methods are effective on certain metrics but not others. However, it may also require careful selection of metrics and evaluation protocols to ensure fairness and comparability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Test-Time Adaptation vs. Fine-Tuning: An Empirical Comparison
PROPOSAL: We will compare the performance of TTA methods with fine-tuning at training time on various pre-trained VLM models, including CLIP and other models used in proposal 2. Specifically, we will fine-tune the models using labeled data and then evaluate their performance on the same test set as the TTA methods. This will allow us to assess whether TTA can serve as a complementary or alternative to fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: Same VLM models and test sets as before, fine-tuning using labeled data, ablation of fine-tuning parameters and TTA methods.
COST: 405000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that fine-tuning provides better performance than TTA methods on certain tasks or models, while TTA methods may be more effective in scenarios where labeled data is scarce or fine-tuning is not feasible. However, the comparison may also reveal interactions and dependencies between fine-tuning and TTA methods that require further investigation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Episodic Test-Time Adaptation: Ablation Study
PROPOSAL: Conduct an ablation study to compare the performance of different components within the episodic adaptation strategy, such as attention over input patches, input prompt, and fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: The study will evaluate the following baselines:
- No attention over input patches
- Default input prompt
- No fine-tuning
- Combination of above modifications
Additionally, we will evaluate the ablations of popular episodic adaptation methods like LXMERT and Visual-BERT.

PREDICTION: This study will provide insights into the role of individual components in the episodic adaptation strategy, and might reveal which components are critical for performance improvements. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Open-Ended Evaluation of Test-Time Adaptation for VLMs
PROPOSAL: Introduce the open-ended evaluation of test-time adaptation methods, where the primary goal is not to achieve high accuracy, but to evaluate the robustness and trustworthiness of VLMs in the face of various real-world challenges, such as class imbalance, out-of-distribution inputs, and corrupted images.
CONTROLS: We will add the following controls to assess the impact of adaptation on model robustness and trustworthiness:
- OOD evaluation on ImagVista-2019 dataset with corruption and masking
- Class balance evaluation on the validation set of the iNaturalist2018 dataset
- Inversion-based dataset corruption task
- Two-stage adaptation evaluation: adapt the model on the in-distribution training set and then test its performance on the out-of-distribution testing set
The baseline will be a non-adapted CLIP model trained on the same training set.
COST: 180
PREDICTION: This evaluation will reveal whether the adaptation process compromises or preserves the trustworthiness of VLMs in real-world scenarios and might indicate potential limitations of VLMs. We predict that fine-tuning can exacerbate the issue of overfitting and reduce model robustness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-Scale Comparison of Online and Episodic Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of state-of-the-art online and episodic adaptation methods on a diverse set of real-world benchmarks and datasets, with the goal of identifying the range of scenarios in which each approach excels.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate a selection of online methods like AOTL and Adapters, and episodic adaptation methods like FreezeCLIP and CC-DETR on the following datasets and benchmarks:
- ImageNet validation set
- iNaturalist2018 validation set
- GTSRB validation set
- Conceptual Captions validation set
We will also evaluate the performance of non-adapted CLIP baseline and compare it to the best-performing adaptation methods.

PREDICTION: This comparison will provide a comprehensive understanding of the trade-offs between online and episodic adaptation methods and will give insights into the scalability and needs of each adaptation technique under different scenarios. We expect online methods to excels in the scenarios with varying amounts of training and testing data but we are uncertain about the performance under previously unseen categories.

PROPOSAL: Perform a detailed case study on the effects of test-time adaptation on a downstream task using a VLM (e.g., CLIP), elucidating how adaptation impacts performance, robustness, and model interpretability in the context of a specific real-world application.
CONTROLS: The case study will assess the impact of adaptation on the following dimensions:

- Robustness: Test the robustness of adaptation to various real-world challenges such as noise, missing features, or variations in the input data
- Model interpretability: Investigate the effect of adaptation on model saliency maps and feature importance
The study will compare the performance of adaptation to the non-adapted model and explore how adaptation impacts model behavior in the context of the domain.

PREDICTION: This case study will provide valuable insights into how test-time adaptation can impact real-world applications and will facilitate a deeper understanding of the strengths and limitations of adaptation techniques.
