PROPOSAL: We propose a revised discrete video tokenizer that combines a convolutional projector with a sequence of causal transformers to recursively compute token activations from input frames. Unlike existing tokenizers, which use convolutions or a fixed anchor grid to divide the frame into tokens, our tokenizer partitions frames into spatially-aligned tokens with contextualized token boundaries. By avoiding the need for a predefined grid, our approach can adapt to videos with varying spatial resolutions and frame rates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Feedback Alignment for Temporally Consistent Discrete Autoregressive Video Generation
PROPOSAL: To stabilize training and maintain temporal consistency, we propose a feedback alignment mechanism that uses an auxiliary loss to compute a temporal connectivity graph among tokens. This graph is then used to align the predicted tokens with the input context, ensuring that tokens are updated in a consistent temporal order. The feedback alignment loss encourages the model to learn a mapping between token representations and their corresponding temporal contexts, thus improving the coherence and fidelity of generated videos.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effect of our feedback alignment mechanism on the stability of training and quality of generated videos, compared to the same discrete autoregressive video model with random token update order, and inject our implementation into our Hierarchical Video Generation with Token-Level Conditioning to enhance benchmark performance.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: This feedback alignment mechanism is expected to significantly improve the stability and coherence of generated videos, especially for long sequences, and may lead to better text-video alignment; it may introduce some computational overhead, particularly during training, which could hinder its adoption in settings where memory or computational resources are limited.

TITLE: Investigating Hierarchical Discrete Video Tokenizers
PROPOSAL: Train a hierarchical discrete video tokenizer using a combination of 2D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to capture spatial and temporal dependencies in videos. This model will be trained on the Heroes dataset, a large-scale video captioning dataset, and evaluated on the text-to-video benchmark, S2VT. CONTROLS: Compare with non-hierarchical tokenizers and tokenizers trained from scratch.

PREDICTION: This approach may achieve better performance than non-hierarchical tokenizers, but may struggle with capturing long-range dependencies due to the hierarchical structure, leading to suboptimal performance on long videos.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Discrete AutoRegressive Video Generation with Alternate Mode and Sub-Pixel Resampling
PROPOSAL: Develop a discrete autoregressive video generation model that alternates between predicting token coordinates using a sub-pixel resampling mechanism and predicting token values. This will allow the model to capture spatial and temporal dependencies while maintaining computational efficiency. The model will be trained on the VLOG17 dataset, a large-scale raw video dataset, and evaluated on the visual fidelity and temporal coherence of generated videos.
CONTROLS: Compare with models that only use sub-pixel resampling or only use alternate modes, as well as with diffusion-based video generation models.
COST: 16,560
PREDICTION: This approach may achieve better visual fidelity and temporal coherence than previous discrete autoregressive models, but may struggle with maintaining stability during training, leading to mode collapse or divergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Temporal Consistency through Self-Attention in VAR-based Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the Visual AutoRegressive (VAR) architecture, introduced in Infinity for image generation, to video synthesis while incorporating spatiotemporal self-attention. This will allow our model to capture temporal consistency and enable coherent motion in long videos. Specifically, we will modify the attention mechanism within Infinity to attend across both spatial and temporal dimensions.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments will be performed on the same architecture without spatiotemporal self-attention and with standard next-frame prediction, as implemented in Nova for comparison. We will also explore the regime where only spatial or only temporal attention is used, to isolate their contributions.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: By incorporating spatiotemporal self-attention, Infinity-Video should outperform the baselines in terms of visual quality and temporal consistency, especially for complex videos with coherent motion. However, extremely long videos may still incur very high computational costs due to the exploding tensor size.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Video Tokenization through Transfer Learning and Meta-Weighting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel video tokenizer that leverages transfer learning by initializing the tokenizer's weights with a pre-trained static image tokenizer (such as the one in Infinity) and fine-tuning on our video dataset. Furthermore, we introduce meta-weighting to adapt the importance of each token's features across different video content. This will help to focus the tokenizer on the most relevant aspects of the video.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed tokenizer to a scratch-trained tokenizer and one that is initialized from a discrete image tokenizer but without meta-weighting. We will also evaluate the robustness of our tokenizer by fine-tuning it on different datasets.
COST: 24000
PREDICTION: Our proposed tokenizer should significantly improve the reconstruction quality of the video data while reducing training costs and convergence times. However, the pre-trained weights from the static image tokenizer may not always be optimal for video processing, potentially leading to subpar results for certain video styles.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Streaming Generation through Parallelized VAR and Efficient Token Buffering
PROPOSAL: We will modify our VAR-based video generation model to enable streaming generation by introducing a parallel processing pipeline and an efficient token buffering mechanism. The parallel processing pipeline will be responsible for generating video tokens in real-time, while the token buffer will store the generated tokens and enable the model to adapt to changing input conditions. This will allow our model to generate videos in real-time and adapt to complex and dynamic inputs.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed streaming generation model to a traditional VAR-based model that generates videos sequentially. We will also evaluate the impact of varying the number of parallel processing threads and token buffering size on the model's performance.
COST: 42000
PREDICTION: Our proposed streaming generation model should enable our VAR-based model to generate videos in real-time and adapt to complex and dynamic inputs. However, the increased parallel processing requirements may lead to higher computational costs and memory usage.

TITLE: Efficient Discrete Video Tokenization
PROPOSAL: Develop an optimized discrete video tokenizer, which significantly reduces the computational cost of training and inference while maintaining high-quality reconstruction. Specifically, we shall adapt existing video tokenizers, like INN-LS, to the spatio-temporal domain, perform pruning and knowledge distillation to reduce token counts, and optimize tokenizer training using data augmentation and reduced self-supervision. We aim for a flexibility in design, such that the tokenizer can be easily combined with different autoregressive models.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing discrete video tokenizers, applying the same optimization strategies to existing architectures like INN-LS and IAF.
COST: 2583.689
PREDICTION: Our tailored tokenizer should exhibit notably improved performance in efficiency and quality, particularly when compared to out-of-the-box applications of existing discrete tokenizers, but it might be challenging to effectively prune down the tokenizer's vocabulary while preserving its ability to capture complex pixel-and-frame relationships and temporal dependence, potentially leading to knowledge underrepresentation or a handicap in model's generative capacity.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Attention for Efficient Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Design a novel, high-capacity attention mechanism that jointly captures the temporal and spatial coherence of videos. Specifically, we propose the Temporal-Spatial Unified Attention (TSUA) module, which aggregates information along both axes by conducting a two-stage aggregation. In the first stage, TSUA utilizes a spatial attention to capture the inter-frame coherence, followed by a temporal attention to distill the sequential motion patterns. Building on this, we will implement this mechanism within a discrete autoregressive model for text-to-video generation and compare its performance against state-of-the-art diffusion and autoregressive models.
CONTROLS: Baseline models including U-Net-based diffusion models and Emu3 will be used for comparison. Additionally, we will implement an ablation study to investigate the effect of TSUA on performance.
COST: 19200
PREDICTION: TSUA is expected to yield a 20-30% reduction in inference latency for high-resolution videos while achieving comparable visual quality to state-of-the-art diffusion models. If successful, this could be a crucial step towards addressing the need for efficient video generation. However, it might fail to generalize across different datasets due to the highly specific design of TSUA.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Discrete Video Tokenizers via Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether transfer learning from image tokenizers can accelerate the training of discrete video tokenizers without significant performance degradation. Specifically, we will freeze the spatial components of a pre-trained discrete image tokenizer and fine-tune the temporal components for video reconstruction. To ensure effective transfer, we will use a reinitialized video tokenizer with a temporal triple encoder based on a CNN LSTM architecture. We will then compare the performance of the fine-tuned tokenizer against one trained from scratch and against an image-tokenizer-initialized tokenizer.
CONTROLS: The experiment will be conducted with the fine-tuned tokenizer as a primary baseline, against which both a tokenizer trained from scratch and an image-tokenizer-initialized tokenizer will be compared. We will also consider an ablation study to determine the importance of the pre-trained components.
COST: 13824
PREDICTION: Fine-tuning the tokenizer is expected to reduce video reconstruction time by 30-40% while maintaining a similar level of visual quality. However, if fine-tuning does not work well, this could prevent a scalable, efficient method for video generation due to high training cost of video tokenizers.

TITLE: Unified Attention for Efficient Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Design a novel, high-capacity attention mechanism that jointly captures the temporal and spatial coherence of videos. Specifically, we propose the Temporal-Spatial Unified Attention (TSUA) module, which aggregates information along both axes by conducting a two-stage aggregation. In the first stage, TSUA utilizes a spatial attention to capture the inter-frame coherence, followed by a temporal attention to distill the sequential motion patterns. Building on this, we will implement this mechanism within a discrete autoregressive model for text-to-video generation and compare its performance against state-of-the-art diffusion and autoregressive models.
CONTROLS: Baseline models including U-Net-based diffusion models and Emu3 will be used for comparison. Additionally, we will implement an ablation study to investigate the effect of TSUA on performance.
COST: 57600
PREDICTION: TSUA is expected to yield a 20-30% reduction in inference latency for high-resolution videos while achieving comparable visual quality to state-of-the-art diffusion models. If successful, this could be a crucial step towards addressing the need for efficient video generation. However, it might fail to generalize across different datasets due to the highly specific design of TSUA.

We will then compare the performance of the fine-tuned tokenizer against one trained from scratch and against an image-tokenizer-initialized tokenizer.

TITLE: Investigating Invariant Representations Under Gradient-Based Training for Associative Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Prove that gradient-based training using a transformer model for knowledge injection can preserve invariant representations of atomic facts, such as (s, r, a), even when these facts are not directly observed during training, under the assumption that the affine coupling layers in the transformer's feed-forward network (FFN) provide a bottleneck for feature compression. This result could imply that the model Learn's invariant representations through its FFN, ultimately enabling associative reasoning.
CONTROLS: Compare with a variant of the transformer with its FFN layers replaced by a simpler MLP.
COST: 36
PREDICTION: If successful, this result would suggest that invariant representations are a key factor in LLMs' associative reasoning capabilities, which could be leveraged to design more effective reasoning mechanisms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Gradient Flow Across Atomic Triads for Associative Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the gradient flow between the input encoding of an atomic fact (s, r, a), its corresponding implication (s, r', a'), and an unseen implication (s, r``, a'') in a transformer model during knowledge injection. This analysis aims to understand whether the gradients of the loss function are consistently flowing between the atomic facts and their implications, or if they hop over unseen implications. Study this gradient flow using a custom visualization tool and a synthetic dataset of atomic triples.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline model without attention mechanisms.
COST: 108
PREDICTION: If successful, this analysis would provide insights into how gradients are transmitted between atomic facts and their implications, shedding light on the associative reasoning mechanisms of transformer models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Layer-by-Layer Training on Inference of Unseen Implications
PROPOSAL: Train a transformer-based LLM on synthetic data for factual knowledge injection, where some subjects appear in both a fact and its corresponding implication, and fine-tune it layer-by-layer using knowledge graph embeddings to inject new factual knowledge. Measure the model's ability to infer unseen implications at different layers and relate this to the effectiveness of generalization versus hallucination. Use multi-tasking by sampling implicative triplets of facts for the model to learn as generalization examples.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline transformer trained with the same amount of knowledge injected at once (broadcasting), a layer-by-layer trained model with the knowledge injection turned off, and the same method but using self-supervised pre-training with lies on the more heavy fact retrieval on the Litwit.
COST: 786.1
PREDICTION: Layer-by-layer training should unlock significant gains in the model's ability to infer unseen implications, as the model has time to learn the connections and relationships between different pieces of knowledge. However, this approach may also exacerbate hallucinations by allowing the model to overfit at the early stages, making it particularly challenging to achieve balance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Effect of Multiplicative Variance in Knowledge Embeddings on Hallucination vs. Generalization
PROPOSAL: Perform an ablation study on the input layer of the transformer to compare the results of knowledge embeddings with multiplicative variance to those with constant variance, injecting new factual knowledge through fine-tuning on synthetic data with subjects in both fact and implication. Evaluate the model's ability to generalize and hallucinate on unseen implications across different radiation settings (regular, slight variation, zero variance).
CONTROLS: Compare to the baseline having knowledge graph embeddings with constant variance, knowledge embeddings where the dimensional variance span between single sampled inpainting concepts slightly changed.
COST: 1229.783
PREDICTION: Multiplicative variance in knowledge embeddings should significantly enhance the model's ability to generalize on unseen implications while reducing hallucinations, as it allows the model to distinguish between relevant and irrelevant relationships more effectively.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Physically-Inspired Focus Features for Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Design a depth estimation model that leverages physically-inspired focus features, such as the circle of confusion and the focus gradient, derived from the focal stack. For each pixel in the stack, extract these features and feed them into a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to jointly estimate depth and a heatmap of focus cues. Use the NYUv2 dataset, a benchmark for indoor scene depth estimation.
CONTROLS: Compare with state-of-the-art focus-based depth estimation models and a variant of our model using standard RGB features instead of physically-inspired focus features.
COST: 1656
PREDICTION: Our model should outperform state-of-the-art focus-based models in terms of accuracy and robustness to texture-induced artifacts. It might fail in regions with strong image gradients or abrupt depth changes, where the physically-inspired focus features might be insufficient to disambiguate noisy focus cues.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Focal Stack Normalization for Robust Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Proposal a novel data normalization technique tailored to focal stacks, which we term Focal Stack Normalization (FSN). FSN aims to mitigate the artifacts caused by varying light conditions, camera settings, and focus changes across the stack. Specifically, FSN normalizes the focal stack in both spatial and focal dimensions to have unit variance and zero mean, using separate normalization parameters for each focal plane. Evaluate FSN's impact on depth estimation using the Focal Stack dataset and compare its performance to baseline models without normalization.
CONTROLS: Compare with state-of-the-art depth estimation models with and without access to focal information, as well as models that apply standard image normalization techniques.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: Our method should significantly improve depth estimation accuracy and robustness in challenging real-world scenes by reducing artifacts caused by varying input conditions. However, FSN might be less effective in scenes with homogeneous texture or under-exposure.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Depth-from-Focus with Focus-Structure Disentanglement
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel depth estimation approach that disentangles focus-related features from structural cues in the focal stack. This is achieved by introducing a multidimensional generative adversarial network (GAN) architecture that learns to separate the focus information from the structural information in the input images. The model comprises two generators: one estimates the depth map, and the other generates a focus heatmap. Use the AI2-THINGS dataset, which provides detailed 3D scene geometry and high-quality image sequences.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art focus-based depth estimation models, as well as models that do not use disentanglement.
COST: 2500
PREDICTION: The proposed approach should lead to a more accurate separation of focus-related features from structural cues in the focal stack, ultimately improving depth estimation performance. It may fail to capture situations where the focus and structural information are highly correlated or intertwined, leading to inconsistencies in the disentanglement.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Constrained Optimization for Depth Estimation from Focal Stacks
PROPOSAL: Develop a constrained optimization framework for depth estimation from focal stacks. The framework integrates with physically-inspired focus features (PROPOSAL 1) and preserves depth consistency across the focal stack. The optimization algorithm is formulated as a variational problem, where the goal is to minimize the difference between the predicted depth map and the input stack while encouraging spatial smoothness and focus-related cues. Implement this framework on the Focal Stack dataset and benchmark against ground truth depth maps.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art focus-based depth estimation models, as well as ablation experiments examining the importance of each individual objective term in the constrained optimization.
COST: 2750
PREDICTION: The proposed constrained optimization framework should improve depth estimation accuracy and robustness to noise and blurring in the focal stack. However, it might require extensive fine-tuning for each scene type, potentially introducing calibration issues that reduce its overall performance.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Focal Stack Augmentation for Diverse Training Conditions
PROPOSAL: Propose focal stack augmentation (FSA) to increase the diversity and representativeness of training data for depth estimation models. FSA involves artificially combining multiple focal stacks using geometric transformations (e.g., rotations, translations) and then blending the frames using alpha-blending. FSA can produce a diverse set of simulated focal stacks that are more representative of real-world scenarios and can train the model to be more robust to variations in focus changes and depth complexity. Use the AI2-THINGS dataset, which provides detailed 3D scene geometry and high-quality image sequences.
CONTROLS: Compare with state-of-the-art focus-based depth estimation models trained on regular and augmented focal stacks, as well as ablation experiments examining the impact of different augmentation techniques.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: The proposed focal stack augmentation should improve the robustness and accuracy of depth estimation models. However, it might require careful adjustment of augmentation parameters to avoid over-smoothing of depth features and ensuring that the changes in the augmented focal stack are realistic and representative of real-world variations.

PREDICTION: The revised physically-inspired focus feature pipeline should provide more accurate estimates of depth and corresponding focus cues, translating to improved performance in sparse scenes. TITLE: Photometric Stability Preserving Module for Multi-Focus Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: We design a novel neural network module, Photometric Stability Preserving (PSP), that preserves photometric stability across different focal planes by learning to adopt and refine focus cues from a multi-focus stack. PSP consists of a feature extractor, a mutually recurrent Refocus engine, and a refocused spatial attention mechanism that infers spatial relationships while tracking sharpest focus planes. To learn how each point's focus evolves over the focal stack, PSP progressively adopts and leverages more refined focus patterns from each slice. This approach ensures a gradual shift of focus, rather than sharp focus-based estimates, providing shred representation of depth cues and thus stabilizing predictions across different images in the stack.
CONTROLS:  We compare it to several state-of-the-art architectures: APF, Shelf Partitioned Relative Depth, Restored DF in CNNs, Latent Space-C attention, Learned Defocus Map Refining (with both pure CNN and mixture CNN-Ensemble.
COST: 2036.7

PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel framework for depth estimation, Physics-Informed Depth Estimation using Focus-Aware Normalization (PIDE FN). PIDE FN incorporates a physics-informed loss function that encourages the model to align with the physical principles of focusing and Gaussian blur, while also utilizing a focus-aware normalization layer to adapt to the varying levels of sharpness across focal planes. This approach enables the model to learn a more accurate and robust representation of depth cues, even in the presence of noise or texture ambiguities.

Specifically, the Focus-Sensitive Spatial-Aware Network (FSSAN) will utilize a dual-branch architecture, where the spatial-branch receives RGB inputs and incorporates spatial regularization, while the focal-branch receives the focal stack inputs, employing focus-sensitive features learned from a synthetic training dataset and distilled with spatial attention mechanisms to refine the depth estimation.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Exploring Focal-Specific Feature Learning for Depth-from-Focus
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a novel Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model, dubbed FocusNet, specifically designed to learn focal-dependent features. FocusNet will be composed of a stacked encoder-decoder architecture where each convolutional block is followed by a focus-aware attention mechanism that computes feature importance based on the focus gradient within the image slice. During training, FocusNet will be supervised using a novel loss function that incorporates both focal-specific information from a focal stack and ground truth depth maps, with the latter obtained from a separate stereo vision system. 
CONTROLS: We will compare FocusNet against the current state-of-the-art learning-based DFF methods, including the self-supervised depth and defocus simulation (SDDS) model, and a standard baseline that uses a pre-trained all-in-focus network. Ablations of our proposed focus-aware attention mechanism and the focal-specific loss function will also be performed to evaluate their individual contributions to the model's performance.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: We expect FocusNet to outperform existing learning-based DFF methods by achieving better depth accuracy, especially in regions with fine textures and abrupt depth changes. However, it may struggle with noisy or misleading focus cues, which could result in depth errors in such areas.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Focus Gradient Information on Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: To better understand the potential benefits of focus gradient information in learning-based DFF, we propose a series of experiments to analyze the effect of incorporating focus gradient maps as an additional input channel to existing depth estimation models. We will specifically use the FocusNet model proposed in experiment 1 as the baseline, and modify it to accept focus gradient maps as an additional input, obtaining FocusNet+FG. We will then evaluate the performance of FocusNet+FG on a range of tasks, including single-image depth estimation, focal-stack depth estimation, and ablation studies.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results of FocusNet+FG to FocusNet (from experiment 1) and the state-of-the-art SDDS model, using metrics such as mean absolute error (MAE) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) to quantify the quality of estimated depth maps.

PREDICTION: We anticipate that incorporating focus gradient maps will result in improved depth estimation accuracy, especially in regions with fine textures or complex depth structures. However, it may lead to overfitting or increased noise sensitivity if not carefully calibrated.

TITLE: Synthetic-to-Real Depth Transfer for Robust Depth-from-Focus
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of domain mismatch between synthetic and real-world data, we propose a novel synthetic-to-real depth transfer approach that leverages a generator network to translate synthetic focal-stack depth estimations to corresponding real-world depth maps. We will use a generator network, specifically designed for depth transfer, and train it using a paired dataset of synthetic and real-world focal stacks. The generator will learn to map the synthetic depth estimations to their real-world counterparts, allowing us to leverage the vast amount of synthetic data available for DFF while improving the robustness of our models to real-world variations.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our synthetic-to-real depth transfer approach to state-of-the-art GAN-based transfer methods, and evaluate its effect on real-world depth estimation performance using metrics such as MAE and PSNR.
COST: 6700
PREDICTION: We expect our synthetic-to-real depth transfer approach to improve the robustness of our DFF models to real-world variations, but it may require careful tuning of the generator network to avoid introducing new biases or artifacts.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Exploring Focal-Specific Feature Learning for Depth-from-Focus
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a novel Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model, dubbed FocusNet, specifically designed to learn focal-dependent features. FocusNet will be composed of a stacked encoder-decoder architecture where each convolutional block is followed by a focus-aware attention mechanism that computes feature importance based on the focus gradient within the image slice. During training, FocusNet will be supervised using a novel loss function that incorporates both focal-specific information from a focal stack and ground truth depth maps, with the latter obtained from a separate stereo vision system. 
CONTROLS: We will compare FocusNet against the current state-of-the-art learning-based DFF methods, including the self-supervised depth and defocus simulation (SDDS) model, and a standard baseline that uses a pre-trained all-in-focus network. Ablations of our proposed focus-aware attention mechanism and the focal-specific loss function will also be performed to evaluate their individual contributions to the model's performance.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: We expect FocusNet to outperform existing learning-based DFF methods by achieving better depth accuracy, especially in regions with fine textures and abrupt depth changes. However, it may struggle with noisy or misleading focus cues, which could result in depth errors in such areas.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Focus Gradient Information on Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: To better understand the potential benefits of focus gradient information in learning-based DFF, we propose a series of experiments to analyze the effect of incorporating focus gradient maps as an additional input channel to existing depth estimation models. We will specifically use the FocusNet model proposed in experiment 1 as the baseline, and modify it to accept focus gradient maps as an additional input, obtaining FocusNet+FG. We will then evaluate the performance of FocusNet+FG on a range of tasks, including single-image depth estimation, focal-stack depth estimation, and ablation studies.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results of FocusNet+FG to FocusNet (from experiment 1) and the state-of-the-art SDDS model, using metrics such as mean absolute error (MAE) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) to quantify the quality of estimated depth maps.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that incorporating focus gradient maps will result in improved depth estimation accuracy, especially in regions with fine textures or complex depth structures. However, it may lead to overfitting or increased noise sensitivity if not carefully calibrated.

PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of domain mismatch between synthetic and real-world data, we propose a novel synthetic-to-real depth transfer approach that leverages a generator network to translate synthetic focal-stack depth estimations to corresponding real-world depth maps. We will use a generator network, specifically designed for depth transfer, and train it using a paired dataset of synthetic and real-world focal stacks. The generator will learn to map the synthetic depth estimations to their real-world counterparts, allowing us to leverage the vast amount of synthetic data available for DFF while improving the robustness of our models to real-world variations.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our synthetic-to-real depth transfer approach to state-of-the-art GAN-based transfer methods, and evaluate its effect on real-world depth estimation performance using metrics such as MAE and PSNR.
COST: 20000
PREDICTION: We expect our synthetic-to-real depth transfer approach to improve the robustness of our DFF models to real-world variations, but it may require careful tuning of the generator network to avoid introducing new biases or artifacts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Token Similarity for MoE Routing in DiT Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the distribution of visual tokens in diffusion transformer embeddings using a set of real-world text-to-image datasets, such as DALL-E, Artbreeder, and Google's LAION-5B. We will compute the similarity between tokens using different metrics (e.g., cosine similarity, Jensen-Shannon divergence) and analyze their spatial distribution in embedding space to understand whether tokens exhibit comparable separability and organization as text tokens in language models. This analysis will help identify potential challenges for routing and expert specialization in DiT-based MoE models.
CONTROLS: Compare token similarity distributions using clustering algorithms (e.g., K Means, Hierarchical clustering) and analyze the effect of different token similarity metrics on the distribution of expert assignments.
COST: 13,320
PREDICTION: The visual tokens will exhibit complex and continuous spatial distributions, resembling patterns, edges, and textures, but lacking the clear separability of text tokens. This could imply that routing and expert specialization in MoE DiTs require a fundamentally different approach from language modeling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Token Similarity for MoE Routing in DiT Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the distribution of visual tokens in diffusion transformer embeddings using a set of real-world text-to-image datasets, such as DALL-E, Artbreeder, and Google's LAION-5B. We will compute the similarity between tokens using different metrics (e.g., cosine similarity, Jensen-Shannon divergence) and analyze their spatial distribution in embedding space to understand whether tokens exhibit comparable separability and organization as text tokens in language models. This analysis will help identify potential challenges for routing and expert specialization in DiT-based MoE models.
CONTROLS: Compare token similarity distributions using clustering algorithms (e.g., K Means, Hierarchical clustering) and analyze the effect of different token similarity metrics on the distribution of expert assignments.
COST: 40,000
PREDICTION: The visual tokens will exhibit complex and continuous spatial distributions, resembling patterns, edges, and textures, but lacking the clear separability of text tokens. This could imply that routing and expert specialization in MoE DiTs require a fundamentally different approach from language modeling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Designing Spatial Awareness for MoE Routers in DiTs
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate spatial-aware routing modules for MoE DiTs, leveraging the insights from analyzing token similarity in turn 1. Specifically, we propose using a graph neural network (GNN) type of router that models the relationships between neighboring tokens in the spatial embedding space, allowing the router to consider the local context and structure of tokens when selecting experts. We will adapt the existing DiffMoE architecture to incorporate the new spatial-aware routing scheme and evaluate its performance on text-to-image generation.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of spatial-aware routing with existing routing approaches, such as token-choice routing and expert-choice routing, and analyze the effect of different GNN architectures (e.g., Graph Attention Network, Graph Convolutional Network) on routing efficiency and expert specialization.
COST: 90,000
PREDICTION: The spatial-aware router will outperform existing routing approaches in terms of expert specialization and threshold for convergence, enabling more accurate and efficient routing decisions, and allowing MoE DiTs to better leverage the capabilities of individual experts.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Expanded Spatial Awareness for MoE Routers in DiTs
PROPOSAL: (Combines and expands 2 with a new goal) Develop and evaluate a complete system for incorporating spatial awareness and expert specialization into MoE DiTs. The system will include a GNN-based spatial-aware router (building on turn 2) and a hierarchical clustering algorithm to group nearby experts together based on their complexity and diversity of processed tokens. Additionally, we will propose a weighted assignment scheme to allow the router to dynamically adjust the number of experts assigned to each token, based on the token's spatial location, similarity, and the surrounding tokens' complexity. We will evaluate this architecture on text-to-image generation tasks and assess its performance, efficiency, and scalability.
CONTROLS: Compare the effectiveness of the proposed system with respect to state-of-the-art DiT architectures (e.g., DiffMoE, EC-DiT) and analyze the impact of different GNN architectures on routing efficiency and expert specialization, in addition to testing multiple clustering and weighting methods.
COST: 150,000
PREDICTION: The system will clearly demonstrate improved efficiency, scalability, and quality of generated images, setting a new standard for MoE DiTs, but the evaluation might identify limitations in handling images with highly variable token densities or portions with meaningful patterns.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Expanded Spatial Awareness for MoE Routers in DiTs
PROPOSAL: (Maintains the previous goal, with refinements) Develop and evaluate an advanced spatial-aware router with attention on adaptive clustering and weighted assignment. We will integrate a Graph Attention Network with continuous clustering using agglomerative clustering based on a similarity metric (e.g., Jensen-Shannon) to form groups of experts with diverse and comparable processing requirements. Additionally, a learnable per-token weighting scheme will be implemented, taking into account spatial context, expert specializations, and the complexity level of tokens for dynamically adjusting the assignment of experts to tokens. This architecture will be evaluated in text-to-image generation and compared to state-of-the-art DiT architectures and existing routing strategies.
CONTROLS: Compare the effectiveness of various graph neural network variants and different aggregated metrics for spatiotemporal attention, including analyzing the interplay of spatial, temporal, and inter-expert similarity.
COST: 110,000
PREDICTION: This advanced spatial-aware router will significantly reduce routing conflicts and exhibit clear expert specialization, yielding better image generation quality while maintaining a comparable computational overhead to state-of-the-art DiTs. However, further tuning and ablation analysis may be required to identify and mitigate potential over-specialization or over-clustering cases.

PROPOSAL: We introduce two metrics, overlap ratio and homogeneity rate, to quantify the degree of overlap and specialization within DiT-MoE experts. CONTROLS: We ablate the token choice routing scheme, focusing on instance-level and global token distribution to understand their relative importance.

PREDICTION: We anticipate positive correlations between high overlap, low homogeneity and lower quality outputs, with instance-level token distribution being more corrosive to specialization than global strategies.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Hierarchical Expert Routing for DiEF-MoE with Local Contextualization
REVISED PROPOSAL: Building on the hierarchical routing design, we extend the DiEF-MoE with local contextualization at the routing process. This involves incorporating context-sensitive layer relations and adaptive token selection based on local information flows to boost information exchange between experts. The goal is to achieve improved token understanding, facilitating enhanced specialization and lower accuracy floors. We propose to integrate domain-specific pretrained weights for leveraging domain knowledge in hierarchical routing and expect improved results in text-to-image synthesis.

PREDICTION: Local contextualization may lead to improved token understanding, resulting in better expert specialization and quality scores, but also requires careful tuning of trainable parameters.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Token Diversity in DiT Outputs
PROPOSAL: To identify visual token properties that could impede expert specialization, we will experimentally quantify the diversity of DiT output tokens. We will use a StyleGAN3 diffusion model as a baseline, trained on the LSUN bedroom dataset. For a given input, we will compute the token similarity matrix to assess the overall similarity structure of DiT outputs. We will also calculate the token importance weights learned by a separate T5-sentence-transformer model and use these to reorganize the outputs, analyzing whether tokens with high contrast in importance weights correlate with reduced token similarity.
CONTROLS: Dense DiT output distributions without reorganization, T5-sentence-transformer model without access to DiT outputs.
COST: 550 GPU hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe a clear ordering of token similarities and find that tokens with high importance weights indeed are more dissimilar. If our reasoning is correct, this should be a critical clue to designing more effective routing for MoE DiTs. However, if DiT output tokens exhibit an implicit hierarchical structure that does not necessarily foster specialization, things might fail.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Experimenting with Multiscale Token Analysis
PROPOSAL: To better understand how the properties of DiT tokens impact expert specialization, we will analyze token distributions across different spatial scales of the image. By applying a multi-scale convolutional neural network to the image before passing it to the DiT, we will extract a set of representative tokens at various resolutions. We will then compare the similarity structures of these tokens to examine how coarser or finer resolutions influence the emergence of distinct expert functions in MoE DiTs. Experiments will be run using ImageNet as the dataset and the MDFI-DiT as the baseline model.
CONTROLS: Experiment 1's dense DiT output distributions without reorganization, experiment 2 without multiscale token analysis.
COST: 1,800 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Analyzing token distributions across multiple scales can help identify how token attributes are embedded throughout the diffusion process, revealing insights into suitable routing strategies for MoE DiTs. However, if the application of multiscale convolution only serves to destabilize the representation of visual tokens, things might fail or lead to unfavourable results.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Experimenting with Multiscale Token Segmentation and Routing
REVISION: (proposal field updated) 
PROPOSAL: In experiment 3, we will modify the multiscale token analysis to not only examine token distributions at different scales but also develop a custom routing scheme for the MoE DiT that takes into account the presence of tokens with varying spatial resolutions. We will apply a hierarchical token segmentation process, splitting the input image into regions that each corresponds to specific spatial scales. We will then use a separate neural network to classify tokens within each segment and dispatch them to experts based on their predicted category. Experiments will be run using ImageNet as the dataset and the MDFI-DiT as the baseline model, with detailed comparisons to the original routing scheme, including studying the impact of different parameters in the hierarchical token segmentation.
CONTROLS: Experiment 1's dense DiT output distributions without reorganization, experiment 2 without hierarchical token segmentation, experiment 3 without custom routing scheme.
COST: 2,800 GPU hours
PREDICTION: This revised experiment should help identify whether exploiting multiscale tokens can lead to significantly improved performance of MoE DiTs, revealing the impact of tailored routing on specialized expert functions. However, if the custom routing scheme ends up introducing a brittle system that fails under certain input conditions or tasks, our findings might not generalize effectively.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Evaluating Token-Rejection Mechanisms for MoE DiTs
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effectiveness of token-rejection mechanisms in MoE DiTs by introducing a soft rejection token that can dynamically decide whether to keep or reject a given token's contribution to the output. We will implement and compare two types of rejection mechanisms, one based on a learnable gate and the other based on a learned binary mask. This experiment will be performed using StyleGAN3-DiT and will evaluate performance across diverse images and collections of text prompts for two settings: standard DiT and the setup involving multiscale token routing.  
CONTROLS: Experiment 1's dense DiT output distributions without reorganization, experiment 2 without t-SNE dimensionality reduction, experiment 3 without hierarchical token segmentation and custom routing scheme.
COST: 4,080 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Integrating a token-rejection mechanism into MoE DiTs can significantly improve the quality of generated images by learning how to abandon tokens that are likely to result in incorrect spatial structures. However, things might fail if the rejection mechanisms become overly restrictive or inconsistent, potentially destroying any true area of the structure generated.

TITLE: Investigating Asymmetric Token Routing: Separating Forgetting from Exploration
PROPOSAL: To gain deeper insight into token routing mechanisms and resolving the issue of expert balance in MoE DiTs, we will experiment with an asymmetric token routing approach by combining forgetting with exploration. This involves designing a novel routing scheme that controls when to retain old experts and update new knowledge within models. For a comprehensive study, we will evaluate these proposed routing strategies on large classes of images drawn from a variety of recognized collections (CIFAR-100 and ImageNet), the routing mechanism being utterly necessary and gaining results using StyleGAN3-DiT and LSUN settings and base model as reference.
CONTROLS: Experiment 1's dense DiT output distributions without reorganization, experiment 2 without t-SNE dimensionality reduction, experiment 3 without hierarchical token segmentation and custom routing scheme, and experiment 4 without token rejection mechanism.
COST: 6,020 GPU hours
PREDICTION: This new routing scheme, which combines the forgetting and exploration mechanisms, could lead to MoE DiTs that better learn knowledge distributions of high-fidelity images, mainly because it decreases the resource loading and rejects object tokens of minimal necessity. However, our analysis may encounter the obstacle of the widely variable connection characteristics within expert modules over epoch iterations if a redundant structure gets coupled through societal node copying --negatively compromising outcomes.

ACTION: REVISE 6
TITLE: Replica Exploiter MoE DiT for Enhanced Local Consistency
REVISION: 
PROPOSAL: To improve MoE DiT's ability to merge expert outputs and achieve more consistent local structures, we will focus on refining the replica exploiter module's learning process by: (1) enabling dynamic weighting of expert contributions, (2) leveraging a more sophisticated contrastive loss function for harder negatives mining, and (3) incorporating a swap regularization technique to alleviate mode collapse. ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Token Diversity in DiT Outputs
PROPOSAL: To identify visual token properties that could impede expert specialization, we will experimentally quantify the diversity of DiT output tokens. We will use a StyleGAN3 diffusion model as a baseline, trained on the LSUN bedroom dataset. For a given input, we will compute the token similarity matrix to assess the overall similarity structure of DiT outputs. We will also calculate the token importance weights learned by a separate T5-sentence-transformer model and use these to reorganize the outputs, analyzing whether tokens with high contrast in importance weights correlate with reduced token similarity.
CONTROLS: Dense DiT output distributions without reorganization, T5-sentence-transformer model without access to DiT outputs.
COST: 1,656 GPU hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe a clear ordering of token similarities and find that tokens with high importance weights indeed are more dissimilar. If our reasoning is correct, this should be a critical clue to designing more effective routing for MoE DiTs. However, if DiT output tokens exhibit an implicit hierarchical structure that does not necessarily foster specialization, things might fail.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Visualizing DiT Token Similarity through t-SNE
PROPOSAL: Building on the previous experiment, we will use t-SNE dimensionality reduction to visualize the high-dimensional token similarity matrix obtained in experiment 1. This representation will allow us to better understand the intrinsic structures and relationships between DiT tokens. We will compare the visualized token spaces for the stability transform and the diffusion process to identify regions with distinct properties. These insights can provide critical information about learning distinct expert functions for MoE DiTs.
CONTROLS: Experiment 1's dense DiT output distributions without reorganization, and a baseline t-SNE without access to token similarity matrix.
COST: 3,746 GPU hours
PREDICTION: By revealing potential cluster structures or trajectories in DiT token space, we anticipate gaining actionable insights into how DiT tokens are systematically organized. However, if t-SNE fails to preserve crucial information about the original token similarity structure, our ability to gain meaningful conclusions could be impaired.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Experimenting with Multiscale Token Analysis
PROPOSAL: To better understand how the properties of DiT tokens impact expert specialization, we will analyze token distributions across different spatial scales of the image. By applying a multi-scale convolutional neural network to the image before passing it to the DiT, we will extract a set of representative tokens at various resolutions. We will then compare the similarity structures of these tokens to examine how coarser or finer resolutions influence the emergence of distinct expert functions in MoE DiTs. Experiments will be run using ImageNet as the dataset and the MDFI-DiT as the baseline model.
CONTROLS: Experiment 1's dense DiT output distributions without reorganization, experiment 2 without multiscale token analysis.
COST: 5,380 GPU hours
PREDICTION: Analyzing token distributions across multiple scales can help identify how token attributes are embedded throughout the diffusion process, revealing insights into suitable routing strategies for MoE DiTs. However, if the application of multiscale convolution only serves to destabilize the representation of visual tokens, things might fail or lead to unfavourable results.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Experimenting with Multiscale Token Segmentation and Routing
REVISION: In experiment 3, we will modify the multiscale token analysis to not only examine token distributions at different scales but also develop a custom routing scheme for the MoE DiT that takes into account the presence of tokens with varying spatial resolutions. We will apply a hierarchical token segmentation process, splitting the input image into regions that each corresponds to specific spatial scales. We will then use a separate neural network to classify tokens within each segment and dispatch them to experts based on their predicted category. Experiments will be run using ImageNet as the dataset and the MDFI-DiT as the baseline model, with detailed comparisons to the original routing scheme.
CONTROLS: Experiment 1's dense DiT output distributions without reorganization, experiment 2 without hierarchical token segmentation, experiment 3 without custom routing scheme.
COST: 8,400 GPU hours
PREDICTION: This revised experiment should help identify whether exploiting multiscale tokens can lead to significantly improved performance of MoE DiTs, revealing the impact of tailored routing on specialized expert functions. However, if the custom routing scheme ends up introducing a brittle system that fails under certain input conditions or tasks, our findings might not generalize effectively.

TITLE: Evaluating Token-Rejection Mechanisms for MoE DiTs
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effectiveness of token-rejection mechanisms in MoE DiTs by introducing a soft rejection token that can dynamically decide whether to keep or reject a given token's contribution to the output. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Non-stationary Environments using Adaptive Exploration
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of transfer learning and adaptive exploration to enable agents to adapt to non-stationary environments. Specifically, we will use a pre-trained policy and fine-tune it using a new dataset collected from the target environment, but with a twist: the agent will use adaptive exploration to actively solicit information about the new environment, and use that information to refine its policy. We will compare the performance of agents using adaptive exploration to baseline agents that do not use it.
CONTROLS: Baseline agents trained without transfer learning and adaptive exploration, comparison with agents that use transfer learning but not adaptive exploration.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: Agents that use adaptive exploration and transfer learning are expected to adapt more quickly and robustly to non-stationary environments, as they can actively solicit information about the new environment and refine their policy accordingly. However, the effectiveness of this approach will depend on the quality of the pre-trained policy and the amount of information the agent is able to gather from the environment.

TITLE: REVISED Minimum Perturbation-based Incremental Learning (MPIL) for Offline RL
PROPOSAL: We propose MPIL, which incorporates a minimum perturbation algorithm that periodically adjusts the agent's policy by identifying areas of the observation function where updates have the smallest impact on the objective. ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Minimum Perturbation-based Incremental Learning (MPIL) for Offline RL
NUMBER: 3
PROPOSAL: We propose MPIL, which incorporates a minimum perturbation algorithm that periodically adjusts the agent's policy by identifying areas of the observation function where updates have the smallest impact on the objective. MPIL will alternate between collecting experience in the offline dataset and applying the minimum perturbation updates, while accounting for non-stationarity. We will modify our previous proposal to include the introduction of "offset buffers" that efficiently store learned offsets to stabilize the training process and reduce the frequency of updates. By doing so, we can minimize overfitting to specific episode offsets and improve the overall robustness of the agent. Additionally, we will incorporate a "prediction module" that predicts future offsets based on the agent's previous experience, allowing for more efficient and adaptive adjustment of the policy.
CONTROLS: Baseline agents trained without offset buffers, comparison with MPIL without the introduction of offset buffers and prediction module, low disengagement.
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: With the introduction of the prediction module, MPIL is expected to significantly outperform the baseline agent and the previous MPIL implementation without the prediction module, as it will be able to better handle the non-stationarity of the observation function and adapt to changing environments. However, this may come at the cost of increased computational complexity and training time.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Sample Efficiency in Non-stationary Environments
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the effectiveness of different sample efficiency techniques (e.g., importance sampling, weighted expert Q-Learning, optimistic planning) in conjunction with MPIL (Proposal 3) for handling non-stationary observation functions. By combining these techniques, we aim to further improve the robustness and adaptability of the agent in changing environments. We will compare the performance of agents using these techniques to baseline agents trained without sample efficiency techniques.
CONTROLS: Baseline agents trained without sample efficiency techniques, comparison with MPIL without sample efficiency techniques.
COST: 8100
PREDICTION: Combining sample efficiency techniques with MPIL is expected to lead to improved performance in non-stationary environments, especially in scenarios with high degrees of change. However, the specific choice and combination of techniques used is crucial, and improper selection may lead to decreased performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Non-stationary Environments using Adaptive Exploration
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of transfer learning and adaptive exploration to enable agents to adapt to non-stationary environments. Specifically, we will use a pre-trained policy and fine-tune it using a new dataset collected from the target environment, but with a twist: the agent will use adaptive exploration to actively solicit information about the new environment, and use that information to refine its policy. We will compare the performance of agents using adaptive exploration to baseline agents that do not use it.
CONTROLS: Baseline agents trained without transfer learning and adaptive exploration, comparison with agents that use transfer learning but not adaptive exploration.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: Agents that use adaptive exploration and transfer learning are expected to adapt more quickly and robustly to non-stationary environments, as they can actively solicit information about the new environment and refine their policy accordingly. However, the effectiveness of this approach will depend on the quality of the pre-trained policy and the amount of information the agent is able to gather from the environment.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Use of Model-Based Reinforcement Learning for Non-stationary Environments
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) to handle non-stationary environments. Specifically, we will use a learned model of the environment to predict the future outcomes of actions, and use this model to plan and execute actions in the presence of changing dynamics. We will compare the performance of MBRL agents to baseline agents using model-free RL.
CONTROLS: Baseline agents trained using model-free RL, comparison with agents that use MBRL but with a static model.
COST: 13500
PREDICTION: MBRL agents are expected to perform better than baseline agents in non-stationary environments, as they can adapt to changing dynamics by updating their model. However, the effectiveness of MBRL will depend on the quality of the learned model and the ability of the agent to update it effectively.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Unified Framework for Handling Non-stationarity in Offline RL
PROPOSAL: We will develop a unified framework that combines the strengths of different approaches for handling non-stationarity in offline RL. This framework will incorporate elements from MPIL, transfer learning with adaptive exploration, and MBRL, and will provide a flexible and adaptive mechanism for handling changing dynamics. We will evaluate the performance of the framework on a range of tasks and compare it to state-of-the-art approaches.
CONTROLS: Baseline agents trained using individual approaches (MPIL, transfer learning with adaptive exploration, MBRL), comparison with agents trained using a combination of these approaches.

However, the effectiveness of the framework will depend on the quality of the individual components and the ability to effectively combine them.

TITLE: Experimental Evaluation of amortized feature learning for non-stationary observation functions
PROPOSAL: Implement the widely used deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) algorithm and its twin-delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) variant to learn, offline, a deterministic policy that maps states to actions, through a feature extractor that also maps static, noisy observation outcomes to a stationary latent space. Then, amplify the feature extractor's output with an additive offset adjustment learned under amortized meta-objective optimization, aiming to find an offset-invariant policy.

PREDICTION: This method should provide robustness to some simple, slowly evolving per-episode offsets; however, it might fail with abrupt changes, which is a big question mark given the computationally space of possible offsets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of offset-invariant learning with unknown observation shifts
PROPOSAL: Assume a stationary MDP with unknown per-dimension time-varying additive offsets in observations, and analyze the learnability of an offset-invariant policy under the total variation distance metric, focusing on the offline setting where the agent only has access to a dataset of static transitions and rewards. Using Fano's inequality and a covering argument, derive a lower bound on the sample complexity of such an offset-invariant policy in the episodic online learning setting.
CONTROLS: Compare the lower bound with existing results on the sample complexity of learning a stationary policy in the same setting, which can serve as a baseline.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: This result may provide an new perspective on why robust offline learning remains challenging for evolving observation shifts, but achieving a tighter bound may require further work.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Episodic Observation Shift Robustness in Offline RL via Auxiliary Dynamics Learning
PROPOSAL: Modify the behavior cloning (BC) algorithm by introducing a novel auxiliary dynamic model that captures the per-episode shift in observations by learning a temporal Gaussian process with a localized kernel, which captures complex, abrupt time-series patterns without requiring a specific pattern of future non-stationarity. Use this auxiliary model to augment the BC objective with an offset-invariant penalty, which encourages learning a policy that adapts to changes in the observation function across episodes.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the robustness of this method against various types of per-episode shifts and compare it with existing offline RL methods.
COST: 2880
PREDICTION: This method should be more robust to abrupt shifts in the observation function than existing offline RL methods, but optimizing the kernel of the temporal Gaussian process might require significant hyperparameter tuning, which adds uncertainty.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offset-Invariant Exploration in Offline RL with Shift-Adaptive Upper Confidence Bound
PROPOSAL: Modify the advantage-weighted architecture critic (AWAC) algorithm by introducing an offset-estimation network that, for each episode, predicts the shift in observations from the stationary offline data to the current online environment. Then, use this estimate to compute a shifted version of the advantage function, and explore with the shifted upper confidence bound (UCB) entropy regularized policy, aiming to adapt to changes in the observation function despite the lack of exploration data.
CONTROLS: Compare this method with existing AWAC variants, and evaluate its performance in robot navigation and manipulation tasks with episodic observation shifts.
COST: 3519
PREDICTION: While this method is likely to outperform AWAC in scenarios with significant episodic observation shifts, it may not provide robust performance if the estimation of the shift is inaccurate, which can easily happen in scenarios with complex time-series patterns.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporal Hierarchical Offsets Modeling for Robust Offline RL
PROPOSAL: We propose Hierarchical Offset Networks (HONs) for offline RL, which factorize the observation function into a hierarchical structure of additive offsets, using learned temporal transition dynamics among these offsets to account for episodic non-stationarity. At test time, the agent can transparently utilize this hierarchical structure to adaptively refine its perceptions and compensate for per-dimension offsets. Our HON architecture consists of a valuefunction network and an offset prediction network, using truncated backpropagation through time (BPTT) for temporal offset dynamics estimation. 
CONTROLS: We compare HONs to two baselines: (i) the Noam context discriminator [1](implemented as a standard multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with two hidden layers), which tends to learn the full stationary observation function and fails to adapt to non-stationarity; and (ii) an OUNN (Off- UNcertainty Network) that uses the offset estimates to correct the observations but does not model the temporal dynamics of offsets.
COST: 200
PREDICTION: We expect HONs to significantly outperform both baselines (by at least 10% improvement in terms of success rate) and demonstrate robustness to various non-stationary offsets in episodic control tasks, particularly when compared to OUNN. However, we predict OUNN to still perform better than Noam in tasks with moderate or frequent offset changes. 

[1]https://www.aclweb.org/anthology/P19-1417

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Per-Episode Offset Component Adaptation for Efficient Offline RL Experiments
PROPOSAL: We introduce a Per-Episode Offset Component (PEOC) sharing strategy to efficiently tackle various non-stationary offset patterns by learning a shared, high-level representation of the offset component that can be transferred and fine-tuned across episodes. This adaptability enables offline RL agents to learn efficiently from episodic development data and align with increasingly varied offsets. During an episode, the learned shared layer's representation serves as a side-input to refine the base network's observation embedding, which captures offset changes, thereby allowing the basic model to adapt quickly to new experiments. We implement the PEOC algorithm with the addition of a condensation network, which reduces the size of the shared layer's representation via zero-encoding. This leads to considerable efficiency in adaptive reinforcement learning from the same dataset.
CONTROLS: We test PEOC against local offset learning methods, naive offset implementation, and a version without the condensation network as key ablations to validate its efficiency benefits.
COST: 280
PREDICTION: Compared to other ablated settings, PEOC is expected to greatly benefit (by at least 15% per episode, though cancelling potentially negative net results) the agent's ability to adapt to shifted observations by extracting knowledge that's broadly applicable across episodes and refining it to the specifics of each learned trajectory, significantly boosting learning efficiency on non-stationary offline RL experiments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offline RL with Learning-Invariant Offset Embeddings for Non-Stationarity
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel offline RL framework, where we learn invariant embeddings of the observation function that capture the essence of non-stationarity and are agnostic to the specific patterns of offset changes. By leveraging these invariant embeddings, our method can adapt to unseen non-stationary patterns at test time without requiring additional training or fine-tuning. We achieve this by pre-training an autoencoder to extract robust, learning-invariant feature representations of the observation function, which are then used as input to a value function Q-function. This Q-function is trained to predict the expected cumulative reward under the learnt invariant feature representations, leading to a robust offline RL policy that is resilient to non-stationarity.
CONTROLS: We compare our method to standard offline RL methods, including HON, PEOC, and Baseline, and also test its ability to adapt to unseen non-stationary patterns in a variety of robotic tasks such as robot navigation and manipulation.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: We expect our method to outperform standard offline RL methods in tasks with moderate to high levels of non-stationarity, and also demonstrate its ability to adapt to novel non-stationary patterns without additional training, while HON and PEOC may perform reasonably well but will likely fail to adapt when they encounter totally unseen non-stationarity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off for Offline RL in Non-Stationary Environments
PROPOSAL: We propose an exploration-exploitation trade-off algorithm for offline RL in non-stationary environments, which balances exploration and exploitation using a novel, dataset-based metric that captures the uncertainty of the observation function. By adaptively adjusting the trade-off between exploration and exploitation, our method can adapt to the changing offset patterns and optimize its performance over time. We implement our algorithm using a Kalman filter-based exploration strategy and a Q-function-based exploitation strategy, which are integrated using a switching mechanism that depends on the dataset-based metric.
CONTROLS: We compare our method to state-of-the-art offline RL methods, including HON, PEOC, and Baseline, and also test its ability to adapt to various non-stationary patterns in robotic tasks such as robot navigation and manipulation.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: We expect our method to outperform standard offline RL methods in tasks with high levels of non-stationarity, and also demonstrate its ability to adapt to changing offset patterns over time, while HON and PEOC may perform reasonably well but may get stuck in local optima.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: CLONADE: Clustered Local Offset Network for Adapting to Non-Stationarity in Offline RL
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel method, CLONADE, that learns a representation of the observation function by clustering similar offset patterns and adapting to each cluster locally. CLONADE consists of a local offset network, which is trained for each cluster of offset patterns separately, and a cluster assignment network, which assigns each observation to the most similar cluster. By learning local representations for each cluster, CLONADE can adapt to changing offset patterns and improve its performance over time. We also propose a novel training scheme that combines the cluster assignment network with the local offset network.
CONTROLS: We compare CLONADE to standard offline RL methods, including HON, PEOC, and Baseline, and also test its ability to adapt to various non-stationary patterns in robotic tasks such as robot navigation and manipulation.
COST: 450
PREDICTION: We expect CLONADE to outperform state-of-the-art methods, and also demonstrate its ability to adapt to changing offset patterns over time, by leveraging local representations of the observation function and cluster-based adaptation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theory of Non-Stationary Offline Reinforcement Learning with Temporally Varying Offset Functions
PROPOSAL: We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of offline reinforcement learning (RL) in non-stationary environments, where the observation function evolves over time due to temporally varying offset functions. We derive bounds on the expected regret of offline algorithms when learning from stationary data collected offline and deployed to non-stationary environments. We assume that the offset function is Lipschitz with respect to time, and the update rule is restricted to a parameterized family of algorithms. The expected regret bound depends on the time horizons of the online and offline learning, and the characteristics of the Lipschitz function.
CONTROLS: We analyze the convergence properties of standard offline RL algorithms in this setting and develop new algorithms that achieve better regret bounds.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: We expect our theoretical analysis to provide new insights into the limitations of offline RL in non-stationary environments and the design of new algorithms that can adapt to changing offset patterns.

During an episode, the learned shared layer's representation serves as a side-input to refine the base network's observation embedding, which captures offset changes, thereby allowing the basic model to adapt quickly to new experiments. We implement the PEOC algorithm with the addition of a condensation network, which reduces the size of the shared layer's representation via zero-encoding. This leads to considerable efficiency in adaptive reinforcement learning from the same dataset.
CONTROLS: We test PEOC against local offset learning methods, naive offset implementation, and a version without the condensation network as key ablations to validate its efficiency benefits.

TITLE: Offline RL with Learning-Invariant Offset Embeddings for Non-Stationarity
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel offline RL framework, where we learn invariant embeddings of the observation function that capture the essence of non-stationarity and are agnostic to the specific patterns of offset changes. By leveraging these invariant embeddings, our method can adapt to unseen non-stationary patterns at test time without requiring additional training or fine-tuning. We achieve this by pre-training an autoencoder to extract robust, learning-invariant feature representations of the observation function, which are then used as input to a value function Q-function. This Q-function is trained to predict the expected cumulative reward under the learnt invariant feature representations, leading to a robust offline RL policy that is resilient to non-stationarity.

TITLE: Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off for Offline RL in Non-Stationary Environments
PROPOSAL: We propose an exploration-exploitation trade-off algorithm for offline RL in non-stationary environments, which balances exploration and exploitation using a novel, dataset-based metric that captures the uncertainty of the observation function. By adaptively adjusting the trade-off between exploration and exploitation, our method can adapt to the changing offset patterns and optimize its performance over time. We implement our algorithm using a Kalman filter-based exploration strategy and a Q-function-based exploitation strategy, which are integrated using a switching mechanism that depends on the dataset-based metric.
CONTROLS: We compare our method to state-of-the-art offline RL methods, including HON, PEOC, and Baseline, and also test its ability to adapt to various non-stationary patterns in robotic tasks such as robot navigation and manipulation.

TITLE: CLONADE: Clustered Local Offset Network for Adapting to Non-Stationarity in Offline RL
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel method, CLONADE, that learns a representation of the observation function by clustering similar offset patterns and adapting to each cluster locally. CLONADE consists of a local offset network, which is trained for each cluster of offset patterns separately, and a cluster assignment network, which assigns each observation to the most similar cluster. By learning local representations for each cluster, CLONADE can adapt to changing offset patterns and improve its performance over time. We also propose a novel training scheme that combines the cluster assignment network with the local offset network.
CONTROLS: We compare CLONADE to standard offline RL methods, including HON, PEOC, and Baseline, and also test its ability to adapt to various non-stationary patterns in robotic tasks such as robot navigation and manipulation.

PREDICTION: We expect CLONADE to outperform state-of-the-art methods, and also demonstrate its ability to adapt to changing offset patterns over time, by leveraging local representations of the observation function and cluster-based adaptation.

We also propose a novel meta-update scheme that combines the updates from the agent's experience and the meta-learner's optimization.

PROPOSAL: We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of offline reinforcement learning (RL) in non-stationary environments, where the observation function evolves over time due to temporally varying offset functions. We derive bounds on the expected regret of offline algorithms when learning from stationary data collected offline and deployed to non-stationary environments. We assume that the offset function is Lipschitz with respect to time, and the update rule is restricted to a parameterized family of algorithms. The expected regret bound depends on the time horizons of the online and offline learning, and the characteristics of the Lipschitz function.

TITLE: Multi-Modal Learning of Offset Representations
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-modal learning approach that leverages the availability of partially observable information at test time, such as past offset values or auxiliary sensor readings, to improve the estimation of per-dimension additive offsets. This is achieved by learning a neural network that takes a concatenation of different modalities as input and outputs a probability distribution over potential offset values.
CONTROLS: We compare our method to a variant of the previous proposal (Adaptive Shift Estimation via Context-Conditioned Embeddings) that only uses the main observation data, as well as to a standard state-estimation method (e.g., Kalman filter) with a learned transition model.

PREDICTION: Our approach should perform better than the previous proposal on tasks with limited or no past offset information, but may be computationally more expensive and require more data to train; we also expect it to fail if the auxiliary sensor readings or past offset values are noisy or biased.

TITLE: Online-Offline Learning Synthesis for Non-Stationary RL
PROPOSAL: We propose an online-online learning synthesis approach that combines the benefits of offline learning with the adaptability of online learning. Our method trains an agent offline using a dataset that includes simulated scenarios with various shift patterns, and then adapts this agent online by incorporating new observations and rewarding the agent for its ability to compensate for non-stationarity.
CONTROLS: We compare our method to the original Adaptive Shift Estimation via Context-Conditioned Embeddings and Multi-Modal Learning of Offset Representations proposals, as well as to a standard online RL baseline.
COST: 13320
PREDICTION: Our approach should improve offline RL performance in scenarios with sudden and unexpected changes in the observation function, and should be particularly effective in adapting to novel scenarios beyond those seen during offline training; however, it may require significant online data to adapt and may not transfer well to cases with partially observable environments.
