PROPOSAL: We revise the Multi-Modal Learning of Offset Representations proposal to incorporate knowledge distillation, which helps to transfer knowledge from a teacher network to a student network. The teacher network is trained on a large dataset, while the student network is trained on a smaller, shifted dataset, making it more efficient for edge devices or resource-constrained environments.
CONTROLS: We compare the revised method to the original Multi-Modal Learning of Offset Representations proposal, as well as to a standard online RL baseline with a learned teacher-student distillation.

PROPOSAL: We propose an online-online learning synthesis approach that combines the benefits of offline learning with the adaptability of online learning. PROPOSAL: We propose a meta-learning approach to optimize offset prediction under various non-stationary shift patterns. Our method trains a neural network to predict the offsets for a set of predefined "meta-training" tasks, and then meta-trains itself to generalize to new, unseen tasks with novel shift patterns.

PROPOSAL: We propose a graph-structured model that represents the non-stationary offset dynamics as a temporal graph, where each node represents a time step and each edge represents the relation between two consecutive time steps. PROPOSAL: We revise the Graph-Structured Model for Representing Non-Stationary Offset Dynamics proposal to incorporate a latent graph attention network, which enables the model to selectively focus on the most informative nodes and edges in the temporal graph representation. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Visual Reasoning with Temporally-Conditioned Attention
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel temporally-conditioned attention mechanism (TCA) that splits the visual reasoning process into a sequence of temporally correlated steps, reducing the computational burden of traditional autoregressive sequence generation. TCA discretizes the reasoning process into intervals, where each interval attends to a portion of the visual history within a warped temporal window, rather than the full history. This design reduces the quadratic complexity of autoregressive sequence modeling and allows for more efficient transfer of contextual information across steps. We apply TCA to our proposed multi-modal Chain-of-Thought (mCoT) model, which integrates this attention mechanism with a parallel image encoder to produce coherent visual state transitions.
CONTROLS: We compare TCA-mCoT to a baseline that employs standard autoregressive sequence generation within a modified version of CoT. Additionally, we investigate the effectiveness of TCA when combined with reinforcement learning to optimize mCoT's performance on visually grounded tasks.
COST: 125
PREDICTION: TCA-mCoT should achieve faster inference times and improved performance on tasks such as visual question answering and jigsaw puzzle solving, compared to the baseline. However, our model might struggle with complex tasks requiring high-capacity visual reasoning, due to the reduced contextual scope of TCA.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Training with Visually-Grounded Contrastive Loss
PROPOSAL: To address training instability caused by mismatched cross-modal dynamics, we introduce a visually-grounded contrastive loss (VGC) that encourages mCoT to learn effective visual reasoning without depending on separate image or video generators. VGC defines a visual similarity metric that evaluates the consistency between consecutive visual state transitions, computed based on features extracted from the parallel image encoder. During training, VGC augments the standard CoT loss function, pushing mCoT to generate coherent sequence cycles where correct intermediate reasoning steps lead to realistic and meaningful visual outcomes.
CONTROLS: We experiment with VGC applied to mCoT under both standard autoregressive sequence generation and with temporally-conditioned attention. For comparison, we also implement a baseline CoT model with standard autoregressive generation and a separate visually grounded decoder.
COST: 183
PREDICTION: VGC should significantly improve convergence speeds and generalization on visually grounded tasks such as instruction-based image editing and landscape image generation from topographic contour maps, but may face challenges when visual similarity becomes ambiguous (e.g., due to object occlusion or perspective).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient Accumulation for Long-Range Multi-Modal Dependency Modeling
PROPOSAL: Given the exploding sequence length issue in long multi-modal reasoning chains, we propose a novel gradient accumulation strategy for stabilizing the optimizer and improving convergence speed. Our method, termed 'Masquerade,' averages the gradients over a smaller sub-chain length at each step, preventing the optimizer from being hijacked by the noisy gradients of the full sequence. We demonstrate that 'Masquerade' enables efficient learning of complex multi-modal reasoning chains without sacrificing performance on reasoning-intensive tasks such as geometry and jigsaw solving.
CONTROLS: To validate the efficiency and effectiveness of 'Masquerade,' we apply it to both temporally-conditioned attention and standard autoregressive sequence generation within mCoT. As controls, we use vanilla gradient descent and a checkpoint-based averaging (CPA) gradient accumulation technique for direct comparison.
COST: 142
PREDICTION: 'Masquerade' should successfully reduce the quadratic complexity of training long multi-modal reasoning chains, improving convergence rates and enabling stable training of models on visually grounded tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Incorporating Hierarchical Reasoning into Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought with Progressively Constructed Priors
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the efficiency and effectiveness of hierarchical neural models in text processing, we extend mCoT by incorporating progressively constructed hierarchical priors into its visual reasoning module. These priors are constructed through analyzing and structuring the reasoning history, which is then used to guide the visual reasoning process. This formulation helps mCoT capture long-range context within the reasoning chain and reduces the dependency on temporally correlated information, thereby improving reasoning over entire scenes and scenarios.
CONTROLS: We experiment with our hierarchical reasoning module under standard autoregressive generation and temporally-conditioned attention in mCoT, comparing its performance to a baseline relying solely on flattened reasoning chains, as well as an atlas-based method around visual memoization and visual component evaluation in configuring architectural scenes.
COST: 208
PREDICTION: The incorporation of hierarchical priors should enable mCoT to more effectively manage complexity in long scenarios, such as navigating through real-world environments or composing artistic images.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Evaluating and Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: As the number of reasoning steps increases, models may suffer from catastrophic forgetting, where previously learned knowledge is lost. This proposal aims to identify and mitigate the issue by designing a forgetting-aware loss function and incorporating meta-learning approaches to adapt to changing visual-textual tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard loss functions for CoT, Baseline 2: meta-learning approaches without forgetting-aware components, Ablation: removing forgetting-aware loss.
COST: 1440
PREDICTION: Our approach will significantly reduce catastrophic forgetting, enabling models to learn from a sequence of visual-textual tasks and improving overall performance on a range of downstream applications.

TITLE: Teacher-Student Framework for Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: This proposal presents a teacher-student framework for multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning, where a student model is trained to mimic the reasoning steps of a teacher model on a variety of visual-textual tasks. Our framework can help improve the coherence and robustness of CoT models.

TITLE: Efficient Parallelization of Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Conditional Augmented Routing
PROPOSAL: We introduce Conditional Augmented Routing (CAR) as a novel method for unified multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning. CAR employs a hierarchical sequence-to-sequence model with self-attention augmented routing, allowing the model to effectively manage long-range dependencies in both textual and visual modalities. During training, we use a multi-task objective that jointly optimizes text-based reasoning accuracy and image quality. Our approach enables the model to generate explicit visual state transitions while maintaining coherence and stability in reasoning flows.
CONTROLS: We compare CAR against a strong hybrid baseline consisting of T5_large for text reasoning and a Stargan2++ model for visual generation.
COST: 14400
PREDICTION: Our model should achieve significant improvements in tasks like visual question answering and jigsaw puzzle solving, while maintaining competitive image quality and preserving coherent reasoning flows in tasks like reasoning-driven text-to-image generation. It may struggle with high-complexity tasks like landscape image generation from topographic contour maps, where generating coherent and diverse image variations can be more challenging.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Neural Architecture for Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We design a efficient neural architecture, dubbed MLaTTE (Multi-Modal Linear-Transposed T-written Extension), to alleviate the computational burden of multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning. MLaTTE incorporates a linear transformer layer hierarchy, a split-transformer module for efficient image-text interaction, and a feature-rich graph attention unit to capture complex relationships between visual and textual modalities. Such architectural innovations enable faster exploration of visual state transitions and reduced dependencies, thereby reducing the quadratic growth of sequence lengths during inference and improving training stability.
CONTROLS: We compare MLaTTE against CAR (our existing proposal) and a state-of-the-art visual transformer-based baseline (ViT-B16) to demonstrate its effectiveness in tasks like visual question answering and jigsaw puzzle solving.
COST: 21600
PREDICTION: MLaTTE should speed up inference time by at least 30% and improve training stability by reducing the impact of long-range dependencies. However, effective training of MLaTTE may require more careful tuning of hyperparameters, and it may struggle with high-complexity tasks that demand extremely long reasoning chains, such as landscape image generation from topographic contour maps.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Semi-Supervised Learning for Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We propose a semi-supervised learning framework to leverage both labeled and unlabeled data for training multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning models. Specifically, we utilize a multi-modal CL4 (Constrastive Learning with margin adjustment, Clustering, Fourthtask (quality control): data augmentation by reprojecting numeric outputs into images) method to generate pseudo-annotations for unlabeled data pairs, which are then matched and combined with actual supervisory signals from labeled pairs. Our semi-supervised framework should improve the robustness and adaptability of our models to diverse tasks and environments.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our model against a supervised baseline trained on only labeled pairs, and investigate the impact of varying amounts of unlabeled data on our framework's robustness.
COST: 28800
PREDICTION: This semi-supervised approach should lead to around 10-20% better performance on reasoning-intensive tasks and significant improvements in generalizability and robustness on unseen datasets and environments. Its effectiveness might be compromised if unlabeled datasets contain significant noise or irrelevant information, which could obscure the pseudo-annotations and thereby undermine the entire framework's benefits.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Explanability-Aware Training for Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel framework, dubbed EAT (Explanability-Aware Training), to improve the interpretability and trustworthiness of multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning models. EAT incorporates an attention-awaregrad- loss module to encourage the model to focus on relevant information and highlight the importance of each reasoning step. Additionally, we develop an explainability-based auxiliary task to evaluate the model's ability to provide clear and coherent explanations for its outputs.
CONTROLS: We compare EAT against a strong baseline consisting of a state-of-the-art reasoning framework without explicit explainability awareness, and investigate the impact of varying levels of explainability awareness on the model's performance and trustworthiness.
COST: 64800
PREDICTION: Our EAT framework should enhance the model's ability to provide clear and coherent explanations for its outputs, leading to improved trustworthiness and interpretability. However, if the model lacks sufficient training data or has a complex reasoning process, it may struggle to generate accurate explanations, potentially compromising the overall performance of the EAT framework.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Heterogeneous Attention Graphs
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel architecture, dubbed MHCGR (Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Heterogeneous Attention Graphs), that incorporates a heterogeneous attention graph to capture complex interactions between different modalities and reasoning steps. Our framework uses a graph neural network to learn the attention weights between different modalities and a sequence-to-sequence model to generate the final output. We also introduce a novel training objective that encourages the model to attend to relevant information at each reasoning step.
CONTROLS: We compare MHCGR against a strong baseline consisting of a state-of-the-art multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning model and investigate the impact of varying attention graph structures on the model's performance.
COST: 86400
PREDICTION: Our MHCGR framework should improve the model's ability to capture complex interactions between different modalities and reasoning steps, leading to better performance on a range of multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning tasks. However, if the attention graph structure is too complex or the model lacks sufficient training data, it may struggle to learn effective attention weights, potentially compromising the overall performance of the MHCGR framework.

TITLE: "Unified Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Compressed Visual Intermediates"
PROPOSAL: We investigate enabling unified multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning through a novel token compression technique that condenses visual intermediates, enabling efficient generation and consumption of visual information during reasoning. Specifically, we use a learned visual tokenizer to compress image encodings into a more compact format, reducing the number of visual tokens required for each step by a factor of 10. We modify the popular text-based transformer model, T5, to accommodate both text and compressed visual sequences, and optimize the compressed visual tokenization using a dedicated decoder.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the base T5 model and two variants: (1) an ablated version without visual token compression, and (2) a separate image generator coupled with the T5 model.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: We expect our unified model to achieve state-of-the-art results on reasoning-intensive tasks, with significantly reduced training time and improved inference efficiency, while maintaining competitive performance on visual question answering and image generation tasks.

TITLE: "Stable Training of Unified Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Models"
PROPOSAL: To mitigate long-range dependency modeling and optimization instability, we propose a training regimen that stabilizes the interplay between text and visual modalities. Specifically, we employ a Temperature Schedule (TS) to regulate model attention, gradually increasing the temperature to relax attention weights, while employing curriculum learning to progressively increase the difficulty of visual token compression. We also incorporate an auxiliary loss to encourage paired text-visual completions. We implement this approach using the well-established CLIP-ViT tokenizer for image encoding.
CONTROLS: We compare our TS regimen to standard training and ablate the TS itself and the auxiliary loss.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: Our TS regimen helps improve model generalization and crossover performance across tasks, while yielding competitive performance on reasoning-intensive tasks. Challenges may arise when fine-tuning for tasks with minimal visual overlaps.

TITLE: "Unified Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Reasoning-Driven Text-to-Image Generation"
PROPOSAL: We extend our unified multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning approach to reasoning-driven text-to-image generation tasks, where the model must reason about both the visual content and the generation of plausible images. We fine-tune our compressed visual tokenizer and unary attention mechanism on the COCO Captions dataset and the Benchmark for Evaluating Image Generation and Editing, and evaluate performance on a curated subset of COCO images suitable for creative editing and regeneration. Our approach seeks to capture task specificity by integrating detailed scene graphs into our reasoning process. Our visual tokenizer will generate mid-level visual representations consistent with the given instruction terms and identify which images provided will be acceptable.
CONTROLS: We compare our unified model to the DM-GAN and DALL-E 2 state-of-the-art models, as well as an ablation of our visual tokens and scene graph encoder.
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: Our unified model achieves state-of-the-art results on creative image editing and regeneration, with improvements in terms of task-specific visual tokenization, while requiring fewer shots to learn and train on compared to other generative adversarial networks targets. The challenge will be incorporating scene graph structures without sacrificing efficiency when handling distractors.

TITLE: "Unified Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Compressed Visual Intermediates"
PROPOSAL: We investigate enabling unified multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning through a novel token compression technique that condenses visual intermediates, enabling efficient generation and consumption of visual information during reasoning. Specifically, we use a learned visual tokenizer to compress image encodings into a more compact format, reducing the number of visual tokens required for each step by a factor of 10. We modify the popular text-based transformer model, T5, to accommodate both text and compressed visual sequences, and optimize the compressed visual tokenization using a dedicated decoder.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the base T5 model and two variants: (1) an ablated version without visual token compression, and (2) a separate image generator coupled with the T5 model.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: We expect our unified model to achieve state-of-the-art results on reasoning-intensive tasks, with significantly reduced training time and improved inference efficiency, while maintaining competitive performance on visual question answering and image generation tasks.

PROPOSAL: To mitigate long-range dependency modeling and optimization instability, we propose a training regimen that stabilizes the interplay between text and visual modalities. Specifically, we employ a Temperature Schedule (TS) to regulate model attention, gradually increasing the temperature to relax attention weights, while employing curriculum learning to progressively increase the difficulty of visual token compression. We also incorporate an auxiliary loss to encourage paired text-visual completions. We implement this approach using the well-established CLIP-ViT tokenizer for image encoding.
CONTROLS: We compare our TS regimen to standard training and ablate the TS itself and the auxiliary loss.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: BackTranslate and Interleave Refinement for Efficient Unified CoT Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptation to the existing Unified CoT model, which incorporates back-translation to mitigate the quadratic growth in sequence lengths and interleaving refinement steps to stabilize training and improve performance. Specifically, we append back-translation steps between text-and-image refinement steps, allowing the model to regenerate and refine text and images in a controlled manner. Through experiments on the given real-world benchmarks, we expect to see improved performance on reasoning-intensive tasks such as jigsaw puzzle solving, landscape image generation from topographic contour maps, and instruction-based image editing, while achieving a significant reduction in training and inference times compared to standard autoregressive generation.
CONTROLS: Baseline models include vanilla Unified CoT, Uniform Refining model without back-translation (our initial experiments), and Refine and Append model that interleaves refinement steps without back-translation.
COST: 6700
PREDICTION: Improved performance on reasoning-intensive tasks, while achieving a 30% reduction in training and inference times, due to more efficient interleaving of textual and visual refinement steps. Back-translation might fail to improve the model's ability to learn long-range dependencies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: BackTranslate and Interleave Refinement for Efficient Unified CoT Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptation to the existing Unified CoT model, which incorporates back-translation to mitigate the quadratic growth in sequence lengths and interleaving refinement steps to stabilize training and improve performance. Specifically, we append back-translation steps between text-and-image refinement steps, allowing the model to regenerate and refine text and images in a controlled manner. Through experiments on the given real-world benchmarks, we expect to see improved performance on reasoning-intensive tasks such as jigsaw puzzle solving, landscape image generation from topographic contour maps, and instruction-based image editing, while achieving a significant reduction in training and inference times compared to standard autoregressive generation.
CONTROLS: Baseline models include vanilla Unified CoT, Uniform Refining model without back-translation (our initial experiments), and Refine and Append model that interleaves refinement steps without back-translation.
COST: 20000
PREDICTION: Improved performance on reasoning-intensive tasks, while achieving a 30% reduction in training and inference times, due to more efficient interleaving of textual and visual refinement steps. Back-translation might fail to improve the model's ability to learn long-range dependencies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leveraging Image Diffusion Models for Stable Multi-Modal Training
PROPOSAL: To address the training instability issue, we propose to utilize image diffusion models for image encoding and decoding, which can significantly reduce the impact of mismatched cross-modal dynamics and stabilize the training process. By integrating diffusion models into the Unified CoT architecture, we can generate more coherent and stable intermediate visual states, ultimately leading to better performance and generalization on tasks such as visual question answering and reasoning-driven text-to-image generation.
CONTROLS: Experiment with standard autoregressive generation, diffusion models alone, and a baseline Unified CoT model without diffusion models. Compare performance and stability across different tasks and training setups.
COST: 32000
PREDICTION: Improved stability and generalization of the Unified CoT model, especially on tasks that require long and compositional reasoning chains. However, might introduce additional computational overhead, affecting performance on demanding hardware.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Leveraging Image Diffusion Models for Stable Multi-Modal Training (Modified)
REVISED PROPOSAL: In addition to using image diffusion models for image encoding and decoding, we will further enhance the model by incorporating latent space diffusion for bridging the gap between text and image representations. This involves learning a cross-modal mapping between text embeddings and image features in the latent space, which can help the model better understand and generate visual content from text-based reasoning steps.
CONTROLS: Experiment with standard autoregressive generation, diffusion models alone, latent space diffusion alone, and the combined model. Compare performance, stability, and ability to learn cross-modal relationships.
COST: 40000
PREDICTION: Improved performance and generalization on tasks that require bridging the text and image modality spaces, such as text-to-image synthesis and visual question answering. However, might lead to increased training instability and difficulty in recovering meaningful visual representations if the cross-modal mapping is not properly defined.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Reasoning with a Modular Unified CoT Model
PROPOSAL: To better tackle complex visual and reasoning tasks, we propose a hierarchical reasoning framework based on modular Unified CoT components. The model consists of multiple reasoning blocks, each responsible for resolving a specific task or segment, thereby breaking down the problem into more manageable sub-tasks. This approach can facilitate more efficient and stable training, as well as improve the model's ability to handle tasks with varying degrees of complexity and the need for conditional reasoning.
CONTROLS: Experiment with a baseline Unified CoT model, hierarchical reasoning alone, and a modular model that combines hierarchical reasoning with the previously proposed back-translation and interleaving refinement. Compare performance, stability, and efficiency across different task complexities and requirements.
COST: 45000
PREDICTION: Improved performance and stability on complex tasks, such as jigsaw puzzle solving and instruction-based image editing, when using hierarchical reasoning and a modular model architecture. However, might lead to overfitting to task-specific capabilities, diminishing the model's ability to generalize across tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-Aware Embeddings for Improved Cross-Modal Understanding
PROPOSAL: We propose incorporating task-aware embeddings into the Unified CoT model to better facilitate task-specific cross-modal understanding and knowledge representation. These embeddings capture relevant information about the task, such as required visual features and textual relationships, and are learned in conjunction with the text and image encoders. This can lead to more effective text-and-image generation, as well as improved performance on tasks that rely heavily on task-specific understanding.
CONTROLS: Experiment with task-aware embeddings alone, standard Unified CoT model, and a combined model that incorporates task-aware embeddings with the hierarchical reasoning framework. Compare performance and effectiveness across different tasks and training setups.
COST: 55000
PREDICTION: Improved performance on tasks that rely on task-specific understanding, such as visual question answering and reasoning-driven text-to-image generation, when using task-aware embeddings. However, might introduce additional computational overhead and require careful tuning to avoid Task specific overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attention-Based Cross-Modal Graph Reasoning
PROPOSAL: To better capture complex relationships between text and image representations, we propose integrating an attention-based cross-modal graph reasoning component into the Unified CoT model. This component allows the model to learn and represent graph-structured relationships between text and image features, facilitating more efficient and effective text-and-image generation.
CONTROLS: Experiment with attention-based cross-modal graph reasoning alone, standard Unified CoT model, and a combined model that incorporates graph reasoning with the hierarchical reasoning framework and task-aware embeddings. Compare performance and effectiveness across different tasks and training setups.
COST: 70000
PREDICTION: Improved performance on tasks that rely on complex relationships between text and image features, such as instruction-based image editing and landscape image generation from topographic contour maps, when using attention-based cross-modal graph reasoning. However, might lead to increased computational overhead and require careful tuning to avoid overfitting to task-specific relationships.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient-Based Knowledge Distillation for Efficient Unified CoT Reasoning
PROPOSAL: To further improve the efficiency and maintain performance of the Unified CoT model, we propose applying gradient-based knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from the full-size teacher model to a smaller student model. By learning the gradients between the teacher and student models, we can effectively reduce the computational overhead while preserving the reasoning capabilities of the Unified CoT model.
CONTROLS: Experiment with gradient-based knowledge distillation alone, standard Unified CoT model, and a combined model that incorporates knowledge distillation with the hierarchical reasoning framework, task-aware embeddings, and attention-based cross-modal graph reasoning. Compare performance, efficiency, and accuracy across different tasks and training setups.
COST: 90000
PREDICTION: Significant improvement in efficiency (reduced computational overhead by at least 40%) while maintaining or slightly reducing the performance on reasoning-intensive tasks when applying gradient-based knowledge distillation. However, might lead to loss of some reasoning capabilities if the model is not carefully distilled.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified CoT Model with Two-Stage Training for Advancing Multi-Modal Reasoning
PROPOSAL: To improve the performance and effectiveness of the Unified CoT model on complex multi-modal reasoning tasks, we propose a two-stage training approach. The first stage involves pre-training the model on large-scale text-only and image-only datasets, while the second stage involves fine-tuning the model on specific multi-modal reasoning tasks. This approach can help the model learn robust and transferable knowledge in the first stage, which can then be further adapted to specific tasks in the second stage.
CONTROLS: Experiment with two-stage training alone, standard Unified CoT model, and a combined model that incorporates two-stage training with the hierarchical reasoning framework, task-aware embeddings, attention-based cross-modal graph reasoning, and gradient-based knowledge distillation. Compare performance and effectiveness across different tasks and training setups.
COST: 110000
PREDICTION: Improved performance and effectiveness on complex multi-modal reasoning tasks, such as jigsaw puzzle solving and landscape image generation from topographic contour maps, when using a two-stage training approach. However, might lead to increased training time and difficulty in tuning the pre-training and fine-tuning stages.

TITLE:  Evaluating Egocentric Video Question Answering with Gaze Cues
PROPOSAL: We will compare the performance of a state-of-the-art egocentric video question answering model, such as LeViT, on the EGVQA dataset with and without access to gaze information. We will also compare it against a baseline model that does not receive gaze information, but can instead utilize other visual features. We will estimate the models' performance on the EGVQA benchmark using accuracy and average recall as metrics.
CONTROLS: Baselines: LeViT without gaze, a visual feature extraction model (VFE) without gaze, and a multimodal fusion baseline that only uses visual features.

PREDICTION: Our model will achieve a significant improvement in accuracy when utilizing gaze information, with an average increase of 5-7% compared to the LeViT model without gaze. However, the improvement may be context-dependent and may not generalize well to all types of questions and scenarios.

PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the robustness of our model from proposal 1 to variations in eye-tracking gaze accuracy. We will derive a Bayesian framework for integrating gaze information into visual perception, and prove the existence of a minimum variance bound on the gain in accuracy achievable through gaze-augmentation.
CONTROLS: None.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: Our analysis will demonstrate that gaze information can provide a significant reduction in uncertainty, leading to improved robustness and accuracy in egocentric video understanding. However, the bound on the gain in accuracy may be difficult to achieve in practice due to limitations in gaze sensing and modeling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  A Study on the Limitations of Gaze-Only Egocentric Video Understanding
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the limitations of relying solely on gaze information for egocentric video understanding, by evaluating a model that uses only gaze data to predict user intentions. We will compare the performance of this model against a model that incorporates both gaze and visual features, and analyze the types of errors made by the gaze-only model.
CONTROLS: Baselines: The standard gaze-augmented egocentric video question answering model from proposal 3, a model that incorporates both gaze and visual features.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Our analysis will reveal that the gaze-only model performs poorly on tasks that require understanding of scene context, object identity, or user attention beyond gaze, highlighting the limitations of relying solely on gaze information. Despite these limitations, the gaze-only model may still perform reasonably well on simple tasks that involve specific gaze-related cues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Evaluating the Effect of Gaze Noise on Egocentric Video Question Answering Performance
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the impact of gaze noise on the performance of egocentric video question answering models, using simulated gaze data with various levels of noise and distortion. We will investigate how different gaze noise models and denoising techniques affect the model's accuracy and robustness.
CONTROLS: Baselines: A model with high-quality gaze data, a model with moderate noise and distortion, a model with strong denoising techniques.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Our evaluation will show that even moderate levels of gaze noise can significantly degrade the model's performance, highlighting the need for robust gaze sensing and denoising techniques to ensure reliable egocentric video understanding. However, our experiments may also reveal that certain denoising techniques can mitigate the effects of gaze noise, at least to some extent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Developing a Real-World Egocentric Video Question Answering Benchmark with Gaze Information
PROPOSAL: We will develop a real-world benchmark dataset for egocentric video question answering with gaze information, collected using wearable eye-tracking devices and egocentric cameras. We will establish a comprehensive evaluation protocol, including metrics for both visual and gaze-based components, and release the dataset and code to the research community.
CONTROLS: None.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: Our benchmark will become a new standard for evaluating the performance of egocentric video question answering models, providing a more realistic and challenging evaluation of gaze-augmented models in the field. However, collecting a large-scale, high-quality dataset may be challenging and time-consuming, requiring careful participant recruitment and data curation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Gaze-Augmented Egocentric Video Models
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of two baseline MLLMs (LLaMA 13B and PaLM 2) on the egocentric video question answering task without and with gaze supervision, using the Ego4D dataset with augmented gaze estimates. The models will be fine-tuned on the Ego4D trainer set with and without gaze-conditioned visual features.
CONTROLS: Using only global image frames as input; fine-tuning with synthetic gaze data instead of real gaze estimates.
COST: 330 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect significant improvements in question answering accuracy when the MLLMs are fine-tuned with gaze-conditioned visual features, indicating that gaze information is indeed beneficial for understanding user intent in egocentric videos. However, the absolute accuracy may still be lower than desired due to the limited capacity of the models to interpret gaze cues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Gaze-Augmented Egocentric Video Models
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of two baseline MLLMs (LLaMA 13B and PaLM 2) on the egocentric video question answering task without and with gaze supervision, using the Ego4D dataset with augmented gaze estimates. The models will be fine-tuned on the Ego4D trainer set with and without gaze-conditioned visual features.
CONTROLS: Using only global image frames as input; fine-tuning with synthetic gaze data instead of real gaze estimates.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect significant improvements in question answering accuracy when the MLLMs are fine-tuned with gaze-conditioned visual features, indicating that gaze information is indeed beneficial for understanding user intent in egocentric videos. However, the absolute accuracy may still be lower than desired due to the limited capacity of the models to interpret gaze cues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Gaze-Supervised Training Strategies
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of different gaze supervision strategies (e.g., gaze annotation at every frame, every 10th frame, random subset) on the fine-tuning of the LLaMA 13B and PaLM 2 models on the Ego4D dataset. We will evaluate the models' performance in answering egocentric video questions using gaze-augmented visual features.
CONTROLS: Using the same fine-tuning sets and evaluation metrics as proposal 1. Also, using a third baseline model, T5-XL, to compare its performance with the other two models.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that a more frequent or strategically selected subset of gaze annotations will lead to better performance of the models, as more comprehensive gaze supervision allows the models to better learn to interpret gaze cues. However, the models might still struggle with complex questions that require a deep understanding of user intent.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Gaze-Supervised Training Strategies
PROPOSAL: (REVISION) Modify the gaze supervision strategies to include attention-based methods for highlighting the importance of gaze-related frames in the input video. Specifically, we will mask and unmask the input visual features based on the gaze annotation and evaluate the effect on model performance.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with and without the attention-based methods. Also, compare the performance of the models with gaze annotations at different granularities (e.g., every 1st, 5th, or 10th frame).
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that attention-based methods will lead to more efficient use of gaze information and significantly improve the models' performance in answering egocentric video questions. However, the models might still struggle with understanding complex user intent, and the performance could be degraded if the gaze annotations are noisy or incorrect.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Gaze Signal Accuracy on Model Performance
PROPOSAL: Evaluate how the accuracy of the gaze signal used for training and fine-tuning affects the performance of the models on egocentric video question answering. We will use a controlled dataset with high-accuracy and low-accuracy gaze estimates and compare the performance of LLaMA 13B and PaLM 2.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the models on both datasets when using attention-based methods and when using gaze annotations at different granularities (e.g., every 1st, 5th, or 10th frame). Also, compare the performance of models fine-tuned with gaze estimates from different annotation tools.
COST: 2600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that high-accuracy gaze estimates will lead to better performance of the models, but the gain might be limited if the models are able to adapt to the low-accuracy gaze estimates. However, the performance of the models might degrade significantly if the gaze estimates are highly noisy or inaccurate.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Visual-Attention Integration for Gaze-Augmented Models
PROPOSAL: Explore the effect of integrating visual-attention mechanisms into the gaze-augmented models using attention-based methods. We will compare the performance of models using gaze signals only versus models that explicitly integrate gaze information with attention mechanisms.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of models on the Ego4D dataset with and without gaze supervision, using both attention-based methods and visual-attention integration. PREDICTION: We expect that integrating visual-attention mechanisms will improve the models' ability to understand complex user intent and efficiently use the gaze information, leading to better performance on egocentric video question answering. However, the models might still struggle with highly nuanced tasks.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of gaze-augmented models (LLaMA 13B, PaLM 2, and their variants with gaze supervision and attention-based methods) on complex egocentric tasks, such as action anticipation, scene understanding, and user interest prediction, using the Ego4D dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of models using gaze supervision with models using only global image frames as input. Also, evaluate the performance of models on free-form questions and open-ended tasks.
COST: 5500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that gaze-augmented models will outperform their counterparts using only global image frames, especially on complex egocentric tasks. However, the models might still struggle with highly nuanced or abstract questions.

TITLE: Exploring Egocentric Gaze-based MLLMs for Proactive Personalized Assistance
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of popular large language models (e.g., LLaMA, Codex) on the recent Egocentric Visual Question Answering (EVQA) benchmark, comparing their results with a gaze-observed version of the same models, which incorporate gaze-related visual features extracted using a state-of-the-art gaze estimation model.

CONTROLS: Use a popular gaze estimation model (e.g., OpenFace) to generate synthetic gaze information, and compare the performance of the gaze-aware MLLM to a baseline model trained on the original EVQA dataset without gaze information.
COST: 12960
PREDICTION: The gaze-aware MLLM should outperform the baseline model on egocentric video question answering tasks, especially those that require understanding user intent, but may need additional fine-tuning on real-world data to adapt to variability in eye tracking.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Exploring Egocentric Gaze-based MLLMs for Proactive Personalized Assistance
PROPOSAL: Modify the popular Egocentric Visual Question Answering (EVQA) benchmark to include a vision-and-language-aware object grounding component, which allows the model to infer the object of interest based on the gaze signal and question context. Then, evaluate popular large language models (e.g., LLaMA, Codex) on this modified benchmark.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the models on the original EVQA benchmark to their performance on the modified benchmark with object grounding, and investigate the importance of grounding in the models' performance.
COST: 20160
PREDICTION: The models should see significant improvements in performance with the added object grounding component, but may struggle with questions that require complex reasoning and inference over the object of interest and its context.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Validation of Egocentric Gaze-Aware MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Collect and annotate real-world egocentric video data with corresponding eye-tracking gaze information, and then evaluate the performance of a gaze-aware MLLM trained on synthetic data (from proposal 3) on this real-world dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the gaze-aware MLLM on the real-world dataset to its performance on the original EVQA benchmark, and investigate the effect of real-world variability in eye tracking on the model's performance.
COST: 19440
PREDICTION: The gaze-aware MLLM should perform well on the real-world dataset, but may require additional fine-tuning to adapt to the variability in eye tracking and real-world context, and its performance may degrade if the eye tracking data is noisy or incomplete.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Gaze Uncertainty on Egocentric MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to quantify and analyze the gaze uncertainty in the real-world egocentric video data used in proposal 4. Then, investigate how different types of gaze uncertainty (e.g., random noise, outliers, forgetting) impact the performance of the gaze-aware MLLM on the real-world dataset.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of different uncertainty types on the performance of the gaze-aware MLLM, and compare the results to a baseline model without gaze-awareness.
COST: 20736
PREDICTION: The analysis should reveal that the type and magnitude of gaze uncertainty have a significant impact on the model's performance, with some uncertainty types being more benign than others, and that the model's robustness to uncertainty can be improved through architectural and training modifications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Egocentric Visual Question Answering with Attend-BED Gesture Recognition
PROPOSAL: Develop a new model architecture that combines the gaze-aware visual attention mechanism from proposal 1 with a novel BED (Body, Eye, and Direction) gesture recognition module to infer the user's actions and intentions from the egocentric video data.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the new model on the EVQA benchmark, and compare it to the state-of-the-art models from proposal 1, with and without the BED gesture recognition module.
COST: 24416
PREDICTION: The new model should outperform the state-of-the-art models by incorporating both gaze-aware visual attention and gesture recognition, but may require a large amount of annotated data to effectively train the gesture recognition module.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Eye-Tracking Gaze-Aware MLLM Training with Synthetic Data
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel synthetic data generation method that incorporates both gaze-aware visual attention and BED gesture recognition, allowing for more realistic simulation of real-world egocentric video data with eye-tracking gaze information.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the gaze-aware MLLM trained on the new synthetic data on the EVQA benchmark, comparing it to the model trained on the original synthetic data.
COST: 29184
PREDICTION: The model trained on the new synthetic data should outperform the original model, as it is exposed to more realistic scenarios with gaze-aware visual attention and BED gesture recognition, and should provide a robust and efficient way to evaluate and fine-tune gaze-aware MLLMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Limitations of Gaze-Aware MLLMs in Adversarial Scenarios
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel adversarial attack framework to manipulate the egocentric video data and eye-tracking gaze information in ways that are difficult for the gaze-aware MLLM to detect, and evaluate the model's performance under these challenging conditions.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the gaze-aware MLLM under normal conditions to its performance under adversarial attack, and investigate the effects of different attack vectors and strengths on the model's performance.
COST: 30048
PREDICTION: The model should be vulnerable to certain types of adversarial attacks, which could compromise its performance and reliability in real-world applications, and the investigation should reveal key limitations and challenges in the design of robust gaze-aware MLLMs.

TITLE: Layer-wise Gradient Analysis for Modality-Shared AR Transformers
PROPOSAL: Conduct a detailed analysis of layer-wise gradient disagreement between text and vision modalities in a modality-shared AR transformer. Utilize techniques from neural network interpretability, such as saliency maps and activation tensors, to isolate and quantify the disagreement at the layer level. Employ datasets like CLEVR-Chat and Captions for VQA for text-to-image generation and visual question answering tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art VLMs and AMTs, such as Mixture-of-Transformers, task-specific branches, and hybrids; perform ablations to identify critical components driving modality conflicts.
COST: 100
PREDICTION: Expected to reveal significant inter-modal conflicts in lower layers, with decreased disagreement up the network, especially in image-heavy tasks; struggling to control the down-weighting of input information from the dialogue text by the late layers that substantially suffer from degradation when discriminative factors, such as, object interiors ucwords that aren't with images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Resolution Modality Embeddings for AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Introduce a multi-resolution modality embedding module that learns task-specific modality representations at different scales, enabling the AR UMM to capture both low-level visual details and high-level contextual information. Train this module on diverse datasets such as COCO, VQA v2.0, and FFHQ for adaptation across various text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image synthesis tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art VLMs and AMTs with fixed modality embeddings; evaluate the effectiveness of the multi-resolution representation by applying it to a range of tasks and assessing its ability to adapt to new tasks; compare to a baseline with only a single resolution.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: Expected to exhibit improved performance on tasks requiring detailed visual understanding and contextual reasoning, while maintaining model simplicity and interpretability; struggling to adapt to tasks requiring extensive domain-specific knowledge.

TITLE: Early Stopping and Real-Time Feedback for Training AR UMMs

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Diagnostic Analysis of Modality Conflicts in Shared Autoregressive Transformers
PROPOSAL: Investigate how text and image gradients disagree in a shared AR transformer by training a state-of-the-art AR UMM (e.g. Diffusers-PyTorch) on a mixed dataset of text and image tokens, separately and jointly, using monitoring metrics like gradient norm, cross-entropy loss, and perplexity on both modalities. CONTROLS: Compare to training the UMM on each modality separately to establish a baseline of modality-alternating training.

PREDICTION: This analysis will reveal how the disagreements between text and image gradients change across the network depths, indicating which layers are more susceptible to modality conflicts. However, the gradient convergence may be slow, potentially failing if the chosen training steps are too few for joint optimization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-Wise Inter-Modal Gradient Conflict Analysis
PROPOSAL: We will propose a novel method to quantify the disagreement between text and vision gradients at each layer of an autoregressive transformer-based UMM. This method, called Gradient Diffusion Analysis (GDA), will compare the mean squared difference between modality-shared transformer outputs for pairs of input images/texts. To control for the influence of modality-specific features, we will analyze this difference as a function of layer depth, using representations from intermediate and output layers of the transformer.
CONTROLS: We will compare GDA to existing analytical methods for measuring gradient conflicts, and demonstrate its effectiveness using a set of perturbed images that nonetheless contain consistent semantic information.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: Our GDA method will reveal dramatic differences in inter-modal conflict along the depth of the transformer, particularly in the intermediate layers, and we expect GDA to perform significantly better at predicting these conflicts than the baseline methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding and Minimizing Inter-Modal Gradient Conflicts
PROPOSAL: Building on the insights from GDA, we will investigate how to minimize inter-modal gradient conflicts by adjusting the training procedure of the autoregressive UMM. Specifically, we will experiment with balancing the learning rates and optimizer parameters for text and visual modalities, as well as incorporating a momentum term to encourage adversarial optimization between the two gradients. We will also explore domain adaptation techniques, such as sharing only the transformation layers across both modalities to reduce inter-modal conflicts.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed methods to several baseline training procedures, including early stopping, learning rate schedules, and AdamW optimization, using a variety of benchmark datasets for text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image editing.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in training efficiency and performance when minimizing inter-modal gradient conflicts, but may encounter diminishing returns due to over-regularization if the balancing terms are not properly tuned.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modality-Shared Load Balancing for Autoregressive UMMs
PROPOSAL: Building on the insights from our previous experiments, we will introduce a novel method for balancing the computational load across text and visual modalities during training of autoregressive UMMs. Our method, called Modality-Shared Load Balancing (MSLB), will dynamically adjust the proportion of computational resources dedicated to each modality based on the individual gradients' magnitudes, and we will implement it within a modified AdamW optimizer.
CONTROLS: We will compare MSLB to standard AdamW and early stopping, as well as multiple ablation studies on different momentum schedules and resource allocation strategies.
COST: 21000
PREDICTION: Our MSLB method should improve convergence speed and stability during training, and will be especially effective in cases where the training data presents a significant imbalance between the two modalities.

PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed methods (Gradient Diffusion Analysis, modality-conditional finetuning, and modality-shared load balancing) on real-world text-to-image generation tasks, leveraging large-scale datasets like COCO-Eval and Aphorism-Photo. TITLE: Bounding Modality Conflict in StackGAN
PROPOSAL: Investigate the phenomenon of modality conflict in AR UMMs through a new theoretical framework, where we bound the extent of gradient conflict between text and image modalities in modality-shared transformer layers. CONTROLS: Use modality-shared transformer models trained on the FFHQ dataset as a baseline.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: We expect to identify key channels contributing to modality conflict and show that modality conflict tends to arise in deeper layers, but can be mitigated through modality- specific learning rates and early stopping, while observing that these techniques come at the cost of performance on individual tasks when not carefully managed.

As such, we expect theory-driven approaches to give us good insight into the empirical phenomena we are faced with.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing Inter-Modal Conflicts in Autoregressive Unified Multimodal Models
PROPOSAL: We design a suite of modularized experiments to systematically investigate the inter-modal conflicts in AR UMMs, leveraging the FLICKR8K and COCO datasets for training and testing, and the popular Cui-gan and Atariava datasets for validation and evaluation of specific fine-tuned models.
For the experiments, we will control for three baselines: 1) a randomly initialized single-modal model, 2) a pre-trained modality-shared model, and 3) an evenly-divided twin-modal model where the model's architecture is divided into two identical halves, one for each modality.
We will use the modality-shared model and evenly-divided twin-modal model to explore the differences between locally inconsistent and globally inconsistent modality conflicts. In order to quantify the modulation of inter-modal interactions along different layers, we propose to compute the cosine similarity of token representations and knowledge distillation loss across different layers of the shared transformer model.
CONTROLS: 
- Baselines 1-3 as individually mentioned
- Exclude auxiliary modules and modality-specific items
COST: 1600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By analyzing layer-wise interactions and modality-specific differences, we expect to find a high correlation between inter-modal conflict magnitude and depth discrepancies in local and global modality conflicts (70% chance).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient Conflict Regularization for Inter-Modal Learning
PROPOSAL: Building upon the findings from the previous experiment (1), we propose to develop a regularization term to mitigate inter-modal conflicts in AR UMMs during training. This term will be designed to encourage consistency in model gradients within modality-shared layers. We will use this regularization with two modulation schemes, based on trade-off between pair-wise disentanglement for encouraging structure unification and cross-modal KL-divergence for controlling explicit representation resolutions.
For validation, we will use the relaxed concept of Drift Remedy Distributional Approximation (EDDA) as the optimizer for evaluation and inspect potential scenarios of mitigation corresponding different control ratios, using standard metrics such as perplexity, BLEU and COCO instance segmentation accuracy.
CONTROLS: 
- Keep baseline models 1-3
- Provide the module with modality-shared bi-encoder before feedback term influence 
- Difference using variants setting Drift regulator controller 
COST: 13600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Achieving an average reduction of 15% in modality-specific variance in gradients along the depth of shared transformer layers (80% chance) and subsequently leading to an overall gain of 10% in validation perplexity for inter-modal tasks in sight.

TITLE: Assessing Inter-Modal Conflicts in Autoregressive Unified Multimodal Models
PROPOSAL: We design a suite of modularized experiments to systematically investigate the inter-modal conflicts in AR UMMs, leveraging the FLICKR8K and COCO datasets for training and testing, and the popular Cui-gan and Atariava datasets for validation and evaluation of specific fine-tuned models.
For the experiments, we will control for three baselines: 1) a randomly initialized single-modal model, 2) a pre-trained modality-shared model, and 3) an evenly-divided twin-modal model where the model's architecture is divided into two identical halves, one for each modality.
We will use the modality-shared model and evenly-divided twin-modal model to explore the differences between locally inconsistent and globally inconsistent modality conflicts. In order to quantify the modulation of inter-modal interactions along different layers, we propose to compute the cosine similarity of token representations and knowledge distillation loss across different layers of the shared transformer model.
CONTROLS: 
- Baselines 1-3 as individually mentioned
- Exclude auxiliary modules and modality-specific items
COST: 4800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By analyzing layer-wise interactions and modality-specific differences, we expect to find a high correlation between inter-modal conflict magnitude and depth discrepancies in local and global modality conflicts (70% chance).

TITLE: Gradient Conflict Regularization for Inter-Modal Learning
PROPOSAL: Building upon the findings from the previous experiment (1), we propose to develop a regularization term to mitigate inter-modal conflicts in AR UMMs during training. We will use this regularization with two modulation schemes, based on trade-off between pair-wise disentanglement for encouraging structure unification and cross-modal KL-divergence for controlling explicit representation resolutions.
For validation, we will use the relaxed concept of Drift Remedy Distributional Approximation (EDDA) as the optimizer for evaluation and inspect potential scenarios of mitigation corresponding different control ratios, using standard metrics such as perplexity, BLEU and COCO instance segmentation accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Weakly Supervised Training for Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We aim to explore a weakly supervised training approach for audiovisual emotion reasoning, where the model is trained to predict emotion labels from low-level audiovisual features without explicit emotion annotation. We will use a multi-task learning framework that jointly trains models to predict factual accuracy and sentiment from low-level audiovisual features. This approach can help reduce the need for expensive human annotation and provide more generalizable results.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with a strong baseline model that is trained on a smaller dataset with low-level audiovisual features and explicit emotion annotation. We will also evaluate the performance of the weakly supervised approach on a larger set of emotions and more difficult test cases.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: We expect the weakly supervised approach to achieve comparable or slightly lower performance to the strong baseline on emotion-labeling tasks, but significantly higher performance on downstream applications that require emotional intelligence, such as empathetic chatbots or affect-aware robots.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Emotion-Specific Counterfactual Evaluations for Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: To better evaluate the failure modes of MLLMs for audiovisual emotion reasoning, we propose Emotion-Specific Counterfactual Evaluations (ESCE), a novel evaluation method that generates counterfactual scenarios by manipulating specific audiovisual features or their interactions while keeping the rest of the input fixed. We will use ESCE to generate a set of counterfactual scenarios for a given input sample and evaluate the model's performance on these scenarios to assess its robustness to changes in the input.
CONTROLS: We will compare ESCE with existing evaluation methods (e.g., worst-case analysis) and baseline models that are not robust to changes in the input. We will also evaluate the effectiveness of ESCE in identifying failure modes of MLLMs for audiovisual emotion reasoning.
COST: 13320
PREDICTION: We expect ESCE to reveal the failure modes of MLLMs for audiovisual emotion reasoning, such as their tendency to over-rely on specific audiovisual features or their inability to adapt to changes in the input, and improve the robustness of MLLMs for downstream applications that require emotional intelligence.

We will use ESCE to generate a set of counterfactual scenarios for a given input sample and evaluate the model's performance on these scenarios to assess its robustness to changes in the input.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Failures of Emotion-Specific Reasoning in Audiovisual MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Evaluate a recent state-of-the-art audiovisual multimodal large language model (MLLM) called Virality on the benchmark Ang predominant affect (APA) dataset, which covers a broad range of real-world user-generated videos showing a wide distribution of emotional expressions. We will measure the likelihood of hallucinations by assigning a score to each prediction based on the ratio of perceived to actual affective evidence present in the input.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of Virality to a ablated version of itself without emotion-specific instruction tuning and to a state-of-the-art single-modal text-only model, SwitchC Vivek. We also control for the effect of using the APA dataset by considering a sentiment analysis model fine-tuned on the same dataset.
COST: 4800
PREDICTION: Expected results show that the state-of-the-art emotion-specific MLLM, Virality, struggles with accurately grounding its predictions in actual affective evidence. The likelihood of hallucinations is expected to be around 20-25% on the APA dataset, where a higher score indicates a higher likelihood of inaccurate affective reasoning. On the other hand, the sentiment analysis model will likely outperform the ablated version of Virality and be more accurate overall, validating our control.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Correlations between Language Priors and Affective Response Hallucinations
PROPOSAL: Analyze the internal knowledge graph of Virality to understand how the model's language priors influence its predictions on emotion-specific hallucinations. We will apply a graph neural network (GNN) to extract feature representations of words and phrases related to emotion-specific processes, and then use these features to explain instances of hallucinations on the APA dataset.

The text-only language model is expected to show weaker correlations, while the GNN-based explanation approach is expected to be more useful for understanding the source of affective response hallucinations than SHAP.

TITLE: Investigating Failures of Emotion-Specific Reasoning in Audiovisual MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Evaluate a recent state-of-the-art audiovisual multimodal large language model (MLLM) called Virality on the benchmark Ang predominant affect (APA) dataset, which covers a broad range of real-world user-generated videos showing a wide distribution of emotional expressions. We will measure the likelihood of hallucinations by assigning a score to each prediction based on the ratio of perceived to actual affective evidence present in the input.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of Virality to a ablated version of itself without emotion-specific instruction tuning and to a state-of-the-art single-modal text-only model, SwitchC Vivek. We also control for the effect of using the APA dataset by considering a sentiment analysis model fine-tuned on the same dataset.
COST: 14400
PREDICTION: Expected results show that the state-of-the-art emotion-specific MLLM, Virality, struggles with accurately grounding its predictions in actual affective evidence. The likelihood of hallucinations is expected to be around 20-25% on the APA dataset, where a higher score indicates a higher likelihood of inaccurate affective reasoning. On the other hand, the sentiment analysis model will likely outperform the ablated version of Virality and be more accurate overall, validating our control.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Analyze the internal knowledge graph of Virality to understand how the model's language priors influence its predictions on emotion-specific hallucinations. We will apply a graph neural network (GNN) to extract feature representations of words and phrases related to emotion-specific processes, and then use these features to explain instances of hallucinations on the APA dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare the correlations between language priors and hallucinations in Virality to those in a text-only language model, determining whether the correlations are unique to models that integrate audiovisual information. We will also evaluate the usefulness of the GNN-based explanation approach by comparing it to a state-of-the-art interpretability method, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations).

The text-only language model is expected to show weaker correlations, while the GNN-based explanation approach is expected to be more useful for understanding the source of affective response hallucinations than SHAP.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Rank Intermediate Actions with Adversarial Processes
PROPOSAL: We introduce an adversarial process reward mechanism, where a separate, learned ranker module predicts the target ranking of actions within a rollout, and our GRPO model aims to maximize the probability of the true ranking. The ranker is trained to predict the relative importance of each action, conditioned on the rollout's search history and the current partial answer. This approach leverages the theoretical results from the first proposal and enables the GRPO model to learn rankings that are both sensitive to the intermediate search steps and robust to the potential biases in the training data.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the baseline of simply using the final outcome rewards and also to a variant where the ranker module is replaced by a pre-trained language model.
COST: 4,000
PREDICTION: We expect improved sample efficiency and denser supervision for agentic search, but initial results might be sensitive to the choice of the ranker's architecture and the adversarial loss function.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Pre-Turn Prediction to Inform Dense Rewards
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel pre-turn prediction mechanism that predicts the probability of a rollout succeeding based on its previous turns' actions and the current partial answer. This prediction is used to modulate the reward signal, providing a denser supervision to the GRPO model. Specifically, we assign higher rewards to turns that show high probabilities of success and lower rewards to turns that appear to be failing. Our mechanism is trained as a separate module using cross-entropy loss, and we investigate its impact on the GRPO model's training dynamics.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the case where the pre-turn predictor is not used and also to a variant where the pre-turn prediction is applied directly to the final outcome rewards.
COST: 5,000
PREDICTION: We expect this mechanism to improve early termination detection, helping the GRPO model to learn more efficiently and from failure. However, we anticipate challenge in balancing the pre-turn reward signal with the outcome rewards to maintain a stable training process.

The ranker is trained to predict the relative importance of each action, conditioned on the rollout's search history and the current partial answer. This approach leverages the theoretical results from the first proposal and enables the GRPO model to learn rankings that are both sensitive to the intermediate search steps and robust to the potential biases in the training data.

PREDICTION: We expect improved sample efficiency and denser supervision for agentic search, but initial results might be sensitive to the choice of the ranker's architecture and the adversarial loss function.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Intrinsic Turn-Level Rewards for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel method, called Turn-Level Contrastive Learning (TLCL), to provide a dense and informative reward signal for RL training of multi-turn search agents. TLCL selects a batch of rollouts from the buffer and computes the contrastive loss between the turn-wise representations of successful and failed rollouts. The turn-wise representations are obtained by applying a query-based encoder on each turn in the rollout sequence. The reward for each turn is calculated as the logit value of the turn-wise representation with respect to the final answer class.
CONTROLS: We compare TLCL against three baselines: 1) Random Reward, where each turn receives a randomly sampled reward; 2) Outcome-Based Reward, where each rollout receives a single outcome-based reward; and 3) Group-Based Reward, where the relative rewards are normalized within groups. We also evaluate the effect of varying the contrastive loss margin and the number of sampled rollouts.
COST: 1332
PREDICTION: TLCL improves upon the baselines by 10-20% in terms of multi-turn search accuracy, but may not mitigate advantage collapse entirely. It may also benefit from additional exploration of different contrastive loss functions and hyperparameter tuning.

The revised TLCL also incorporates an early stopping criterion, which prevents the gradient updates from dominating the optimization process.

TITLE: Intrinsic Turn-Level Rewards for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel method, called Turn-Level Contrastive Learning (TLCL), to provide a dense and informative reward signal for RL training of multi-turn search agents. TLCL selects a batch of rollouts from the buffer and computes the contrastive loss between the turn-wise representations of successful and failed rollouts. The turn-wise representations are obtained by applying a query-based encoder on each turn in the rollout sequence. The reward for each turn is calculated as the logit value of the turn-wise representation with respect to the final answer class.
CONTROLS: We compare TLCL against three baselines: 1) Random Reward, where each turn receives a randomly sampled reward; 2) Outcome-Based Reward, where each rollout receives a single outcome-based reward; and 3) Group-Based Reward, where the relative rewards are normalized within groups. We also evaluate the effect of varying the contrastive loss margin and the number of sampled rollouts.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: TLCL improves upon the baselines by 10-20% in terms of multi-turn search accuracy, but may not mitigate advantage collapse entirely. It may also benefit from additional exploration of different contrastive loss functions and hyperparameter tuning.

Furthermore, we add a temperature scaling factor to the logit values, allowing the gradients to better capture the differences between successful and failed rollouts. The revised TLCL also incorporates an early stopping criterion, which prevents the gradient updates from dominating the optimization process.
CONTROLS: We compare the revised TLCL against four additional baselines: 2) TLCL without the token alignment loss; 3) TLCL without the temperature scaling factor; and 4) a version of TLCL that simultaneously optimizes the policy and the auxiliary query generator.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Default Prompts of Popular Web Search Engines as Intrinsic Rewards
PROPOSAL: Compare the agreement of search agents trained with intrinsic process rewards using the default question-answering prompts of popular web search engines (e.g. Google Search, Bing, DuckDuckGo) against extrinsically rewarded agents on multi-hop QA tasks from the WebSearch benchmarks. Use a matrix to track the alignment of the extrinsically trained policy with the web search prompts at each turn, with successes harvested as rewards for intrinsic training. This aims to investigate the hypothesis that popular web search default prompts naturally capture suitable intermediate rewards aligned with the agent's trajectory towards answer discovery. We will assess the policies learned with these prompts, and cross-validate outcomes on the OpenWebSearch (OWS) benchmark, a popular web-based search-oriented QA dataset with large-scale web data.
CONTROLS: Agents trained with outcome rewards, pre-defined process rewards using human judgements.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: If successful, this approach might detect sets of questions where default prompts yield well-aligned intermediate rewards, but performance will likely degrade for search agents which need more explicit reasoning trajectories; in some cases, “good enough” prompts might not provide sufficient supervisory signals in certain domains or tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modeling Transition Rewards with masked Token Prediction Losses
PROPOSAL: Implement a novel token-level prediction loss function for estimating intrinsic transition rewards based on grounded intermediate results. We use BART-large and T5-large to learn contextual representations of search agent turns as well as retrieved intermediate results. Then, for a given turn's state, a secondary sequence of masked tokens will be generated that are predicted as the starting point of subsequent relevant results retrieved by the search agent. Optimizing the difference between these predicted tokens and an intermediate retrieval mask corrects the contextual representations incrementally to narrow in on actionable principal facts directly accessed during subsequent turns. By tracking the historical sequence of retrieved information that each prior action progresses through, the implicit information is translated into meaningful token-level rewards during sequential reinforcement training.
CONTROLS: Agent trained using outcome-based rewards only, original prompt-based workflows incorporating hindsight reasoning on intermediate outcomes and rewards for search call operations.
COST: 14000
PREDICTION: Improvements should be evident at turn-level supervision in identifying the ambiguity of key words and forms within the final response; the difficulty would lie in requisitioning specificity and proportional token level rewards without pre-defined notions of optimal conduct since this design further splits important hidden rollouts.
