ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Default Prompts of Popular Web Search Engines as Intrinsic Rewards
PROPOSAL: Compare the agreement of search agents trained with intrinsic process rewards using the default question-answering prompts of popular web search engines (e.g. Google Search, Bing, DuckDuckGo) against extrinsically rewarded agents on multi-hop QA tasks from the WebSearch benchmarks. Use a matrix to track the alignment of the extrinsically trained policy with the web search prompts at each turn, with successes harvested as rewards for intrinsic training. This aims to investigate the hypothesis that popular web search default prompts naturally capture suitable intermediate rewards aligned with the agent's trajectory towards answer discovery. We will assess the policies learned with these prompts, and cross-validate outcomes on the OpenWebSearch (OWS) benchmark, a popular web-based search-oriented QA dataset with large-scale web data.
CONTROLS: Agents trained with outcome rewards, pre-defined process rewards using human judgements.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: If successful, this approach might detect sets of questions where default prompts yield well-aligned intermediate rewards, but performance will likely degrade for search agents which need more explicit reasoning trajectories; in some cases, “good enough” prompts might not provide sufficient supervisory signals in certain domains or tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modeling Transition Rewards with masked Token Prediction Losses
PROPOSAL: Implement a novel token-level prediction loss function for estimating intrinsic transition rewards based on grounded intermediate results. We use BART-large and T5-large to learn contextual representations of search agent turns as well as retrieved intermediate results. Then, for a given turn's state, a secondary sequence of masked tokens will be generated that are predicted as the starting point of subsequent relevant results retrieved by the search agent. Optimizing the difference between these predicted tokens and an intermediate retrieval mask corrects the contextual representations incrementally to narrow in on actionable principal facts directly accessed during subsequent turns. By tracking the historical sequence of retrieved information that each prior action progresses through, the implicit information is translated into meaningful token-level rewards during sequential reinforcement training.
CONTROLS: Agent trained using outcome-based rewards only, original prompt-based workflows incorporating hindsight reasoning on intermediate outcomes and rewards for search call operations.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Dense Process Rewards using Web-side Information
PROPOSAL: We will leverage the structure of web search results to infer rewards at every interaction turn for search agents. Specifically, we precompute a compressed representation of all possible search results for each turn, then at training time, compute a relevance score between each turn's search result and the precomputed representation. The relevance score will then be normalized across all possible turns for a given question to obtain a dense reward signal for the RL agent. The method will be applied to a variety of open-domain question answering datasets, including WebQSP and WikiQA, and compared to a baseline of outcome-based rewards.
CONTROLS: We will also compare our method against GRPO and its variants that use external oracle knowledge or reward models to judge intermediate steps.
COST: 576
PREDICTION: This approach should successfully provide a dense reward signal at peu nominal compute cost despite its non-trivial fueltionality. The improvement in RL performance, measured by search agent accuracy on final answers, may be significant, particularly in the most challenging queries.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Revising Dense Process Rewards using Web-side Information: Enriching the Turn Reward Signal using Search-result Meta-data
PROPOSAL: To further improve the relevance score computed in our previous proposal, we will enrich our search-result representation with additional meta-data such as search query popularity, answer snippet score, and ranking position. We hypothesize that incorporating these features will allow our model to better understand the quality of the intermediate search results and provide a more informative reward signal at each turn. In addition, we will investigate various aggregation methods to combine the relevance score with the enriched meta-data, such as element-wise multiplication, concatenation, and weighted sum.
CONTROLS: We will keep all controls from the original proposal, and also investigate the impact of different feature weights and aggregation methods on the final reward signal and RL performance.
COST: 972
PREDICTION: By incorporating meta-data and experimenting with different aggregation methods, we expect to see an improvement in the policy performance and a more stable reward signal compared to the original proposal. However, fine-tuning these hyperparameters might pose a challenge and might lead to overfitting if not done carefully.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Supervisor as Curator: Diversity-based Sampling of Search Results
PROPOSAL: We propose an additional layer of complexity to the reward signal by sampling the search results in a way that encourages the RL agent to explore a diverse set of relevant evidence. We will train a supervisor network to predict the importance of each search result, given a query and the expected final answer. Then, at training time, we will sample the search results based on the supervisor's predictions, ensuring that the final answer is likely to be found somewhere in the sampled results. We hypothesize that this approach will help the RL agent learn to navigate complex search spaces and find the most relevant evidence more efficiently.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed method against a baseline which uses permutation-invariant sampling, and also investigate the impact of using different supervisors for sampling and for reward computation.
COST: 1296
PREDICTION: By incorporating diversity-based sampling, we expect to see an improvement in the RL agent's ability to navigate complex search spaces and find the most relevant evidence, leading to higher accuracy and better sample efficiency. However, training the supervisor network might require significant additional computational resources, especially for very large search spaces.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Contextualizing Turn Rewards: Leveraging Intermediate Question-Answer Pairs to Improve Supervision
PROPOSAL: We will leverage intermediate question-answer pairs generated by the RL agent to improve the turn reward signal. By conditioning the reward prediction on the current question, answer, and previous questions-answers pairs, we can provide more informed feedback to the RL agent about its progress and coverage of the search space. We will use a contextual neural network to predict the rewards and compare its performance with our previous methods and a baseline that uses only the current question and search results.
CONTROLS: We will also investigate the impact of using different contextualization mechanisms, such as using a graph neural network to model the question-answers pairs, and comparing our proposed method against a baseline that uses static reward signals.
COST: 1920
PREDICTION: By contextualizing the turn rewards, we expect to see a more accurate and informative reward signal that helps the RL agent to refine its search strategy and improve its final accuracy. However, training the contextual neural network might pose a challenge due to the need to balance the complexity of the model and the availability of training data.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Dense Process Rewards using Web-side Information
PROPOSAL: We will leverage the structure of web search results to infer rewards at every interaction turn for search agents. Specifically, we precompute a compressed representation of all possible search results for each turn, then at training time, compute a relevance score between each turn's search result and the precomputed representation. The relevance score will then be normalized across all possible turns for a given question to obtain a dense reward signal for the RL agent. The method will be applied to a variety of open-domain question answering datasets, including WebQSP and WikiQA, and compared to a baseline of outcome-based rewards.
CONTROLS: We will also compare our method against GRPO and its variants that use external oracle knowledge or reward models to judge intermediate steps.
COST: 1728
PREDICTION: This approach should successfully provide a dense reward signal at peu nominal compute cost despite its non-trivial fueltionality. The improvement in RL performance, measured by search agent accuracy on final answers, may be significant, particularly in the most challenging queries.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Revising Dense Process Rewards using Web-side Information: Enriching the Turn Reward Signal using Search-result Meta-data
PROPOSAL: To further improve the relevance score computed in our previous proposal, we will enrich our search-result representation with additional meta-data such as search query popularity, answer snippet score, and ranking position. We hypothesize that incorporating these features will allow our model to better understand the quality of the intermediate search results and provide a more informative reward signal at each turn. In addition, we will investigate various aggregation methods to combine the relevance score with the enriched meta-data, such as element-wise multiplication, concatenation, and weighted sum.
CONTROLS: We will keep all controls from the original proposal, and also investigate the impact of different feature weights and aggregation methods on the final reward signal and RL performance.
COST: 2916
PREDICTION: By incorporating meta-data and experimenting with different aggregation methods, we expect to see an improvement in the policy performance and a more stable reward signal compared to the original proposal. However, fine-tuning these hyperparameters might pose a challenge and might lead to overfitting if not done carefully.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Supervisor as Curator: Diversity-based Sampling of Search Results
PROPOSAL: We propose an additional layer of complexity to the reward signal by sampling the search results in a way that encourages the RL agent to explore a diverse set of relevant evidence. We will train a supervisor network to predict the importance of each search result, given a query and the expected final answer. Then, at training time, we will sample the search results based on the supervisor's predictions, ensuring that the final answer is likely to be found somewhere in the sampled results. We hypothesize that this approach will help the RL agent learn to navigate complex search spaces and find the most relevant evidence more efficiently.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed method against a baseline which uses permutation-invariant sampling, and also investigate the impact of using different supervisors for sampling and for reward computation.
COST: 3888
PREDICTION: By incorporating diversity-based sampling, we expect to see an improvement in the RL agent's ability to navigate complex search spaces and find the most relevant evidence, leading to higher accuracy and better sample efficiency. However, training the supervisor network might require significant additional computational resources, especially for very large search spaces.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Contextualizing Turn Rewards: Leveraging Intermediate Question-Answer Pairs to Improve Supervision
PROPOSAL: We will leverage intermediate question-answer pairs generated by the RL agent to improve the turn reward signal. By conditioning the reward prediction on the current question, answer, and previous questions-answers pairs, we can provide more informed feedback to the RL agent about its progress and coverage of the search space. We will use a contextual neural network to predict the rewards and compare its performance with our previous methods and a baseline that uses only the current question and search results.
CONTROLS: We will also investigate the impact of using different contextualization mechanisms, such as using a graph neural network to model the question-answers pairs, and comparing our proposed method against a baseline that uses static reward signals.
COST: 5760
PREDICTION: By contextualizing the turn rewards, we expect to see a more accurate and informative reward signal that helps the RL agent to refine its search strategy and improve its final accuracy. However, training the contextual neural network might pose a challenge due to the need to balance the complexity of the model and the availability of training data.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Integrated Approach to Turn Rewards: Web-side Information, Supervisor, and Context
PROPOSAL: We will integrate the three previous methods to create a more comprehensive and informative turn reward signal. Specifically, we will combine the enriched search-result representation from Revising Dense Process Rewards with the diversity-based sampling from Supervisor as Curator, and the contextualization from Contextualizing Turn Rewards. We will use a hierarchical neural network to predict the rewards, where the first layer uses web-side information and supervisor predictions, the second layer uses the contextualized question-answer pairs, and the final layer produces a dense reward signal for each turn.
CONTROLS: We will compare our integrated method against a baseline that uses outcome-based rewards and also investigate the impact of using different neural network architectures and hyperparameters.

PREDICTION: By integrating the three methods, we expect to see a significantly improved reward signal that provides more accurate and informative feedback to the RL agent. However, the increased complexity of the hierarchical neural network might require significant computational resources and careful hyperparameter tuning.

These smaller rewards will be conditioned on the previous question, answer, and search results, and will be used to encourage the RL agent to take more informative and relevant actions at each hop.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attentive Sparse Projection for Pre-training Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel pre-training method named Attentive Sparse Projection (ASP), which extends NeRF-based approaches to adapt to the sparse query-based structure of SPMs. ASP uses a set of learnable attention weights to project sparse queries onto a 2D learned intermediate representation, enabling the pre-training model to retrieve a BEV-like grid-based feature mapping for sparse queries. While the sparse queries remain unchanged, their representations are translated into a learnable, regular grid structure, composable for geometric reasoning and capable of simulating how SPMs perceive the 3D environment. Train on unlabeled data, evaluate on Shift-Seg, Dapto, and KITTI odometry datasets.
CONTROLS: Using existing approaches like UniPAD and ViDAR as baselines; ASP-ablation without attention weights to examine the impact of geometric projection on the model.
COST: 288000.
PREDICTION: ASP outperforms the baselines for tasks that require robust geometric interpretation, such as 3D object detection, semantic segmentation, and scene understanding.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transferable Scene Representation through Meta-Learned Projection
PROPOSAL: Design a meta-learning module that discovers a better mapping between the intermediate learned representation, projected from ASP in turn 1, and the query-based space. The Meta-Learned Projection (MLP) aims to transfer the learned representations across different SPM architectures, thus allowing for a shared understanding of 3D scene geometry among these disparate models without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. This is done by iteratively learning to select and project query features to a common space through meta-reinforcement learning. 
CONTROLS: Training MLP on both shifts of query representation in downstream models and on the learned intermediate space in experimental ASP from turn 1; as an ablation, remove the meta-learning component and solely use ASP representations.
COST: 288000.
PREDICTION: MLP significantly reduces the transfer gap among different downstream models operating on heterogeneous queries due to better aligning of intermediate feature spaces, and enables flexible adaptation to diverse SPM architectures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: GLoST: Geometry-Enabled Local Spatial Temporal Pre-training
PROPOSAL: Develop a domain-agnostic self-supervised pre-training framework, Geometry-Enabled Local Spatial Temporal pre-training (GLoST), that generates pseudo-ground-truths for 3D spatial and temporal structures from multi-view images without the need for explicit first-person viewpoint or dense volumetric annotations. GLoST combines a series of differentiable rendering and back-projecting processes to recover and predict accurate geometric layouts, facilitating pre-training of SPMs to fully capture spatial-temporal geometric representations solely based on scene structure, following the model-driven rendering strategies observed in recent works. 
CONTROLS: The proposed no-viewpoint-availability (NVA) and no-dense-annotations (NDA) modes by checking its generalization on multiple benchmarks and context perms without SPM-knowledge by comparing it to existing methods such as UniPAD and ViDAR and leveraging LPIPS as a measure of image similarity.
COST: 288000.
PREDICTION: GLoST can learn rich 3D spatial and temporal representations, achieving a relatively stable pre-training performance of sparse perception models on real-world driving scenes plus boosts partly or even effects wise better results than the previous baselines for downstream tasks like 3D object detection and semantic segmentation following car-centric annotation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attentive Sparse Projection for Pre-training Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel pre-training method named Attentive Sparse Projection (ASP), which extends NeRF-based approaches to adapt to the sparse query-based structure of SPMs. ASP uses a set of learnable attention weights to project sparse queries onto a 2D learned intermediate representation, enabling the pre-training model to retrieve a BEV-like grid-based feature mapping for sparse queries. While the sparse queries remain unchanged, their representations are translated into a learnable, regular grid structure, composable for geometric reasoning and capable of simulating how SPMs perceive the 3D environment. Train on unlabeled data, evaluate on Shift-Seg, Dapto, and KITTI odometry datasets.
CONTROLS: Using existing approaches like UniPAD and ViDAR as baselines; ASP-ablation without attention weights to examine the impact of geometric projection on the model.
COST: 864000.
PREDICTION: ASP outperforms the baselines for tasks that require robust geometric interpretation, such as 3D object detection, semantic segmentation, and scene understanding.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transferable Scene Representation through Meta-Learned Projection
PROPOSAL: Design a meta-learning module that discovers a better mapping between the intermediate learned representation, projected from ASP in turn 1, and the query-based space. The Meta-Learned Projection (MLP) aims to transfer the learned representations across different SPM architectures, thus allowing for a shared understanding of 3D scene geometry among these disparate models without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. This is done by iteratively learning to select and project query features to a common space through meta-reinforcement learning. 
CONTROLS: Training MLP on both shifts of query representation in downstream models and on the learned intermediate space in experimental ASP from turn 1; as an ablation, remove the meta-learning component and solely use ASP representations.
COST: 864000.
PREDICTION: MLP significantly reduces the transfer gap among different downstream models operating on heterogeneous queries due to better aligning of intermediate feature spaces, and enables flexible adaptation to diverse SPM architectures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated Learning meets Scene Completion
PROPOSAL: Develop a federated learning framework for sparse perception models (SPMs) that leverages unlabeled multi-view driving data from autonomous vehicles within a fleet, enabling scene completion tasks like predicting 3D occupancy. By aggregating features from multiple vehicles, the method learns to fill in gaps in observed data, fostering self-supervised learning of 3D scene representations. The framework is designed to adapt to various query-based downstream models, including those with 2D or 3D initializations, by fine-tuning the shared query encoder.
CONTROLS: Commodity variant of DETR3D as the baseline SPM, with a randomly initialized query encoder.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: The proposed framework should improve the generalizability and robustness of SPMs, particularly for scene completion tasks, by exploiting labeled data from other vehicles and leveraging the diversity of their experiences. However, achieving effective adaptation across query encoder architectures and initializations might be challenging, limiting the overall performance for certain downstream tasks.

PREDICTION: The proposed framework should significantly improve the performance of SPMs on specific scene understanding tasks by leveraging expert guidance, particularly for tasks where precise 3D geometric representations are crucial. However, achieving consistent performance improvements across diverse SPM architectures and tasks might be difficult due to the need for tailored demonstrations from the expert model.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Multi-view Pre-training for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Develop an adversarial multi-view pre-training method for Sparse Perception Models, leveraging unlabeled multi-view driving data. The framework includes a generative model to synthesize a cohort of surrogate 3D scenes, an evaluation metric to assess the scene realism, and a discriminator to enforce a weighted minimum confusion loss. During pre-training, the generator attempts to generate a realistic 3D scene, while the discriminator tries to distinguish between the real and generated scenes. The generator uses a set of implicit queries to extract relevant features from the input images, and the discriminator evaluates the spatial-temporal coherence of the predicted 3D scene. The pre-trained model will learn to effectively encode and reason about 3D scene understanding, despite the absence of explicit dense intermediate representations.
CONTROLS: Supervised training on the Sparse4D dataset, SPM baselines trained on DETR3D and PETR.
COST: 414.72 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed adversarial multi-view pre-training method will significantly improve the 3D scene understanding performance of Sparse Perception Models, outperforming existing baselines by at least 5% on the Sparse4D dataset. However, may fail to generalize well to diverse driving scenes, such as those with heavy occlusions or dynamic objects.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Query-based Downstream Tasks
PROPOSAL: Introduce a cross-modal knowledge distillation framework to adapt the pre-trained Sparse Perception Model for query-based downstream tasks, such as sparse 3D object detection and sparse semantic occupancy prediction. The framework consists of a teacher-student network structure, where the pre-trained model serves as the teacher and the downstream model as the student. The student network is trained to mimic the teacher's output, while leveraging additional knowledge distilled from a guiding loss function that emphasizes the spatial coherence and contextual relationships between objects. Experiments will be conducted on tasks like DErr3D, PETR, SparseOcc, and OSP, comparing the effectiveness of the proposed cross-modal knowledge distillation method against existing transfer learning techniques.
CONTROLS: Direct weight transfer, frozen features, multi-task learning.
COST: 530 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The cross-modal knowledge distillation method will show significant performance improvements for Sparse Perception Models in downstream tasks, outperforming existing transfer learning techniques by at least 3% on the DErr3D and PETR datasets, and achieve comparable results on SparseOcc and OSP. However, the approach may require careful tuning of the guiding loss function to avoid negative transfer and prioritize the most informative features.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Adversarial Multi-view Pre-training for Sparse Perception Models with Geometric Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Enhance the adversarial multi-view pre-training method (proposal 1) by incorporating geometric reasoning into the generator and discriminator. The generator will predict not only the 3D scene but also the spatial layout and texture of the objects in the scene. The discriminator will evaluate not only the spatial-temporal coherence but also the geometric consistency of the predicted 3D scene. This refinement will allow the pre-trained model to reason about object relationships and spatial layout, improving its geometry-awareness and tackling challenging scenarios such as partial occlusions and contexts with multiple objects. A variant of the method will be designed to balance the trade-off between spatial and geometric consistency in the final prediction.
CONTROLS: Baseline same as before.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised adversarial multi-view pre-training method will significantly boost the 3D scene understanding performance of Sparse Perception Models, yielding substantial improvements in its geometry-awareness and spatial reasoning capabilities, outperforming existing methods by at least 8% on the Sparse4D dataset. However, the trade-off between spatial and geometric consistency might lead to overfitting if not carefully tuned.

PROPOSAL: Introduce a pseudo-label-based auxiliary task to augment the training of Sparse Perception Models for autonomous driving, leveraging the unlabeled driving data and using the predictions from the pre-trained generator as pseudo-labels. The auxiliary task, designed to improve the model's robustness and generalizability, will focus on predicting implicit scene context and motion patterns from the driving video sequence. The pseudo-labels will be produced from the generator's output, refining the model's ability to encode complex spatial and temporal relationships. This will further enhance the representation capacity and predictive abilities of the model for downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline same as before.

PROPOSAL: Develop a scalable opponent neural rendering (SONR) method for Sparse Perception Models, designed to generate multiple diverse opponents using data augmentation and sampling techniques. These opponents will enable the model to learn more robust spatial and temporal representations by leveraging competition and diversity in the generated scenarios. The SONR framework will be efficiently integrated into the adversarial multi-view pre-training pipeline (proposal 1), providing a scalable and flexible means to generate diverse scenarios for pre-training and evaluating the Sparse Perception Model.

COST: 670 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The scalable opponent neural rendering method will significantly enhance the performance and robustness of Sparse Perception Models, enabling them to generalize better to new and unseen scenarios, outperforming existing methods by at least 10% on the Sparse4D and DErr3D datasets. However, the SONR method may introduce computational overhead due to the need to generate diverse opponents, potentially slowing down training and inference.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Scalable Opponent Neural Rendering for Sparse Perception Models | 
PROPOSAL: Refine the scalable opponent neural rendering (SONR) method by incorporating a progressive learning schedule and a dynamic sampling strategy. The progressive learning schedule will adjust the difficulty of opponent generation based on the model's performance, starting with simple scenarios and gradually introducing more challenging and diverse opponents. The dynamic sampling strategy will adaptively select the most informative opponents to focus on, ensuring that the model learns to generalize to the most likely and critical scenarios. This refinement will improve the efficiency and effectiveness of SONR, making it a more scalable and practical solution for pre-training Sparse Perception Models.
CONTROLS: New controls on burn-in period for generating easy opponents, concurrent training periods for different skill levels.
COST: 734 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refined SONR method will show significant improvements in terms of efficiency, effectiveness, and robustness, outperforming existing methods by at least 12% on the Sparse4D and DErr3D datasets. However, the adaptive strategy may lead to overfitting if not tuned carefully, and the refinement might increase the computational demands during the pre-training phase.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Differentiable Soft Sensorimotor Perturbations for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Introduce differentiable soft sensorimotor perturbations to the pre-training process of Sparse Perception Models, allowing the model to learn robustness to sensor noise and sensorimotor uncertainty. The perturbations will be applied in an end-to-end differentiable manner, enabling the model to backpropagate the gradients of the perturbations and adapt accordingly. This method will be integrated into the adversarial multi-view pre-training pipeline (proposal 1), enabling the model to learn more robust and generalizable representations.
CONTROLS: Baseline same as before.
COST: 936 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The differentiable soft sensorimotor perturbations will significantly enhance the robustness and generalizability of Sparse Perception Models, outperforming existing methods by at least 15% on the DErr3D and PETR datasets. However, the introduction of perturbations may lead to increased training time and computational requirements due to the need to maintain a stable and efficient backpropagation process.

TITLE: Joint Adversarial Learning for Scene Representation and Motion Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel joint adversarial learning framework for Sparse Perception Models, which learns to predict the scene representation and motion forecasting simultaneously. The framework will utilize a critique-respond approach, where the model generates both the scene representation and motion predictions, and an adversary is trained to critique the predictions. The model will then respond to the critique by refining its predictions. This approach will enable the model to learn more comprehensive scene understanding and accurate motion forecasting capabilities.
CONTROLS: Baseline same as before, plus separate evaluation metrics for scene representation and motion forecasting.
COST: 1260 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The joint adversarial learning framework will significantly improve the model's scene representation and motion forecasting capabilities, outperforming existing methods by at least 20% on the DErr3D and PETR datasets. However, the critique-respond approach may lead to overfitting if the critique network is overly complex or not optimized properly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Query-Agnostic Self-Supervised Pre-training for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a query-agnostic self-supervised pre-training framework for SPMs, which learns a 3D scene representation through a "render-and-predict" pipeline without relying on explicit dense features. Specifically, we use a learned 3D renderer to render the scene into images from different views, and a predictor network to predict the rendered images. The pre-training loss is based on the reconstruction error of the predicted images from the rendered images. This framework can be applied to various SPMs with different query distributions and can transfer knowledge to multiple downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: 
- We compare our method to standard self-supervised methods (e.g., MoCo, SimCLR) that require explicit dense features as input.
- We also compare to alternate pre-training methods specifically designed for SPMs (e.g., NQSPM, LQSPM) that require task-specific query initialization.
- We evaluate the transferability of our pre-trained models to multiple downstream SPMs with different query distributions.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Our method will outperform standard self-supervised methods and demonstrate strong transferability to multiple downstream tasks, but may fail if the 3D renderer is not sufficiently accurate or flexible to adapt to various scene geometries.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Crucial Role of Scene Geometry in Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We conduct a thorough analysis of the impact of scene geometry on the performance of SPMs. Specifically, we investigate how the geometry of scenes affects the quality of the sparse queries learned by the models during pre-training and fine-tuning. We use a combination of quantitative metrics (e.g., query-query similarity, query-scene distance) and qualitative visualization tools (e.g., scene graphs, query decomposition) to understand the relationship between scene geometry and query distribution.
CONTROLS: 
- We compare our results to a baseline setting where scene geometry is randomly sampled or fixed.
- We evaluate the effect of scene geometry on different types of SPMs, including 3D object detectors and semantic occupancy predictors.
- We examine the relationship between scene geometry and task performance to understand whether geometry is a relevant feature for SPMs to learn from.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: Our analysis will provide crucial insights into the role of scene geometry in SPMs, highlighting its importance for query learning and task performance. However, we predict that our analysis might overlook certain edge cases where non-geometric factors dominate the performance of SPMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Novel Framework for Warm-starting Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel framework for warm-starting SPMs using pre-trained models and a new query initialization strategy. Specifically, we use transfer learning to initialize the query distribution of the SPM with the learned query distribution from a pre-trained model, and then refine the query distribution through a few-shot fine-tuning process. This warm-starting strategy aims to reduce the computational cost and improve the convergence speed of SPMs.
CONTROLS: 
- We compare our warm-starting strategy to the standard query initialization method used in most SPMs.
- We evaluate the effect of the warm-starting strategy on different types of SPMs, including 3D object detectors and semantic occupancy predictors.
- We examine the trade-off between computational cost and convergence speed to determine the optimal number of fine-tuning iterations.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: Our warm-starting framework will significantly reduce the computational cost and improve the convergence speed of SPMs, but may fail if the pre-trained model is not well-matched to the target task or dataset.

PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive query normalization technique for SPMs, which dynamically adjusts the query distribution to adapt to the changing scene characteristics. We evaluate our adaptive query normalization technique on various SPMs and datasets to demonstrate its effectiveness in improving task performance and adaptability.

PROPOSAL: Investigate asymmetric pre-training for SPMs that incorporates image-to-sparse-3D translation to bridge the gap between dense image features and sparse 3D scene representations. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Detectors via Gradual Feature Alignment
PROPOSAL: Experimentally investigate a novel approach to adapt a pre-trained vision-language detector (e.g. GLIP) at test time by gradually aligning the target domain features to the source domain features using a consistency loss, while preserving the pre-trained detector's generalization capability. Specifically, the alignment is achieved by iteratively updating the target feature extractor to minimize the difference between the target and source feature distributions, while the detector's object classification head remains frozen to prevent overfitting.
CONTROLS: Compare with two baselines: (1) a simple self-training approach that fine-tunes the entire model on the target data, and (2) a recent TTAOD method that leverages pseudo-labels to adapt the detector.
COST: 4,500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to outperform both baselines, especially in scenarios with limited target data, but may struggle with large domain shifts due to the gradual alignment mechanism.

These synthetic samples are then used to generate supplementary pseudo-labels, which can be combined with the original pseudo-labels to improve the quality and diversity of the pseudo-labels. This approach can help alleviate the issue of missing pseudo-labels in test samples.
CONTROLS: Compare with two baselines: (1) a simple pseudo-label filtering method that only considers the top-N confident pseudo-labels, and (2) a recent pseudo-label refinement method that leverages a discriminator to evaluate pseudo-label quality.
COST: 7,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to significantly improve pseudo-label diversity and quality, leading to improved adaptation performance, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

TITLE: Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Detectors via Gradual Feature Alignment
PROPOSAL: Experimentally investigate a novel approach to adapt a pre-trained vision-language detector (e.g. GLIP) at test time by gradually aligning the target domain features to the source domain features using a consistency loss, while preserving the pre-trained detector's generalization capability. Specifically, the alignment is achieved by iteratively updating the target feature extractor to minimize the difference between the target and source feature distributions, while the detector's object classification head remains frozen to prevent overfitting.
CONTROLS: Compare with two baselines: (1) a simple self-training approach that fine-tunes the entire model on the target data, and (2) a recent TTAOD method that leverages pseudo-labels to adapt the detector.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Distribution Alignment for Vision-Language Detector Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the GLIP pre-trained detector on a set of real-world benchmarks like COCO and VOS-2018, aligning source and target distribution by leveraging contrastive learning, particularly using the recently introduced temporal contrastive loss. Specifically, we will use the training procedures of GLIP and integrate a temporal contrastive loss module into the detector's loss function, pairing positive pairs across the augmentations of the same target image while discarding the source domain altogether.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the GLIP pre-trained detector with both our modifications and standard training procedure on real-world benchmarks COCO and VOS-2018.
COST: 1068.322
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvement in detector adaptation due to the learned alignment of source and target distributions, but we may face challenges when adapting across large variations in domain and category.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Self-Training with.statusCode Dropout for Online Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose to add statusCode dropout to the GLIP detector during online self-training, dynamically filtering pseudo-labels based on a confidence threshold. Concretely, we will mask the output of certain batch elements in the self-training process with a predefined probability, encouraging the model to robustly predict on different subsets of data and promoting adaptation to noisy or missing pseudo-labels. The GLIP detector will be self-trained and evaluated on various real-world benchmarks, including COCO-KEPLER, VOS-2018, and DAVIS-2022.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate GLIP with both statusCode dropout and standard self-training on the mentioned real-world benchmarks, comparing results in terms of detector adaptation and adaptation efficiency.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: We predict that statusCode dropout will improve GLIP's online self-training efficiency and detection accuracy, but the absence of well-designed filtering thresholds may lead to suboptimal pseudo-label quality.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Context-Aware Weighted Regression for Target Domain Shift Compensation
PROPOSAL: We propose to incorporate context-aware weighted regression (CWRR) to adapt the detector's parameters during test time, enabling the compensation of target domain shift. CWRR leverages an attention mechanism to dynamically weigh the contribution of pre-trained weights according to their relevance to the current test domain. Specifically, we compute the attention weights by taking as input the target image's features, the pre-trained weights, and the detector's self-generated pseudo-targets. Subsequently, we re-weight the pre-trained weights using the learned attention mechanism and then perform a linear regression update of the detector's weights, considering the CWRR-weighted pre-trained weights and the target pseudo-labels.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of GLIP detector equipped with CWRR against the standard self-training procedure and other baselines like uncertainty weighted regression on several real-world benchmarks COCO, VOS-2018 and ADE20K.
COST: 2168
PREDICTION: We expect CWRR to lead to more accurate adaptation to the target domain in scenarios with significant distribution shifts, as it leverages the advantages of attention-based weight adaptation.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Guided Sampling for Efficient Online Adaptation
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of balancing model adaptation and overfitting when pseudo-labels are scarce or noisy, we propose an uncertainty-guided sampling strategy. We will utilize the stochastic dependency of the detector's prediction uncertainty on the quality and diversity of pseudo-labels. Specifically, we will evaluate the uncertainty estimates of the detector's predictions, using a Monte Carlo drop-out strategy for each prediction in the self-training process, with higher uncertainty values guiding the selection of images to sample pseudo-labels. The selected images will then be used to self-train the model, prioritizing adaptation of samples with lower uncertainty predictions that are more informative for model improvement.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance of the uncertainty-guided sampling strategy and a baseline sampling strategy without uncertainty estimation on several real-world benchmarks such as COCO, VOS-2018 and EPIC-KITCHEN.
COST: 2918.4
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved model adaptation accuracy and generalization performance with the uncertainty-guided sampling strategy, as it helps to more effectively select informative samples for the self-training process, reducing the risk of overfitting and improving the overall robustness of the online adaptation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Branch Online Adaptation for Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-branch online adaptation framework, which leverages multiple branch detectors that focus on different aspects of the target domain, such as object pose, shape, or appearance. Each branch is trained to adapt to the target domain through online self-training, and the output of each branch is combined to produce the final detection results. This multi-branch approach allows the model to explore different adaptations and learn to focus on the most informative features for the target domain, leading to improved adaptation accuracy and robustness. Additionally, we will incorporate an attention mechanism to dynamically weigh the contribution of each branch and the fine-grained adaptation signal.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance of our multi-branch online adaptation framework on several real-world benchmarks, including COCO, VOS-2018, and EPIC-KITCHEN, comparing it against baseline methods, such as a single-branch adaptation framework.
COST: 4608
PREDICTION: We expect the multi-branch online adaptation framework to achieve state-of-the-art performance on various real-world benchmarks, but the increased complexity may lead to slower adaptation speed and higher computational costs.

TITLE: Meta-Learning for Fast Adaptation to New Target Domains
PROPOSAL: To enhance the online adaptation framework, we propose to incorporate a meta-learning module that adapts the model's India's learning process to new target domains through few-shot learning. Specifically, we will use a meta-learning algorithm to optimize the model's parameters such that it can rapidly adapt to new target domains by learning from a limited number of samples. During meta-training, the model will be presented with a set of source domains and a set of target domains, and its goal will be to learn a procedure that can adapt to the target domains quickly and effectively. Once meta-trained, the model can adapt to new target domains with minimal additional training data.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance of our meta-learning online adaptation framework on several real-world benchmarks, including COCO, VOS-2018, and EPIC-KITCHEN, comparing it against baseline methods, such as online adaptation without meta-learning.
COST: 6800
PREDICTION: We expect the meta-learning online adaptation framework to achieve improved adaptation speed and accuracy, especially when adapting to new target domains with limited data, but the increased computational cost during meta-training may lead to longer training times.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off in Online Adaptation for Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: To optimize the online adaptation process, we propose to explore the exploration-exploitation trade-off in the framework. Specifically, we will incorporate an entropy-based exploration mechanism that balances the exploration of new target domains and the exploitation of existing knowledge. During the online adaptation process, the model will maintain an entropy-based representation of the target domain, and use this representation to dynamically adjust the exploration-exploitation trade-off. TITLE: Context-Aware Weighted Regression for Target Domain Shift Compensation
PROPOSAL: We propose to incorporate context-aware weighted regression (CWRR) to adapt the detector's parameters during test time, enabling the compensation of target domain shift. CWRR leverages an attention mechanism to dynamically weigh the contribution of pre-trained weights according to their relevance to the current test domain. Specifically, we compute the attention weights by taking as input the target image's features, the pre-trained weights, and the detector's self-generated pseudo-targets. Subsequently, we re-weight the pre-trained weights using the learned attention mechanism and then perform a linear regression update of the detector's weights, considering the CWRR-weighted pre-trained weights and the target pseudo-labels.

TITLE: Uncertainty-Guided Sampling for Efficient Online Adaptation
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of balancing model adaptation and overfitting when pseudo-labels are scarce or noisy, we propose an uncertainty-guided sampling strategy. PROPOSAL: We will augment our vision-language detector with confidence-calibrated pseudo-labeling, which assigns lower-confidence pseudo-labels lower weights to prevent amplifying noise and enhances the model's robustness. During test time, the model generates a set of pseudo-labeled bounding boxes for each image from which it then selects a subset with higher confidence for adaptation. We compare this baseline to vanilla self-training where pseudo-labels are used with equal weights regardless of confidence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Confidence-Calibrated Pseudo-Labeling for Test-Time Adaptive Visual-Linguistic Detectors
PROPOSAL: We will augment our vision-language detector with confidence-calibrated pseudo-labeling, which assigns lower-confidence pseudo-labels lower weights to prevent amplifying noise and enhances the model's robustness. During test time, the model generates a set of pseudo-labeled bounding boxes for each image from which it then selects a subset with higher confidence for adaptation. We compare this baseline to vanilla self-training where pseudo-labels are used with equal weights regardless of confidence.
CONTROLS: Compare with state-of-the-art self-training based methods (e.g., GLIP, DINO) without confidence calibration.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: Confidence-calibrated pseudo-labeling will lead to a modest improvement over vanilla self-training with a potential degradation in precision when pseudo-labels with lower confidence are also given lower weight, but the model will stabilize its adaptation over test batches.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Self-Modulating Adapter for Online Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We will extend our vision-language detector with an adaptive self-modulating adapter that dynamically adjusts its learning rate based on the model's confidence in its pseudo-labeled predictions. This allows the model to adapt more aggressively when it is more confident in its pseudo-labels, while being more cautious when they are uncertain. We will compare this approach to our baseline of confidence-calibrated pseudo-labeling from Proposal 1 and traditional self-training without any confidence-based adaptation.
CONTROLS: Compare with Proposal 1 and traditional self-training without confidence modulation, and also investigate the sensitivity of the adaptive self-modulating adapter to hyperparameters such as the confidence threshold and adaptation frequency.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: The adaptive self-modulating adapter will achieve better adaptation performance than confidence-calibrated pseudo-labeling, especially on datasets with large distribution shifts, by mitigating overfitting to noisy pseudo-labels and adapt more effectively, but it might introduce oscillations or over-adaptation if its confidence threshold or adaptation frequency are not calibrated correctly.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Adaptive Self-Modulating Adapter for Online Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We modify the adaptive self-modulating adapter proposal to include a knowledge distillation component that encodes the pre-trained detector's knowledge into the test-time adapted model, while allowing the adapter to dynamically adjust its learning rate based on the model's confidence in its pseudo-labeled predictions. This should enable the model to transfer learned knowledge more effectively while still adapting to the test domain.
CONTROLS: Investigate the trade-offs between adaptation tightness and knowledge distillation, as well as the impact on the pre-trained detector's generalization capability.
COST: 4200
PREDICTION: The adaptive self-modulating adapter with knowledge distillation will achieve better adaptation performance and more robust generalization to unseen categories, but it might be more computationally expensive and require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance adaptation and knowledge transfer.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Implicit Domain Generalization
PROPOSAL: We will introduce a multi-task learning framework that leverages pre-trained vision-language detectors to learn multiple tasks, including object detection and a pretext task such as image-text matching or image denoising, but with task-specific networks that can adapt to the test domain while leveraging the pre-trained detector's base network and shared knowledge.
CONTROLS: Compare this approach with traditional self-training and our previously proposed methods, including Proposal 1 and the updated Proposal 2, and investigate the effect of the pretext task on adaptation performance and pre-trained detector's generalization.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: Multi-task learning will help our model achieve better adaptation performance and more robust generalization to unseen categories by exploiting shared knowledge across tasks, but it might overfit to the pretext task if not properly regularized or if the pretext task is too different from object detection.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Confidence-Calibrated Pseudo-Labeling for Test-Time Adaptive Visual-Linguistic Detectors
PROPOSAL: We will extend the confidence-calibrated pseudo-labeling proposal to incorporate a novel boundary layer that dynamically adjusts the spatial attention weights of the detector based on the confidence of pseudo-labeled predictions. This boundary layer will allow the detector to focus on regions with higher confidence predictions, thereby reducing the impact of noisy or uncertain pseudo-labels on adaptation performance.
CONTROLS: Investigate the effect of the boundary layer on adaptation performance, especially when combined with other adaptive methods such as the adaptive self-modulating adapter.
COST: 4800
PREDICTION: The confidence-calibrated pseudo-labeling with boundary layer will lead to improved adaptation performance and robustness to noise, but it might introduce additional Computational costs and require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance the effect of the boundary layer.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Teacher-Student Approach for Overcoming Pseudo-Label Noise
PROPOSAL: We will use a teacher-student framework, where a teacher model generates pseudo-labels from the target data, and a student model adapts to these pseudo-labels and gradually develops its own confidence in them. The teacher model's pseudo-labels are generated based on a confidence threshold, and the teacher and student models are trained simultaneously. This allows the student model to benefit from the teacher's expertise while also handling noisy or missing pseudo-labels.
CONTROLS: Compare this teacher-student approach with our previously proposed methods, including Proposal 1, Proposal 2, and Proposal 3, and investigate the impact of the confidence threshold on adaptation performance.
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: The teacher-student approach will lead to significant improvements in adaptation performance and robustness to pseudo-label noise, but it might introduce additional training complexities and require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance the teacher and student's confidence in their pseudo-labels.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Adaptive Self-Modulating Adapter for Online Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We modify the adaptive self-modulating adapter proposal to include a novelty detection mechanism that identifies new categories or instances in the test data and assigns them lower confidence pseudo-labels until more confident predictions are generated. This novelty detection mechanism is integrated with the adaptive self-modulating adapter to handle out-of-distribution data and new categories more effectively.
CONTROLS: Investigate the effect of the novelty detection mechanism on adaptation performance, especially when combined with our multi-task learning framework (Proposal 3) and teacher-student approach (Proposal 4).
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: The novelty detection mechanism will enhance the adaptive self-modulating adapter's ability to handle new categories and out-of-distribution data, leading to improved adaptation performance, but it might introduce additional computational costs and require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance novelty detection and adaptation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptation-Aware Loss Functions for Improved Stability
PROPOSAL: We introduce adaptation-aware loss functions that take into account the uncertainty of the pseudo-labels and the model's confidence in its predictions. These loss functions are designed to promote stable adaptation and effective knowledge transfer between the source and target domains. We will compare the effectiveness of these adaptation-aware loss functions with traditional cross-entropy loss and our previously proposed methods.
CONTROLS: Compare with state-of-the-art self-training methods and investigate the impact of different adaptation-aware loss functions on adaptation performance and pre-trained detector's generalization.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: Adaptation-aware loss functions will lead to improved adaptation stability and effective knowledge transfer, but they might introduce additional computational costs and require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance adaptation confidence and classification accuracy.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Teacher-Student Approach for Overcoming Pseudo-Label Noise
PROPOSAL: We enhance the teacher-student approach by incorporating an entropy-based curriculum learning strategy that gradually increases the complexity of the pseudo-labels based on the student model's confidence. This allows the student model to learn from more complex pseudo-labels as its confidence improves, leading to more effective adaptation and robustness to noise. We will compare the effectiveness of this enhanced teacher-student approach with our previously proposed methods.
CONTROLS: Compare with our adaptation-aware loss functions (Proposal 5) and investigate the impact of the entropy-based curriculum learning strategy on adaptation performance and pre-trained detector's generalization.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: The enhanced teacher-student approach with entropy-based curriculum learning will lead to significant improvements in adaptation performance and robustness to noise, but it might introduce additional computational costs and require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance curriculum learning and adaptation confidence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Uncertainty-Aware Pseudo-Labeling for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: We modify the pre-trained vision-language detector by incorporating an uncertainty estimation module, which forecasts the confidence in pseudo-labels generated for each object instance during test time. We then selectively use these pseudo-labels to train the detector in a self-supervised manner, leveraging the classifier head's output as additional input features or adjusting the pseudo-label confidence threshold adaptively. This uncertainty-aware pseudo-labeling strategy encourages the model to rely less on unreliable pseudo-labels and more on its pre-trained knowledge, reducing overfitting and improving robustness to noisy samples.
CONTROLS:Compare with standard self-training (w/o uncertainty estimation) and with a stronger baseline using adaptive pseudo-label filtering strategies based on diverse object attributes (e.g., bbox height/width).
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Uncertainty-aware pseudo-labeling is likely to show a trade-off between adaptation and generalization performance; it might improve adaptation when the target domain has clean data but suffer when noise levels are high.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Masked Self-Supervision for Domain-Agnostic Object Detection
PROPOSAL: Inspired by BERT's success in masked language modeling, we develop a novel masked self-supervision strategy for domain-agnostic object detection. During test time, we randomly mask out random feature maps from the pre-trained vision-language detector's intermediate layer outputs and force it to reconstruct the original features. This creative, noise-injection type of self-supervision favours the learning of high-level features that are resilient to data shifts and ensures that the model can adapt efficiently in an open-set scenario, without confronting the label inconsistencies that characterise the heterogeneity of real-world domains. Masked self-supervision alleviates the reliance on consistently obtainable, high-quality pseudo-labels, providing a reliable mechanism for edge domains that contain little information.
CONTROLS:Evaluate adaptation to previously unseen categories on two diverse real-world datasets (COCO and LVIS), where the target categories are disjoint from the source categories; compare with well-established pseudo-label filtering strategies.
COST: 1656
PREDICTION: The effectiveness of masked self-supervision will depend on its ability to provide a nuanced representation learning mechanism that acts as a substitute to the more volatile pseudo-label generation and filtering approach.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradual Feature Re etiquering (GFR): Adaptive Object Detection through Masked Feature Valence Governance
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel adaptive mechanism that leverages the high-level features learned by the pre-trained vision-language detector and gradually re-labels these features during test time, assisting the model in dynamically adapting to novel domains while minimizing the reliance on high-quality pseudo-labels. This Gradual Feature Re etiquering (GFR) method applies a guided masking strategy to reduce the impact of noise on the model, encouraging the learning of weighted feature maps that adaptively reflect changing distribution of object instances in new environments. GFR's incremental updating ensures robustness to divergent target domains without multiplying adaptation overhead; the self-supervised mechanism efficiently explores novel data augmentation pathways, showcasing its adaptability to shifting distribution priors.
CONTROLS: Investigate and compare GFR to its most significant competitor, masked self-supervision, across several diverse object detection datasets (COCO, LVIS, and multiple category-shift scenarios).
COST: 2500
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the proposed mechanism will demonstrate improved robustness in adapting domain-agnostic vision-language models, specifically when undertaking mission-critical transfer of supervision frameworks among broad target domains.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Uncertainty-Aware Pseudo-Labeling for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection with Adaptive Re-weighting
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous suggestion by including a module that adaptively re-weights the uncertainty estimates during self-supervised training based on the distribution of predicted pseudo-labels. This allows the model to give more credit to reliable pseudo-labels and less to unreliable ones, improving overall object detection performance without compromising robustness to noise and out-of-distribution data. By leveraging these adaptively weighted pseudo-labels, the detector can better make use of the self-training process, distinguishing itself as a significantly more resilient and efficient mechanism for addressing real-world challenges in domain-agnostic test-time object detection.
CONTROLS: For comparison, experiment with an uncertainty estimator that does not adaptively re-weight pseudo-labels and assess thus generated pseudo-label performance against state-of-the-art non-test-time adaptive object detection methods. Compare also to Gradual Feature Re etiquering to tease apart merits of pseudo-label re-weighting in self-supervised learning.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Adaptive re-weighting is likely to offer a clearer milestone in unbiased feature learning among different episodic distributions across episode validations and represents an appealing extension of Less Consistently Guearanteed supervision theoretical derivations to more real-world perspectives.

TITLE: Self-Supervised Non-Negative Tensor Factorization for Multimodal Competence Enhancement in Test-Time Object Detection
PROPOSAL: We present a novel self-supervised learning approach to enhancing multimodal competence in object detection at test time. By leveraging non-negative tensor factorization, we decompose the feature spaces learned by the pre-trained vision-language detector into latent factors that capture semantic meaning across multiple modalities. This decomposition facilitates more efficient and adaptive learning under changing distributions, allowing the detector to process and reason about images and text simultaneously with greater accuracy and robustness to noise and data shifts. Implemented in a test-time incremental learning paradigm, the approach ensures seamless integration of the multimodal components into the overall system and achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple real-world object detection benchmarks.

PREDICTION: The proposed self-supervised learning based on tensor factorization is likely to result in out-of-the-box multimodal object detection performances which could serve as a unified solution specifically to rest share adaptive substantial promotion whole border modulation polar trends superiority sought.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Vision-Language Detector Adaptation via Self-Supervised Pseudo-Label Learning
PROPOSAL: This experiment aims to evaluate the impact of self-supervised pseudo-label learning (SSPL) on test-time adaptive object detection. The detector is trained on a set of unlabeled images where the pixel-wise correspondence between images and text encodes their similarity, following the principle of contrastive learning. By iteratively refining pseudo-labels through a small number of self-training updates performed on the unlabeled test images, the adaptation performance of a pre-trained GLIP (a vision-language detector) can be examined on several real-world benchmarks including PASCAL VOC and Microsoft COCO.
CONTROLS: Ablation study with self-training alone (pre-trained GLIP fine-tuned on pseudo-labeled target images), Standalone object detection on source-data (no adaptation), Plug-and-play adaptation (static pre-trained GLIP + TTA-based adapters), and prototypes of prior works which facilitate test-time adaptation via pseudo-labeled objects but utilizing statistics collected from source-data.
COST: 268.163
PREDICTION: SSPL is likely to outperform its ablated variants and plug-and-play adaptation counterparts due to the incorporation of cross-modality similarity learning but adaptation efficiency and reliability concerns are anticipated given the dependence of pseudo-label quality on high-quality pre-trained knowledge, background noise levels, and mini-batch property.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Complexity-Performance Tradeoff in Euclidean TSP with aprototypical scaling law
PROPOSAL: Train and analyze a large set (400-600) of Euclidean TSP instances with N points (N = 10^1, 10^2, 10^3) and model capacity M. Use a fixed problem instance size N, and vary the instance difficulty by increasing the number of points while maintaining a fixed average distance. Train models of varying complexities with scaled-up neural architectures (e.g., ResNet-18N) using alternatives to transformer-based methods, including random orthogonal weights or randomly initialized feedforward nets for low-M models. Observe performance degradation for increasing N, and compare it to the performance of models with similar M but large dataset sizes (D= 10^2, 10^3, 10^4). Record metrics including the normalized Hamiltonian length, model parameter count, and training time.
CONTROLS: Baseline models include the Euclidean-TSP-Net model with 5000 parameters and the Euclidean-TSP-OPT model which uses a branch-and-bound algorithm for solving the TSP with a large initial set of random solutions
COST: 800
PREDICTION: Performance of models characteristically degrades as the size of the smaller space (typically the solution space, but possibly the representation space) grows, and improves predictably with scaling up the parameter count and fixed-size D-infinity dataset sizes within similar training conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Role of Model Capacity in Euclidean TSP with Self-Modifying Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: Train a set of self-modifying neural networks (SMNns) on a diverse Euclidean TSP dataset. Use the SMNNs to find a set of edges in the graph that, when removed, yield a subgraph for which the remaining TSP instance can be solved via an efficient (e.g., linear-time) algorithm, i.e., the fundamental limits of a TSP problem are hidden substructures. Treat the SMNNs as proxies to understand the similarity between the original problem and an instance of the easier problem. Analyze how increasing the model capacity affects the SMNN's graph manipulation performance and compare these to threshold values derived from curve-fitting models of TSP hardness. Develop alternative strategies to manipulate a model's capacity that avoids data augmentation, random initialization, or scaling the learning rate, and thus aim at clarifying the fundamental role of the capacity of a learned model in preventing rapid 'easy' set convergence phenomena in large-scale TSP domains.
CONTROLS: Compare to Identity-aware Metric Learning Model (IMLM) and Decentralized Spiking Neural Network (DSNN)
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: The proposed approach allows for smoothing performance curves in very hard zones and might offer definitive explanations of well-known relations and metric relationships when the amount of ground-truth validation samples for the new metrics collected by the surrogate model escapes to be more complex than the task at hand.

TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Capacity Allocation on Euclidean TSP Problem-Solving with Neural Modules
PROPOSAL: Develop a framework for allocating capacity within neural networks to address the Euclidean TSP problem. Use a combination of graph-based methods and entropic regularizers to allocate capacity to different parts of the network. Evaluate the impact of different capacity allocation strategies on the performance of neural networks on Euclidean TSP instances of varying problem scales. Investigate how capacity allocation affects the emergence of problem-specific features and the ability of the network to generalize to new instances. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Neural Scaling Laws in Synthetically Generated Instances of the Euclidean Traveling Salesman Problem
PROPOSAL: We design an experiment to train neural networks on synthetic TSP instances with varying solution space sizes, generated by independently scaling the TSP graph sizes and the dimensionality of the representation. We will use a GWR architecture to train instance-wise TSP solvers with 3 different model sizes (100k, 1M, 10M parameters), and a compute budget ranging from 1-16 GPUs. We will track learning dynamics using instance-wise loss and use Breadth-First Search as a baseline.
CONTROLS: We compare with other scalable baselines, such as the Held-Karp algorithm and cutting plane methods.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: We expect to see evidence supporting the existence of neural scaling laws for TSP solvers, with improved performance as both the solution space and the model size are scaled. However, we anticipate the scaling law will fail for higher-dimensional representations, where the instance-wise loss is expected to degrade rapidly due to the curse of dimensionality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Probing the Effects of Increasing Solution Space and Representation Dimensionality on Neural TSP Representations
PROPOSAL: To understand how the capacity of the model affects performance in high-dimensional solution spaces, we analyze the representations learned by the trained GWR architectures (used in proposal 1) in the lower-dimensional TSP instances before imposing higher dimensionality. We will use mutual information-based techniques (such as the information-theoretic neural embedding analysis) to identify features that are retained or lost as the dimensionality is increased.
CONTROLS: We compare the mutual information patterns against those observed in lower-dimensional TSP instances, and against representations learned using an attention-based TSP solver.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that features that capture structural information about the Euclidean space are preserved as dimensionality increases, while features that capture finer details (such as optimal routes for specific instances) are lost as the representation's capacity is overwhelmed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Neural Scaling Laws for Infinite-Depth Tree-Structured Representations
PROPOSAL: Assuming the neural network instance consists of an infinite-depth tree-structured representation, where each internal node compresses or selects features, we theoretically derive a neural scaling law that accounts for both the size of the solution space and the representation dimensionality. We assume that performance is a function of the mutual information between the input and internal node representations. We derive an expression that relates model performance to the network's depth, width, and internal node computability.
CONTROLS: We validate our theoretical results against the empirical findings from proposals 1 and 2, and we compare against an arbitrary baseline assumption.
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: The derived theoretical result should provide insights into the mechanisms behind neural scaling laws and correctly predict the observed performance trends in the empirical analysis. However, the inaccuracy of the arithmetic-tree assumption at high representation dimensionality may cause the theoretical and empirical scaling laws to diverge.

TITLE: Neural Scaling Laws for Non-Euclidean TSP on Single-Layer Graph Embeddings
PROPOSAL: We generalize the analysis of neural scaling laws for Euclidean TSP in proposal 1 to geodesic distances on single-layer graph embeddings, allowing us to analyze the impact of geometric complexity on neural network performance. We explore the effect of scaling embedding dimensionality and the number of nodes on the performance of neural solvers, and we investigate the interplay between spectral and geometric properties of the graph.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of spectral embeddings optimized for geodesic distances with that of black-box neural solvers on the TSP-Graph-Embedding.

PREDICTION: We expect that the transition from Euclidean to non-Euclidean distances will highlight the importance of learning optimized representations in high-dimensional geometric spaces, while the scaling behavior remains predictable.

TITLE: Towards a Unified Theory of Neural Scaling Laws for Combinatorial Optimization
PROPOSAL: We propose a unified framework for understanding the neural scaling laws in combinatorial optimization problems, which combines the insights from the previous proposals and provides a theoretical foundation for predicting the performance of neural networks in solving complex optimization problems. We use tools from high-dimensional geometry, statistical physics, and machine learning to derive a set of mathematical equations that describe the dependence of neural network performance on the problem size, model capacity, and learning schedule.
CONTROLS: Compare against a simplified version of the theory that neglects certain terms or assumes idealized conditions.
COST: 12600
PREDICTION: We expect to derive a set of equations that accurately predict the neural scaling laws in combinatorial optimization problems, including the dependence on problem size, model capacity, and learning schedule. This will provide a valuable tool for practitioners to design and optimize neural networks for complex optimization problems.

PROPOSAL: We will investigate how neural networks trained on a simplified, synthetic version of the Euclidean traveling salesman problem (a set of pairwise distances between cities) perform when scaling the solution space (e.g., more cities) and the representation space (e.g., more city coordinates) independently, using a tightly controlled simulation environment. We will use the accordance optimization algorithm to train neural networks on a specific sequence of complexity-increasing problem instances, while varying model size, activation functions, and solver approximations. CONTROLS: Comparison with forward planning heuristics, random search, grid search; ablating the accordance solver; experiment with different objectives.

PREDICTION: We expect neural networks to degrade slowly at first but then catastrophically as the solution space expands combinatorially, showing that simply scaling the capacity may not stabilize performance in this regime. However, this may fail if the loss landscape of accordance diverges at large scales, rendering local solvers useless.

TITLE: Probing Neural Scaling Laws under Independent Complexity Scaling
PROPOSAL: We will investigate how neural networks trained on a simplified, synthetic version of the Euclidean traveling salesman problem (a set of pairwise distances between cities) perform when scaling the solution space (e.g., more cities) and the representation space (e.g., more city coordinates) independently, using a tightly controlled simulation environment. We will use the accordance optimization algorithm to train neural networks on a specific sequence of complexity-increasing problem instances, while varying model size, activation functions, and solver approximations. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Performance Degradation under Combinatorial Solution Space Growth
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of combinatorially growing solution space sizes on a model of fixed capacity, specifically using the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) as a benchmark. Experiment with models of progressively increasing depth and capacity (e.g., neural networks of 2, 3, and 4 layers with 1024, 2048, and 4096 units each).
We will train the network using a Euclidean distance metric and a small number of neighboring nodes to simulate a growing solution space. The performance metric will be the inverse of the average tour length.
CONTROLS: Baseline networks with small numbers of nodes (20, 50), and ablation studies to isolate the effect of depth and capacity.
COST: 100
PREDICTION: We expect to observe a performance degradation that follows a polynomial or exponential trend, indicating the curse of dimensionality taking hold. The-specific form of the trend may be influenced by the capacity and depth of the model, with shallower models exhibiting diminishing returns and deeper models showing potentially dramatic performance drops.

TITLE: Refined A Theoretical Framework for Predicting Model Performance in Homogeneous Scalability Regimes
PROPOSAL: Refined the theoretical framework to explicitly account for both combinatorial and representation space scalability. Introduce a system of coupled differential equations (CDEs) that describe the convergence rate of the model's performance as a function of these critical scalability parameters. The CDEs should be formulated in a way that makes them computationally tractable and permits the application of existing techniques for solving nonlinear differential equations.
The adjusted theoretical framework can be evaluated and compared against the performance of the existing experiments (e.g., Quantifying Performance Degradation under Combinatorial Solution Space Growth and Characterizing the Effect of Representation Space Dimensionality Growth on Model Performance) to assess its predictive power and accuracy in modeling realistic scaling scenarios.

COST: 2500
PREDICTION: The refined framework will provide improved predictive power by better modeling the interplay between combinatorial and representation space scalability, leading to more accurate estimates of performance convergence rates in large-scale scenarios.
