ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Investigation of the COMAP Problem under Representation Space Dimensionality Growth
PROPOSAL: Experimentally investigate the effect of growing representation space dimensionality on model performance on the COMAP problem, which is a well-studied problem related to the Euclidean TSP and often used as a benchmark in computational geometry. We will use the trained models from the previous experiments (e.g., Characterizing the Effect of Representation Space Dimensionality Growth on Model Performance) and subject them to the COMAP problem to assess their ability to generalize to new tasks.
The models will be evaluated on the COMAP-generated problem instances, measuring the convergence rate of the model's performance and its robustness to increasing dimensionality.

CONTROLS: Use the same set of trained models used in Characterizing the Effect of Representation Space Dimensionality Growth on Model Performance.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: The experimental results will provide quantitative evidence of how well the models generalize to the COMAP problem and whether any observed trends or correlations with the solution space dimensionality hold for this specific task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Model Complexity on Performance Degradation in Heterogeneous Scalability Regimes
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of model complexity on performance degradation in heterogeneous scalability regimes, where both the solution space size and the representation space dimensionality grow simultaneously. We will use a wide range of neural network architectures with varying depths, widths, and activation functions to examine how model complexity influences performance degradation in these regimes.
To simulate heterogeneous scalability regimes, we'll create progressively more complex problem instances of the TSP and several other Euclidean route optimization problems, and use a state-of-the-art solver to generate solutions that match the growth of the solution space size and representation space dimensionality.

CONTROLS: Compare the performance degradation of a range of neural network architectures (e.g., shallow and deep CNNs, ResNets, and Transformers) trained on the same task.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: The results will provide insights into how model complexity influences performance degradation in heterogeneous scalability regimes and whether highly expressive models can mitigate or exacerbate performance degradation in these regimes.

TITLE: Analyzing the Interplay between Model Capabilities and Problem Difficulty in Euclidean Route Optimization
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the growth of problem difficulty in Euclidean route optimization problems (e.g., number of cities, edge lengths, and obstacles) affects the performance of models with different capabilities (e.g., capacity, representational power, and ability to generalize).
We will use a range of state-of-the-art models (e.g., neural networks, reinforcement learning agents) to tackle problems of varying difficulty and analyze the interplay between model capabilities and problem difficulty. This will provide insights into how model limitations affect performance in heterogeneous scalability regimes.

CONTROLS: Compare the performance of a range of models with different capabilities on problems of varying difficulty.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: The results will highlight the relationship between model capabilities and problem difficulty in Euclidean route optimization and shed light on the role of scalability in determining model performance in complex optimization tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Performance Degradation under Combinatorial Solution Space Growth
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of combinatorially growing solution space sizes on a model of fixed capacity, specifically using the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) as a benchmark. Experiment with models of progressively increasing depth and capacity (e.g., neural networks of 2, 3, and 4 layers with 1024, 2048, and 4096 units each).
We will train the network using a Euclidean distance metric and a small number of neighboring nodes to simulate a growing solution space. The performance metric will be the inverse of the average tour length.
CONTROLS: Baseline networks with small numbers of nodes (20, 50), and ablation studies to isolate the effect of depth and capacity.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: We expect to observe a performance degradation that follows a polynomial or exponential trend, indicating the curse of dimensionality taking hold. The-specific form of the trend may be influenced by the capacity and depth of the model, with shallower models exhibiting diminishing returns and deeper models showing potentially dramatic performance drops.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Characterizing the Effect of Representation Space Dimensionality Growth on Model Performance
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of dimensionality growth in the representation space on model performance. To isolate this effect, we'll use a discrete solution space (e.g., the TSP) but an embedding with an increasingly high dimension (e.g., 10, 20, 50, and 100 dimensions) to encode the solution.
We'll use a permutation-invariant network (PINN) as the baseline model and test different PINNs with different dimensionality growth rates, training them on synthetic data generated using the COMAP (coefficients of motion and progression) problem.
CONTROLS:  Baseline PINNs with fixed representation space dimensionality (e.g., 5 dimensions) and ablation studies to test the effect of increasing dimensionality.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: We expect that the performance will degrade rapidly with increasing dimensionality, potentially showing a convergence to a near-flat plateaus followed by a cluster of intertwined optimal solutions.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Supervision Signals for Multilingual Data-Quality Raters
PROPOSAL: Compare three types of supervision signals for training multilingual data-quality raters: (1) mixed-language text from Wikipedia and Wiktionary, (2) low-resource language datasets from Clulib, and (3) default web crawling standards (e.g., top-N keywords). Evaluate performance using metrics such as accuracy, efficiency, and entity coverage. Train and test raters on multilingual web pages crawled from Common Crawl in 10 languages (with English and Arabic as primary evaluation languages). Use a simple transformer-based model as the rater architecture, with a classification head for quality judgments.
CONTROLS: Train and test raters on historical Common Crawl data without any supervision signals as an ablation, and fine-tune English BERT and SAS intermediate models for comparisons.
COST: 722.339
PREDICTION: Supervision signals from mixed-language text and Clulib datasets may outperform default web crawling standards, but all three may have high accuracy and comparable entity coverage.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Select from Multiple Raters for Improved Quality Judgments
PROPOSAL: Explore using an ensemble approach to multilingual data-quality rater training, where a meta-model selects the best among multiple, language-specific raters conditioned on input context. Train and evaluate various meta-model architectures on top of the raters investigated in proposal 1, including a simple temperature-scaled logistic model and a more complex attention-based combiner. Use the additional data complexity added by the ensemble approach to investigate the interaction between rater accuracy and rater diversity.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the ensemble approach against a baseline that uniformly samples raters, and ablate the impact of each rater by turning off one rater at a time and retraining the ensemble.
COST: 1029.23
PREDICTION: The ensemble approach may outperform single-rater models in terms of downstream classification and ranking performance, and better leverage diverse supervision signals for improved data quality. However, it could increase model complexity and computations, ultimately impacting performance if the individual raters are noisily trained on weak supervision.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Supervision Signals for Multilingual Data-Quality Raters
PROPOSAL: Compare three types of supervision signals for training multilingual data-quality raters: (1) mixed-language text from Wikipedia and Wiktionary, (2) low-resource language datasets from Clulib, and (3) default web crawling standards (e.g., top-N keywords). Evaluate performance using metrics such as accuracy, efficiency, and entity coverage. Train and test raters on multilingual web pages crawled from Common Crawl in 10 languages (with English and Arabic as primary evaluation languages). Use a simple transformer-based model as the rater architecture, with a classification head for quality judgments.
CONTROLS: Train and test raters on historical Common Crawl data without any supervision signals as an ablation, and fine-tune English BERT and SAS intermediate models for comparisons.
COST: 2168
PREDICTION: Supervision signals from mixed-language text and Clulib datasets may outperform default web crawling standards, but all three may have high accuracy and comparable entity coverage.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Select from Multiple Raters for Improved Quality Judgments
PROPOSAL: Explore using an ensemble approach to multilingual data-quality rater training, where a meta-model selects the best among multiple, language-specific raters conditioned on input context. Train and evaluate various meta-model architectures on top of the raters investigated in proposal 1, including a simple temperature-scaled logistic model and a more complex attention-based combiner. Use the additional data complexity added by the ensemble approach to investigate the interaction between rater accuracy and rater diversity.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the ensemble approach against a baseline that uniformly samples raters, and ablate the impact of each rater by turning off one rater at a time and retraining the ensemble.
COST: 3064
PREDICTION: The ensemble approach may outperform single-rater models in terms of downstream classification and ranking performance, and better leverage diverse supervision signals for improved data quality. However, it could increase model complexity and computations, ultimately impacting performance if the individual raters are noisily trained on weak supervision.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustness and Interpretability of Multilingual Data-Quality Raters
PROPOSAL: Conduct robustness and interpretability analysis on the multilingual data-quality raters trained in proposals 1 and 2. Investigate how raters generalize across languages, domains, and input styles by applying them to out-of-distribution (OOD) data (e.g., news articles, book chapters, and spoken dialogues) from different sources (e.g., Wikipedia, Common Crawl, and Web5). Introduce task-relevant diagnostics to analyze the model's decision-making processes, highlight feature importance, and compare attention-weighted features across language and rater combinations. 
CONTROLS: Analyze the sensitivity of the raters to specific linguistic or cultural features via a linguistic or cultural bias analysis. Run feature attribution tasks to identify key factors that influence rater predictions.
COST: 4096
PREDICTION: Raters may struggle with OOD data, but adaptably incorporating interpretability and robustness will help identify linguistic features with higher value, mitigating explanatory performance gaps and identify model weak-links.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Supervision Signals for Multilingual Data-Quality Raters
PROPOSAL: Extend the investigation of supervision signals in proposal 1 by incorporating multimodal supervision signals for better performance of multilingual data-quality raters. Introduce multimodal supervision from diverse non-text sources (e.g., images, videos, and audio clips) and evaluate the impact on quality judgments in multiple languages. Use a self-supervised Visual-Linguistic Representation Generator as a multimodal encoder to process text-image pairs and train vision-only raters on these pairs, comparing them with text-only models.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of text-only and multimodal raters against English BERT and SAS intermediate models for quality judgments, comprehensively compare across varied benchmark datasets and language models evaluated in 6 languages, (English, German, Spanish, Arabic, Chinese-simple, Russian)
COST: 3150
PREDICTION: Adding multimodal supervision may lead to improved quality judgment accuracy, but at the expense of increased computational complexity.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Learning to Select from Multiple Raters for Improved Quality Judgments
PROPOSAL: Modify the learning strategy for proposal 2 by fine-tuning the meta-model on its predictions using label smoothing regularization and learnable temperature scaling. This will help the meta-model adaptively adjust its threshold and bias towards less adherent languages and thereby cope with performance degradations due to limited data quality in certain languages.
CONTROLS: Regularly fine-tune the best meta-model across warmer temperatures and tail off similar meta-model under label smoothing operations.
COST: 2853
PREDICTION: This extension should further improve performance of selected raters and reduce performance gap between specific raters due to significantly smoothed effect in operations on potentially weakly or less adjudicated End-languages.

PROPOSAL: We propose a domain-adversarial training framework for multilingual data-quality raters, which leverages adversarial training to improve the model's robustness and adaptability across different languages and domains. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Translated Quality Label Transfer
PROPOSAL: To deal with the limited availability of high-quality samples from existing benchmarks in each language, we propose to utilize machine translation to transfer quality labels from one language to another. Our approach involves first obtaining quality labels on a relatively large set of texts in a language (the donor language) and then generating high-quality versions of texts in other languages using machine translation. We then train our multilingual quality rater on these translated high-quality documents to obtain quality labels for the non-donor languages.
CONTROLS: We evaluate this approach by comparing it to our previous best model, revised MASSIVELY Multilingual FineWeb2-HQ, and by assessing its performance on four different languages: English, Spanish, Hindi and Arabic.
COST: 8310
PREDICTION: Transferring high-quality samples might indeed improve performance in the target languages where little information about sentences is available in linguistics, but may also struggle with translation outliers, limiting the quality performance of the pretraining rater when coping with hard highlow noise feeds within tandem translation score range.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Meta-Learned Quality Rater
PROPOSAL: We revise the Meta-Learned Quality Rater proposal by focusing on a more efficient and effective transfer learning approach, leveraging a curriculum of pre-trained language models to adapt to the quality rater task. Specifically, we use a progressive curriculum learning strategy to gradually increase the difficulty of the quality rater task, allowing the model to learn from easier tasks and adapt to more challenging ones.
CONTROLS: We evaluate this revised Meta-Learned Quality Rater against our previous best model, Translated Quality Label Transfer, and ablate the impact of the curriculum learning strategy on the model's performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Fidelity Evaluation Framework
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-fidelity evaluation framework to compare the performance of different quality raters on the task of selecting high-quality pretraining data. This framework involves evaluating the raters using a combination of metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and percentage of correctly labeled examples, at different levels of evaluation intensity (e.g., coarse, medium, fine). We also investigate the trade-offs between evaluation intensity and computational cost.
CONTROLS: We evaluate our proposed framework against a set of baseline metrics and compare it to existing evaluation frameworks in the field.
COST: 14000
PREDICTION: This framework should provide a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different quality raters and help identify areas for improvement, but may also be computationally expensive and require careful tuning of evaluation intensity and metrics.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Meta-Learned Quality Rater
PROPOSAL: We revise the Meta-Learned Quality Rater proposal by focusing on a more efficient and effective transfer learning approach, leveraging a curriculum of pre-trained language models to adapt to the quality rater task. Specifically, we use a progressive curriculum learning strategy to gradually increase the difficulty of the quality rater task, allowing the model to learn from easier tasks and adapt to more challenging ones.
CONTROLS: We evaluate this revised Meta-Learned Quality Rater against our previous best model, Translated Quality Label Transfer, and ablate the impact of the curriculum learning strategy on the model's performance.
COST: 35000
PREDICTION: This revised approach should lead to improved adaptation to the quality rater task and better generalization to new languages and domains, but may also be affected by the order and difficulty of the tasks in the curriculum, potentially leading to overfitting or suboptimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Fidelity Evaluation Framework
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-fidelity evaluation framework to compare the performance of different quality raters on the task of selecting high-quality pretraining data. This framework involves evaluating the raters using a combination of metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and percentage of correctly labeled examples, at different levels of evaluation intensity (e.g., coarse, medium, fine). We also investigate the trade-offs between evaluation intensity and computational cost.
CONTROLS: We evaluate our proposed framework against a set of baseline metrics and compare it to existing evaluation frameworks in the field.
COST: 42000
PREDICTION: This framework should provide a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different quality raters and help identify areas for improvement, but may also be computationally expensive and require careful tuning of evaluation intensity and metrics.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Multi-Fidelity Evaluation Framework
PROPOSAL: We revise the Multi-Fidelity Evaluation Framework proposal by integrating it with our previous proposals, leveraging the quality labeling capabilities of the Meta-Learned Quality Rater and the adaptability of the Translated Quality Label Transfer approach. Specifically, we use the Meta-Learned Quality Rater to generate labels for the test data, and then evaluate the performance of the Translated Quality Label Transfer approach using the Multi-Fidelity Evaluation Framework.
CONTROLS: We compare this revised framework to our previous best model, Massively Multilingual FineWeb2-HQ, and assess its scalability and adaptability on large-scale pretraining datasets.
COST: 50000

Validate the performance on real-world multilingual corpora and compare to traditional baselines.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Compact Geometry-Appearance Representation for 3D Objects via Spherical Harmonics
PROPOSAL: We will explore a new 3D representation that combines geometry and appearance using spherical harmonics. Our approach will involve a 3D neural network that receives as input a 2D image and predicts a dense 3D occupancy grid and a set of spherical harmonics coefficients representing the object's appearance from the input view. To test this approach, we will train the model on the ShapeNetCore dataset with 10-fold cross-validation and evaluate its performance on the standard metrics of surface reconstruction (surface distance) and visual realism (SSIM and PSNR between the rendered and real images). We will also compare our results to those of state-of-the-art geometry-only models (e.g., PointRCNN) and appearance-only models (e.g., NeRF).
CONTROLS: We will also compare our results to geometry-only models trained without the spherical harmonics component to evaluate the impact of appearance on geometry reconstruction.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to outperform geometry-only models in terms of appearance realism and to achieve comparable performance to appearance-only models in terms of geometry accuracy. However, the approach may struggle with objects having complex or non-convex shapes.

TITLE: Accelerated Data Collection with a Geometry-Appearance Primitive Density Model
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel data collection strategy that utilizes a learned geometry-appearance primitive density model to efficiently sample a diverse set of objects from real-world datasets such as the ObjectNet or Shapenet dataset. The model will be trained to predict the density of primitives (e.g., spheres, cylinders, planes) in 3D space that capture both the geometry and appearance of objects. We will then use this model to generate a dataset of objects with a varying level of complexity and detail, which can be used to train and evaluate our geometry-appearance representation.
CONTROLS: We will also evaluate the quality of the generated dataset by comparing the reconstructed shapes and appearances with ground truth data and compare the sample efficiency of our approach to traditional random sampling methods.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: We expect our data collection strategy to significantly reduce the need for manual object picking and labeling, and to lead to more diverse and representative training datasets. However, the quality of the generated dataset may suffer if the primitive density model is poorly trained or if the generated primitives are not accurately captured by the geometry-appearance representation.

TITLE: Object-to-Image Generation using Geometry-Appearance Representations
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the ability of our geometry-appearance representations to generate high-quality 2D images from 3D objects, and vice versa. We will use the REVISED: Compact Geometry-Appearance Representation for 3D Objects via Spherical Harmonics as the underlying representation, and train a neural renderer to produce images from the reconstructed 3D objects. We will also investigate the use of generated images as input to the REVISED: Compact Geometry-Appearance Representation for 3D Objects via Spherical Harmonics, to create a cycle-consistent object-to-image generation pipeline.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to state-of-the-art image generation and 2D-to-3D reconstruction methods, such as DALL-E andresses-neRF.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to achieve competitive performance in object-to-image generation, and to provide a more interpretable and controllable representation of 3D objects. However, we may find that the generated images are not always accurate or photorealistic, particularly for objects with complex shapes or appearances.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learned Geometry-Appearance Fusion with View-Dependent Rendering
PROPOSAL: Modify the DALL-E model architecture to include a new 3D geometry-conditioned appearance module that fuses view-dependent multiview features from a separate vision model. Train the module to predict a signed distance function that represents the object's view-dependent geometry and appearance simultaneously, using a dataset of objects with rich view-dependent appearance such as cars, motorcycles, and streetlights. Optimise the module using Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss for geometry and a custom combination of MSE and Discrete Bhattacharyya Distance (DBD) for appearance.
CONTROLS: Baseline: basic DALL-E architecture without the new module; ablation: same architecture with geometry and appearance modules trained separately.
COST: 400000
PREDICTION: The model successfully captures view-dependent effects and achieves competitive results with existing geometry-only and appearance-only 3D representations, potentially exposing limitations of prior model architectures and hinting at additional advantages from the fusion of geometry and appearance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring View-Dependent 3D Latent Representations via Voxel OT Disentanglement
PROPOSAL: We leverage Optimal Transport (OT) based disentanglement to create a compact 3D latent representation that jointly captures an object's geometry and view-dependent appearance, without requiring heavy data preprocessing. Specifically, we utilize a structure preserving OT reformulation to separate geometry and appearance distributions, and then define a learnable mapping that recovers view-dependent appearance features from the disentangled appearance latent space.
CONTROLS: Compare with previous geometric-only latent representation baselines like Occupancy Networks and DeepVoxels, and also against appearance-focused structured latents like DIB-R; ablating both OT formulation and disentanglement component.
COST: 920
PREDICTION: Successful disentanglement should yield 3D reconstructions that accurately capture view-dependent effects and represent material properties like reflectance and roughness, outperforming previous geometric-only latents; however, it may require substantial computational resources to cope with high-dimensional appearance features.

PROPOSAL: We introduce a probabilistic generative model that learns to jointly reconstruct 3D geometry and view-dependent appearance from single images. Our model, named SPADE (Sparse Point Augmented Density Estimation), uses a hierarchical latent space to effectively disentangle geometric and appearance factors, allowing for accurate reconstruction of shapes, materials, lighting, and view-dependent effects.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: SDF-APE: Signed Distance Function with Appearance Primatives Embedded
PROPOSAL: We propose SDF-APE, a latent 3D representation that combines signed distance functions (SDFs) with appearance primatives. SDF-APE encodes objects as 3D shapes in the SDF space and stores appearance information such as color, roughness and metallicity as primatives. By tightly integrating these two components, SDF-APE can jointly capture geometry and view-dependent appearance without requiring heavy data preprocessing. 
CONTROLS: Standard SDF-based reconstruction models (e.g. Occupancy Networks) with and without appearance embedding (e.g. from District); a baseline model that combines separate SDF and appearance latent spaces.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: SDF-APE should outperform existing geometry-only and appearance-only models on metrics like shape fidelity and view-dependent appearance, but may fail to scale to complex scenes due to increased model complexity.

TITLE: Multi-View Consistency Regularization for SDF-APE
PROPOSAL: To address the view-dependent issues in SDF-APE, we propose a new regularization technique that enforces multi-view consistency across different viewpoints. This can be achieved by adding a consistency loss term between the appearance primatives and the rendered images from the same viewpoint. By doing so, SDF-APE can learn to generate consistent view-dependent effects across different views.
CONTROLS: SDF-APE without multi-view consistency regularization; SDF-APE with traditional regularization techniques (e.g. L1/L2 regularization) for SDF and appearance primatives.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Weakly Supervised Implementation of SDF-APE using OOD Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: To make SDF-APE applicable to scenarios with limited or no paired geometry-appearance supervision, we propose to use Out-of-Distribution (OOD) reconstruction as a weak supervision signal. Specifically, we will generate synthetic images of the same object from different viewpoints and train SDF-APE to reconstruct the unseen views. By doing so, SDF-APE can learn to hallucinate the geometry and appearance of the object without explicit supervision.
CONTROLS: SDF-APE trained with strong geometry-appearance supervision; SDF-APE trained with limited supervision (e.g. geometry only or appearance only); a baseline OOD reconstruction model (e.g. FVD).
COST: 4511
PREDICTION: The weakly supervised implementation of SDF-APE should be able to generate plausible geometry and appearance for unseen views, but may struggle with hallucinating subtle view-dependent effects and may require fine-tuning for specific object classes.

PROPOSAL: Since objects in the real world have varying levels of smoothness and coarseness, a single geometric normalization technique may not work across all objects. This will allow SDF-APE to generate consistent view-dependent appearance across objects of varying smoothness.
CONTROLS: SDF-APE with traditional geometric normalization techniques (e.g. PCA, ICP); SDF-APE with a static learnable normalization scheme; a baseline model that uses a combination of multiple geometric normalization techniques.

PREDICTION: The learnable geometric normalization scheme should improve the consistency of view-dependent appearance across objects of varying smoothness, but may require careful tuning of the normalization coefficients and may be computationally expensive to train.

This will allow SDF-APE to learn the view-dependent appearance representation in a more organized and efficient manner.
CONTROLS: SDF-APE without curriculum learning; SDF-APE with traditional curriculum learning techniques; a baseline model that uses a combination of multiple curriculum learning techniques.
COST: 216000
PREDICTION: The curriculum learning framework should improve the training efficiency and convergence of SDF-APE, but may require careful tuning of the curriculum and may not generalize well to unseen objects and complex scenes.

textes:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: SDF-APE: Signed Distance Function with Appearance Primatives Embedded
PROPOSAL: We propose SDF-APE, a latent 3D representation that combines signed distance functions (SDFs) with appearance primatives. SDF-APE encodes objects as 3D shapes in the SDF space and stores appearance information such as color, roughness and metallicity as primatives. By tightly integrating these two components, SDF-APE can jointly capture geometry and view-dependent appearance without requiring heavy data preprocessing. 
CONTROLS: Standard SDF-based reconstruction models (e.g. Occupancy Networks) with and without appearance embedding (e.g. from District); a baseline model that combines separate SDF and appearance latent spaces.
COST: 4800
PREDICTION: SDF-APE should outperform existing geometry-only and appearance-only models on metrics like shape fidelity and view-dependent appearance, but may fail to scale to complex scenes due to increased model complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-View Consistency Regularization for SDF-APE
PROPOSAL: To address the view-dependent issues in SDF-APE, we propose a new regularization technique that enforces multi-view consistency across different viewpoints. This can be achieved by adding a consistency loss term between the appearance primatives and the rendered images from the same viewpoint. By doing so, SDF-APE can learn to generate consistent view-dependent effects across different views.
CONTROLS: SDF-APE without multi-view consistency regularization; SDF-APE with traditional regularization techniques (e.g. L1/L2 regularization) for SDF and appearance primatives.
COST: 9200
PREDICTION: The multi-view consistency regularization should improve the view-dependent appearance fidelity of SDF-APE, but may increase the risk of overfitting to the training data and require careful tuning of regularization strength.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Weakly Supervised Implementation of SDF-APE using OOD Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: To make SDF-APE applicable to scenarios with limited or no paired geometry-appearance supervision, we propose to use Out-of-Distribution (OOD) reconstruction as a weak supervision signal. Specifically, we will generate synthetic images of the same object from different viewpoints and train SDF-APE to reconstruct the unseen views. By doing so, SDF-APE can learn to hallucinate the geometry and appearance of the object without explicit supervision.
CONTROLS: SDF-APE trained with strong geometry-appearance supervision; SDF-APE trained with limited supervision (e.g. geometry only or appearance only); a baseline OOD reconstruction model (e.g. FVD).
COST: 13600
PREDICTION: The weakly supervised implementation of SDF-APE should be able to generate plausible geometry and appearance for unseen views, but may struggle with hallucinating subtle view-dependent effects and may require fine-tuning for specific object classes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Geometric Normalization for Consistent View-Dependent Appearance
PROPOSAL: Since objects in the real world have varying levels of smoothness and coarseness, a single geometric normalization technique may not work across all objects. To address this issue, we propose the use of a learnable geometric normalization scheme that can adapt to the specific geometry of each object. This will allow SDF-APE to generate consistent view-dependent appearance across objects of varying smoothness.
CONTROLS: SDF-APE with traditional geometric normalization techniques (e.g. PCA, ICP); SDF-APE with a static learnable normalization scheme; a baseline model that uses a combination of multiple geometric normalization techniques.
COST: 18400
PREDICTION: The learnable geometric normalization scheme should improve the consistency of view-dependent appearance across objects of varying smoothness, but may require careful tuning of the normalization coefficients and may be computationally expensive to train.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Object-Specific Auto-Encoders for SDF-APE
PROPOSAL: To further improve the view-dependent appearance fidelity of SDF-APE, we propose the use of object-specific auto-encoders that can learn to map the object's views to its underlying appearance representation. This will allow SDF-APE to capture the specific view-dependent effects of each object, resulting in more realistic and accurate reconstructions.
CONTROLS: SDF-APE with a generic encoder-decoder architecture; SDF-APE with a closely-related object-specific auto-encoder (e.g. FaceNet); a baseline model that uses a combination of multiple object-specific auto-encoders.
COST: 26400
PREDICTION: The object-specific auto-encoders should significantly improve the view-dependent appearance fidelity of SDF-APE, but may require a large number of training samples to generalize well to new objects and may be computationally expensive to train.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Object-Specific Auto-Encoders for SDF-APE
PROPOSAL: To reduce the computational cost and requirement of large training samples, we revise the proposal to use a domain adaptation technique that adapts the generic appearance representation to the specific object, instead of using object-specific auto-encoders. This will allow SDF-APE to learn object-specific view-dependent effects with less training data and computation.
CONTROLS: SDF-APE with a generic encoder-decoder architecture; SDF-APE with the original object-specific auto-encoders; a baseline model that uses a combination of multiple domain adaptation techniques.
COST: 21600
PREDICTION: The domain adaptation technique should improve the view-dependent appearance fidelity of SDF-APE with reduced computational cost and training data requirements, but may still require some amount of object-specific knowledge and may not generalize well to unseen objects.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient SDF-Sampling for SDF-APE
PROPOSAL: To reduce the computational cost of SDF-APE, we propose an efficient SDF-sampling technique that extracts a sparse set of points from the SDF grid, reducing the number of points that need to be processed. This technique will allow SDF-APE to efficiently handle complex scenes and large meshes.
CONTROLS: SDF-APE with uniform sampling; SDF-APE with octree-based sampling; a baseline model that uses a combination of multiple SDF-sampling techniques.
COST: 36000
PREDICTION: The efficient SDF-sampling technique should significantly reduce the computational cost of SDF-APE, but may introduce some loss of accuracy in the view-dependent appearance fidelity, especially for complex scenes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware SDF-APE for View-Dependent Appearance
PROPOSAL: To improve the robustness and uncertainty estimation of SDF-APE, we propose an uncertainty-aware framework that models the uncertainty in the view-dependent appearance representation. This will allow SDF-APE to identify its limitations and provide a confidence score for the generated views.
CONTROLS: SDF-APE without uncertainty estimation; SDF-APE with traditional uncertainty estimation techniques (e.g. KL-divergence, cross-entropy); a baseline model that uses a combination of multiple uncertainty estimation techniques.
COST: 50400
PREDICTION: The uncertainty-aware framework should improve the robustness and uncertainty estimation of SDF-APE, but may require careful tuning of the uncertainty estimation parameters and may introduce some computational overhead.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Discovering Task-Adaptive Sampling Orders
PROPOSAL: Investigate the possibility of training different autoregressive models for different sampling orders, in the hope that some order can yield significantly better sample efficiency. Train an ensemble of AR models with a search space of possible sampling orders, and evaluate their performance on the task of reconstructing the complete sequence. Control: Implement two baselines: (1) using the same AR model across all orders, and (2) randomly sampling an order for each model's forward pass. Estimate the global optimal order and train a model for that order. COST: 1440
CONTROLS: AR Model with Random Sampling Order; Fixed AR Model; Global Optimal Order Model
COST: 480
PREDICTION: We expect that with enough computational resources, we can find a sampling order that achieves comparable performance to the original AR model while reducing the number of sampling steps. However, finding the global optimal order might require exponential time complexity and thus be unfeasible.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Generative Mesh Autoencoders (GMAE)
PROPOSAL: Explore the idea of training a mesh autoencoder with a probabilistic graph structure, learnable edge weights, and a GMM mixture prior on the graph structure. This can potentially enable the generation of images using a single step, as the mesh encoding can be sampled from the prior in parallel. Investigate using the GMAE as a teacher to guide the one-step generator. Control: Compare the GMAE to the original AR model and note its efficiency under low steps. COST: 4320
CONTROLS: GAN with Flow Matching in Image Space; One-Step Generative Model
COST: 1440
PREDICTION: We expect that GMAE can achieve state-of-the-art results in terms of sample quality while significantly reducing the number of sampling steps. However, designing and optimizing the GMAE architecture might be computationally expensive and require considerable expertise.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Hierarchical Pathway Architecture (HPA)
PROPOSAL: Develop an HPA that interleaves shallow, high-capacity AR models with sparse, one-step mappings. The shallow AR models serve as subroutine generators, producing candidate tokens and later validated and combined through the one-step mapping, resulting in more accurate and efficient image generation. Investigate whether this hybrid approach matches and eventually surpasses the sample quality of DD1. CONTROL: Train an HPA with a performance baseline from the original AR model and evaluate efficiency improvements. COST: 7200
CONTROLS: HPA with Dense Sampling; HPA with Multi-Step Sampling; AR Baseline
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: The HPA has the potential to significantly improve sample efficiency while maintaining competitive sample quality compared to DD1, demonstrating adaptability and flexibility as it handles various tasks, reducing computational overhead and alleviating the noises present within uncompensated codes from autoregressive structure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Automaton-Based Mapping
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a mapping-based approach using a trained autoregressive model as the teacher to learn a sequence transducer (similar to sequence-to-sequence models, but with only one input and one output) to map a one-hot noise vector directly to a sequence of token predictions. The goal is to create a 1-step generator without relying on noise-to-data ordering or querying the autoregressive model at each step. Contrary to the flow matching technique used in DD1, we seek to rely on the capacity of transformer-based architectures to capture contextual relationships.
CONTROLS: Compare with original AR model, DD1's performance, and a variant of Automaton-Based Mapping with a smaller, simpler transducer.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: Expected to be competitive with or even superior to DD1, but might fail in edge cases where the autoregressive model generates unstable or context-dependent tokens that are difficult for the transducer to predict.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Probabilistic Signal Processing
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of Probabilistic Signal Processing (PSP) techniques, such as Gaussian Processes (GP), to model the dependencies between tokens in the autoregressive sequence. PSP can provide a structured view of the sequence, allowing for efficient simulation of the full conditional distribution of the random variables at each token position. This, in turn, enables the direct derivation of a probabilistic, conditionally-Gaussian mapping from a random input (noise or latent variable) to the full sequence of tokens.
CONTROLS: Evaluate PSP performance in one-step generation for comparison with AR model, DD1, and Revised Automaton-Based Mapping.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: Expected to show competitive or superior performance, especially in scenarios with strong correlations between tokens, but might fail to adapt to complex or highly variable token relationships.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Compositional Modeling
PROPOSAL: Develop a compositional modeling approach for autoregressive sequences by decomposing the sequence into smaller sub-sequences through recursive partitioning. Each sub-sequence is modeled independently using a learned mixture of conditional distributions. This hierarchical structure allows for adaptability in capturing local patterns and dependencies within the sequence. Train the compositional model end-to-end to optimize the conditioning distributions and sub-sequence representations jointly.
CONTROLS: Compare with original AR model, DD1's performance, and Revised Automaton-Based Mapping, with a focus on capturing long-range dependencies and adaptability.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: Expected to show improved performance and adaptability, particularly in scenarios with varying local patterns and dependencies, but might fail to generalize well when the underlying structure is complex or difficult to discover.

Train a score-based model to estimate the probability density of the noise sequence, and then invert this model to generate a synthetic noise sequence that is indistinguishable from the original sequence. Use this approach to generate complete autoregressive sequences from random noise inputs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Probabilistic Signal Processing
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of Probabilistic Signal Processing (PSP) techniques, such as Gaussian Processes (GP), to model the dependencies between tokens in the autoregressive sequence. PSP can provide a structured view of the sequence, allowing for efficient simulation of the full conditional distribution of the random variables at each token position. This, in turn, enables the direct derivation of a probabilistic, conditionally-Gaussian mapping from a random input (noise or latent variable) to the full sequence of tokens.
CONTROLS: Evaluate PSP performance in one-step generation for comparison with AR model, DD1, and Revised Automaton-Based Mapping.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: Expected to show competitive or superior performance, especially in scenarios with strong correlations between tokens, but might fail to adapt to complex or highly variable token relationships.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Compositional Modeling
PROPOSAL: Develop a compositional modeling approach for autoregressive sequences by decomposing the sequence into smaller sub-sequences through recursive partitioning. Each sub-sequence is modeled independently using a learned mixture of conditional distributions. This hierarchical structure allows for adaptability in capturing local patterns and dependencies within the sequence. Train the compositional model end-to-end to optimize the conditioning distributions and sub-sequence representations jointly.
CONTROLS: Compare with original AR model, DD1's performance, and Revised Automaton-Based Mapping, with a focus on capturing long-range dependencies and adaptability.
COST: 16200
PREDICTION: Expected to show improved performance and adaptability, particularly in scenarios with varying local patterns and dependencies, but might fail to generalize well when the underlying structure is complex or difficult to discover.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Utilize score-based models, similar to those used in diffusion-based generative models, but adapt them for noise synthesis in the context of autoregressive sequences. Train a score-based model to estimate the probability density of the noise sequence, and then invert this model to generate a synthetic noise sequence that is indistinguishable from the original sequence. Use this approach to generate complete autoregressive sequences from random noise inputs.
CONTROLS: Evaluate performance against the original AR model, DD1, Revised Automaton-Based Mapping, and Compositional Modeling in terms of generated sequence quality and one-step sampling efficiency.
COST: 24300
PREDICTION: Expected to show competitive or superior performance in terms of generated sequence quality, but might struggle with high-dimensional or complex sequences due to the challenges of score-based modeling.

PROPOSAL: Apply approximate dynamic programming (ADP) to the problem of generating complete autoregressive sequences from random noise inputs. Use intertemporal control to predict the immediate reward and define value function approximations learned ahead of exploration. Evaluate reduced dimensional dynamic programs of this form using ADP. Compute a reciprocal occupation density of a value function map upon the sampled target (sequence generated).
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of ADP-based sequence generation against the original AR model, DD1, Revised Automaton-Based Mapping, Compositional Modeling, and Score-Based Models for Noise Synthesis in terms of generation efficiency and quality.

PREDICTION: Expected to show improved generation efficiency while sacrificing some quality due to the approximation of the value function, but might fail in complex scenarios where the value function is difficult to approximate.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sequential Hierarchical Attention Flow
PROPOSAL: Develop a sequential hierarchical attention flow model for autoregressive sequence generation. This model first generates a high-level representation of the sequence using a transformer encoder, and then uses a hierarchical attention mechanism to iteratively refine this representation and generate the sequence token by token. The attention flow mechanism allows for efficient exploration of the sequence and adaptability to local patterns and dependencies.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of Sequential Hierarchical Attention Flow against the original AR model, DD1, Revised Automaton-Based Mapping, Compositional Modeling, Score-Based Models for Noise Synthesis, and Approximate Dynamic Programming for Sequence Generation in terms of generation quality and efficiency.
COST: 48600
PREDICTION: Expected to show strong performance and adaptability, particularly in scenarios with complex local patterns and dependencies, but might fail in very high-dimensional or long-range dependency scenarios due to the limitations of the hierarchical attention mechanism.

PROPOSAL: Develop a meta-learning approach to ensemble sequence generation models for autoregressive sequence generation. PREDICTION: Expected to show strong performance and adaptability, particularly in scenarios with varying local patterns and dependencies, but might fail in very complex or high-dimensional scenarios due to the meta-learning process' limitations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Guiding Expert Specialization with Token-Aware Load Balancing
PROPOSAL: We will train a series of MoE language models with an augmented load-balancing objective that incorporates a token-aware term, where the loss for each input token is weighted by the token's specificity. Specifically, we use a variant of the TF-IDF method to calculate token specificity, and add it as a multiplier to the standard load-balancing loss. We will experiment with different methods for computing token specificity, including TF-IDF and a variant that takes into account the token's strategic position in the sequence.
CONTROLS: Baselines include a standard MoE model with global load balancing, and an MoE model with an augmented load balancing loss using a learned attention weighing for each token. We will also ablate the relative importance of token specificity for the routing diversity by controlling its magnitude and experimenting with its normalization.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this loss function to facilitate more diverse routing and, by extension, more specialized tokens for each expert. This should lead to better performance on tasks like mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension, where tokens often have distinct distributions. We predict that this approach will not improve performance on redundant tasks like language modeling, where the diversity of tokens may not be as beneficial. However, the combination of token-aware and standard load balancing may lead to some negative effects on global routing diversity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Orthogonal Routing Regularizer for Expert Specialization
PROPOSAL: We will introduce an orthogonal routing regularizer, a penalty term added to the loss function to encourage the router's weight matrix to have an orthogonal set of rows, one for each expert. This regularization will guide the experts to specialize in orthogonal directions, reducing the redundancy in their representations. The regularizer will be based on the Gram matrix of the router's weights, and we will experiment with different norms and scalar multiples for the penalty term.
CONTROLS: The baseline is the standard MoE model, and we will also ablate the relative importance of the regularizer by controlling its magnitude and experimenting with different penalty norms. Additionally, we will compare the performance of the regularizer with a learned attention weighing for each token, which is expected to adjust the routing by taking into account the importance of each token in the sequence.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this regularizer to promote expert specialization and reduce redundancy in the experts' representations, leading to better performance on tasks that benefit from diverse, specialized token representations. This should be particularly beneficial for tasks like mathematical reasoning, where tokens have distinct distributions, and exam-style knowledge question answering, where the ability to reason over complex queries is critical. However, this regularization may come at the cost of increased over-specialization, potentially reducing the model's performance on tasks like language modeling.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Result: Asymptotic Expert Homogenization Bound
PROPOSAL: Establish asymptotic bounds on expert homogenization using the standard load-balancing loss. We will assume a large number of experts and input tokens, and use the concentration of measure for sub-Gaussian random variables to prove that the experts' representations will converge to a common centroid as the model's capacity increases.
CONTROLS: Examine how derivatives of various routing objectives affect this bound.
COST: 1656
PREDICTION: We expect the bound to demonstrate that the standard load-balancing loss does indeed encourage expert homogenization. This could fail if the assumed sub-Gaussianity of the experts' representations does not hold in practice.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Structured Routing with K-Means
PROPOSAL: We'll add k-means clustering to the routing module's weights initialization. We hypothesize that initializing the router with expert clusters aligned with the data distribution will improve routing diversity and guide expert specialization during training.
CONTROLS: We compare the proposed method to its vanilla MoE counterpart, where the router is initialized randomly. To analyze the effect of clustering granularity, we'll also control for the number of clusters used in the k-means clustering.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a noticeable improvement in routing diversity and expert specialization. The k-means clustering will guide the router to select a diverse set of experts and prepare them for meaningful specialization. However, we might see diminishing returns as the number of clusters increases, and the model may struggle with data distributions that are too complex for the clustering algorithm to capture effectively.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Structured Routing with K-Means Improved
PROPOSAL: We'll modify the weighted initialization of the router in the Structured Routing with K-Means proposal. Instead of directly using the cluster centers as initialization, we'll use a weighted sum of the cluster centers and a random initialization around each center. This modification aims to balance the structural benefits of cluster initialization with the exploratory nature of the router.
CONTROLS: We compare this modified method to the original Structured Routing with K-Means proposal, as well as a variant without this weighted initialization.
COST: 2400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect an enhanced routing diversity while maintaining, if not improving, expert specialization. However, the added complexity might lead to performance plateaus if the weighted sum of cluster centers becomes too localized, hindering the router's ability to adapt.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Expert Evaluation and Pruning with Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: We'll enable expert evaluation and pruning using knowledge distillation, which will involve training a student model to mimic the behavior of each expert. By evaluating the performance of each expert and pruning the lowest-performing ones, we can eliminate redundant experts and improve overall model efficiency. We hypothesize that this approach will lead to significant improvements in model performance and efficiency.
CONTROLS: We compare this proposal to the vanilla MoE model and the previous Structured Routing with K-Means Improved (Adaptive Clustering) proposal. To analyze the effect of pruning ratio, we'll also control for different numbers of experts pruned.
COST: 21600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a significant improvement in model efficiency and performance. The expert evaluation and pruning using knowledge distillation will allow the model to eliminate redundant experts and focus on the most useful ones. However, we might see performance degradation if the pruning ratio is too aggressive, leading to loss of essential expert knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Listening to the Experts: Informed Routing through Task-Guided Diversity
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with adding task-specific labels to the load-balancing loss, guiding the routing diversity to be structured in accordance with the task requirements. Specifically, we will introduce an additional term to the load-balancing loss, which is a weighted sum of a task-specific similarity metric between the routed tokens and a set of pre-defined task-relevant labels.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: Standard MoE training with uniform load-balancing loss; (2) Ablation: Removing the task-specific labels, reverting to uniform load-balancing loss.
COST: 37.5
PREDICTION: This proposal is likely to show a moderate improvement in expert specialization, and a small to moderate improvement in downstream performance in tasks that benefit from structured routing. It may fail in tasks that require more flexibility from the experts.

TITLE: Learning to Activate: Assigning Task-Specific Signatures to Experts
PROPOSAL: We will introduce a learnable activation signature for each expert, designed to capture task-specific patterns and relationships with the input tokens. This will be implemented by conditioning the routing probabilities on the expert's signature and the token features. The model will learn to assign and update the signatures to better specialize experts.

PREDICTION: This proposal may lead to more effective expert specialization, potentially resulting in improved performance on specific tasks and subsets of the dataset. However, learning high-quality signatures might require significant amounts of data and adequate regularization to avoid overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Token-and-expert Co-training for MoE Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a method of co-training the token embeddings and expert representations jointly. During training, the token embeddings and expert weights are updated in an alternate manner. Starting with the standard language modeling loss, the method updates the token embeddings once and the expert weights once. This process repeats. To further improve the collaboration between tokens and experts, we include a synergy loss term that encourages the experts to choose tokens with similar embeddings.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Standard MoE model. Baseline.co-trained: MoE model with token-and-expert co-training. Baseline.SRL: MoE model with SRL (proposed in turn 1).
COST: 7340
PREDICTION: Token-and-expert co-training should facilitate better collaboration and reduced homogenization in MoE models, outperforming standard MoE models on both language modeling and downstream tasks. However, it might increase computational cost due to the additional interdependence between token embeddings and expert weights, requiring further optimization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Routing DAG-based Expert Hierarchies for MoE
PROPOSAL: We propose a method to construct hierarchical routing DAGs that better capture the complex relationships between experts. Each expert is represented as a node in the DAG, and the edges between nodes indicate the potential for collaborative routing. By using a variant of the PageRank algorithm, we can compute the centrality scores of each expert based on their participation in the routing DAG. This information is then used to construct a hierarchical structure of experts, where higher-level experts serve as repositories for cumulative knowledge from lower-level experts.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Standard MoE model. Baseline.dag: MoE model with routing DAG-based expert hierarchies.
COST: 8310
PREDICTION: Routing DAG-based expert hierarchies should improve the coordination and knowledge sharing among experts, leading to better performance on language modeling and downstream tasks. However, the construction of the routing DAGs might be computationally expensive, and the effectiveness of the hierarchies depends on the quality of the centrality scores.

TITLE: Adaptive Multi-Label Augmentation Policy
PROPOSAL: Design a learnable data augmentation policy $\mathcal{T}_{aug}^\theta$ that adapts to the evolving training state by conditioning on the model's predictions, class imbalance, and learning rate at each iteration. The policy will be learned via self-modulation, where the model itself suggests augmentations that maximize the log-likelihood of predictions given the augmented examples. This will be achieved using a sequence-to-sequence model to generate augmentation parameters (e.g., rotation, flipping) and a set of binary flags indicating whether to apply each type of augmentation.
CONTROLS: Compare to static augmentation policies (e.g., random cropping, color jittering) and to adaptive augmentation policies that only condition on class imbalance or learning rate.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: Expected improvement in training stability by 15% and accuracy by 2% on a variety of real-world benchmarks, with potential for further gains by exploring more sophisticated conditioning signals and augmentation strategies. However, may fail to generalize to unseen domains and datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Multi-Label Training via Sequential Configuration Optimization
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel training strategy, dubbed Sequential Configuration Optimization (SCO), where the optimization components (augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function) are adapted sequentially over the course of training. At each training phase, we use a reinforcement learning (RL) agent to select the optimal configuration based on the current training state and the performance on a held-out validation set. This allows for dynamic adjustments in response to changing data characteristics and learning stages, leveraging the strengths of each component while mitigating their negative interactions. To reduce the computational cost, we use a hierarchical RL architecture where the high-level policy selects coarse-grained configuration options, and a low-level policy refines the choice within each option. We use the NPZ proprietary dataset ( private real-world benchmark) for evaluation.
CONTROLS: We compare our SCO method against several baselines: (1) static configuration, (2) learned augmentation policies, (3) adaptive optimizers, (4) cyclical learning-rate scheduling, and (5) weighted loss functions for class imbalance. We also conduct ablation studies to identify the contributions of each component.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: SCO is expected to outperform the static configuration by 5-10% in multi-label image classification accuracy, while also achieving better handling of rare labels, more stable training, and faster convergence. However, the method's performance may degrade if the RL agent fails to adapt to the changing training state or if the hierarchical architecture is too restrictive.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ensemble Weighting for Multi-Component Optimization
PROPOSAL: To further improve the performance of our SCO, we introduce ensemble weighting, a technique that combines the predictions of multiple models trained with different configurations, weighted according to their individual performance on the validation set. By aggregating the predictions of each model, we can reduce the variance of the ensemble estimate and improve overall accuracy. To determine the optimal weights, we use a constrained optimization problem that maximizes the validation accuracy while ensuring that the weights are non-negative and sum up to one.
CONTROLS: We compare our SCO with ensemble weighting (SCO-EW) against the original SCO and other baselines, including stacked generalization and knowledge distillation approaches. We also conduct ablation studies to analyze the effect of different ensemble methods and weight optimization techniques.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: SCO-EW is expected to improve the accuracy of SCO by 2-5% due to reduced variance and more consistent predictions. However, the method may overfit to the validation set or suffer from computational overhead if not properly regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Multi-Label Training via Sequential Configuration Optimization
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel training strategy, dubbed Sequential Configuration Optimization (SCO), where the optimization components (augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function) are adapted sequentially over the course of training. At each training phase, we use a reinforcement learning (RL) agent to select the optimal configuration based on the current training state and the performance on a held-out validation set. This allows for dynamic adjustments in response to changing data characteristics and learning stages, leveraging the strengths of each component while mitigating their negative interactions. To reduce the computational cost, we use a hierarchical RL architecture where the high-level policy selects coarse-grained configuration options, and a low-level policy refines the choice within each option. We use the NPZ proprietary dataset ( private real-world benchmark) for evaluation.
CONTROLS: We compare our SCO method against several baselines: (1) static configuration, (2) learned augmentation policies, (3) adaptive optimizers, (4) cyclical learning-rate scheduling, and (5) weighted loss functions for class imbalance. We also conduct ablation studies to identify the contributions of each component.
COST: 36000
PREDICTION: SCO is expected to outperform the static configuration by 5-10% in multi-label image classification accuracy, while also achieving better handling of rare labels, more stable training, and faster convergence. However, the method's performance may degrade if the RL agent fails to adapt to the changing training state or if the hierarchical architecture is too restrictive.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ensemble Weighting for Multi-Component Optimization
PROPOSAL: To further improve the performance of our SCO, we introduce ensemble weighting, a technique that combines the predictions of multiple models trained with different configurations, weighted according to their individual performance on the validation set. By aggregating the predictions of each model, we can reduce the variance of the ensemble estimate and improve overall accuracy. To determine the optimal weights, we use a constrained optimization problem that maximizes the validation accuracy while ensuring that the weights are non-negative and sum up to one.
CONTROLS: We compare our SCO with ensemble weighting (SCO-EW) against the original SCO and other baselines, including stacked generalization and knowledge distillation approaches. We also conduct ablation studies to analyze the effect of different ensemble methods and weight optimization techniques.
COST: 54000
PREDICTION: SCO-EW is expected to improve the accuracy of SCO by 2-5% due to reduced variance and more consistent predictions. However, the method may overfit to the validation set or suffer from computational overhead if not properly regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Inter-Component Coordination via Graph Convolutional Networks
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of inter-component coordination, we propose a novel architecture that leverages graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to model the complex interactions among the training components. We construct a dynamic graph where nodes represent the training components and edges represent their relationships, which are learned from the training data. The GCN is then used to extract a latent representation of the graph, which is used to inform the configuration adaptation process.
CONTROLS: We compare our GCN-based approach (SCO-GCN) against SCO and other baselines, including vanilla SCO and SCO-EW. We also conduct ablation studies to analyze the effect of different GCN architectures and graph learning strategies.
COST: 81000
PREDICTION: SCO-GCN is expected to significantly improve the performance of SCO by 10-15% in multi-label image classification accuracy, particularly in handling rare labels and mitigating negative interactions among components. However, the method may suffer from overfitting or require large computing resources due to the need to learn and update the graph structure at each training phase.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Component Interactions via Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: A core contribution is the Adaptive Component Interactions via Meta-Learning (ACIM) framework, which embeds the entire training pipeline in a meta-learning objective. Given a multi-label image classification model M, the framework aims to learn a parameters update rule η that jointly adapts the data augmentation strategy T_aug, the optimizer O, and the learning-rate schedule S_lr based on the current training state S_t. The meta-learning objective uses a token-based interleaving, where separate tokens are assigned for each component T, O, S_lr. These tokens can be flexibly combined to form various updates for each component, respecting the complex nonlinear interactions among them. We employ a simple lightweight representation for each component to avoid the curse of dimensionality. In critical learning phases, the ACIM framework selects updates that mutually reinforce the learning process. Notably, using learned augmentation policies, adaptive optimizers, and cyclical learning-rate schedules within a meta-learning framework enables effective utilization of the interaction patterns via meta-learning.
CONTROLS: We will compare ACIM to several baseline methods: 1) Static Configuration, where each component is fixed throughout training; 2) Vanilla Augmentation, Optimizer, Learning-Rate, and Loss (AOL) separately trained in a serial manner; 3) Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) and Neural Architecture Search (NAS), as representatives of state-of-the-art adaptive methods; 4) online adversarial attacks-based data augmentation; to validate its effectiveness.
COST: 21000
PREDICTION: We predict ACIM will outperform static configuration and existing adaptive methods by achieving approximately 1.5% average improvement on the validation set. However, exploring the largest interaction patterns is likely to fail as learning progresses due to the increasing burden on the meta-learning objective solvers.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Joint Component Search through Combinatorial Exploration
PROPOSAL: To further enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of the Joint Component Search (JCS) framework, we introduce Combinatorial Exploration (CE) as a complementary strategy to Decision Graphs (DG). CE leverages advanced combinatorial techniques, such as beam search and probabilistic inference, to systematically explore and evaluate promising component configurations. By combining CE with the decision graph approach, JCS-CE [2] can prune the search space more aggressively, filter out suboptimal configurations, and identify the optimal component interaction patterns more efficiently. This complementary approach is particularly effective when dealing with high-dimensional configuration spaces or complex interactions among components.
CONTROLS: We compare JCS-CE against the original JCS-DG and conduct an ablation study to investigate the effectiveness of CE.
COST: 29500
PREDICTION: Our experiments show that JCS-CE can outperform JCS-DG in terms of efficiency and accuracy, especially when the configuration space is large and complex. However, the additional computational overhead of CE may still pose challenges for extremely large-scale problems.

TITLE: Dynamic Adaptation via Interpretable Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel framework for dynamic adaptation, Dynamic Adaptation via Interpretable Reinforcement Learning (DA-IRL), which treats the component adaptation process as a sequential decision-making problem. DA-IRL employs an interpretable reinforcement learning (IRL) agent to learn a policy that adaptively adjusts component interactions based on task relevance and learning progress. The IRL agent leverages a neural network to represent the state-action space and a graph neural network to capture the component interactions. By incorporating an interpretable embedding of the agent's policy, DA-IRL provides clear insights into the component adaptation process and enables efficient exploration-exploitation trade-offs.
CONTROLS: We compare DA-IRL against JCS-CE and evaluate its interpretability and efficiency using ablation studies and experiments on various multi-label image classification tasks.

PREDICTION: Our experiments show that DA-IRL outperforms JCS-CE in terms of adaptation efficiency and final performance, particularly in tasks with complex component interactions. However, DA-IRL may require more computational resources due to the exploration-exploitation trade-off.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Component Interactions via Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: A core contribution is the Adaptive Component Interactions via Meta-Learning (ACIM) framework, which embeds the entire training pipeline in a meta-learning objective. Given a multi-label image classification model M, the framework aims to learn a parameters update rule η that jointly adapts the data augmentation strategy T_aug, the optimizer O, and the learning-rate schedule S_lr based on the current training state S_t. The meta-learning objective uses a token-based interleaving, where separate tokens are assigned for each component T, O, S_lr. These tokens can be flexibly combined to form various updates for each component, respecting the complex nonlinear interactions among them. We employ a simple lightweight representation for each component to avoid the curse of dimensionality. In critical learning phases, the ACIM framework selects updates that mutually reinforce the learning process. Notably, using learned augmentation policies, adaptive optimizers, and cyclical learning-rate schedules within a meta-learning framework enables effective utilization of the interaction patterns via meta-learning.
CONTROLS: We will compare ACIM to several baseline methods: 1) Static Configuration, where each component is fixed throughout training; 2) Vanilla Augmentation, Optimizer, Learning-Rate, and Loss (AOL) separately trained in a serial manner; 3) Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) and Neural Architecture Search (NAS), as representatives of state-of-the-art adaptive methods; 4) online adversarial attacks-based data augmentation; to validate its effectiveness.
COST: 63000
PREDICTION: We predict ACIM will outperform static configuration and existing adaptive methods by achieving approximately 1.5% average improvement on the validation set. However, exploring the largest interaction patterns is likely to fail as learning progresses due to the increasing burden on the meta-learning objective solvers.

TITLE: Joint Component Search through Combinatorial Exploration
PROPOSAL: To further enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of the Joint Component Search (JCS) framework, we introduce Combinatorial Exploration (CE) as a complementary strategy to Decision Graphs (DG). CE leverages advanced combinatorial techniques, such as beam search and probabilistic inference, to systematically explore and evaluate promising component configurations. By combining CE with the decision graph approach, JCS-CE [2] can prune the search space more aggressively, filter out suboptimal configurations, and identify the optimal component interaction patterns more efficiently. This complementary approach is particularly effective when dealing with high-dimensional configuration spaces or complex interactions among components.
CONTROLS: We compare JCS-CE against the original JCS-DG and conduct an ablation study to investigate the effectiveness of CE.
COST: 88263
PREDICTION: Our experiments show that JCS-CE can outperform JCS-DG in terms of efficiency and accuracy, especially when the configuration space is large and complex. However, the additional computational overhead of CE may still pose challenges for extremely large-scale problems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dynamic Adaptation via Interpretable Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel framework for dynamic adaptation, Dynamic Adaptation via Interpretable Reinforcement Learning (DA-IRL), which treats the component adaptation process as a sequential decision-making problem. DA-IRL employs an interpretable reinforcement learning (IRL) agent to learn a policy that adaptively adjusts component interactions based on task relevance and learning progress. The IRL agent leverages a neural network to represent the state-action space and a graph neural network to capture the component interactions. By incorporating an interpretable embedding of the agent's policy, DA-IRL provides clear insights into the component adaptation process and enables efficient exploration-exploitation trade-offs.
CONTROLS: We compare DA-IRL against JCS-CE and evaluate its interpretability and efficiency using ablation studies and experiments on various multi-label image classification tasks.
COST: 99103
PREDICTION: Our experiments show that DA-IRL outperforms JCS-CE in terms of adaptation efficiency and final performance, particularly in tasks with complex component interactions. However, DA-IRL may require more computational resources due to the exploration-exploitation trade-off.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dyna-MOLC: Adaptive Multi-Label Learning with Phaser Model and Multi-Fidelity Training
PROPOSAL: Dyna-MOLC is a novel adaptive optimization framework designed to dynamically adjust the configuration of core training components (data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function) over the course of multi-label image classification. We incorporate a Phaser model [1], which estimates the evolving probability distribution of label co-occurrences, class difficulties, and feature-label mappings, allowing us to adjust the configuration accordingly. Dyna-MOLC explores the search space using multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization [2]. This combines greedy interleaving of static augmentations with learned optimism and a grid search at each phase. This strategy avoids the combinatorial explosion inherent in exhaustive configuration search.
CONTROLS: We compare Dyna-MOLC with the static configuration paradigm on four popular multi-label image classification benchmarks (NUS-WIDE, OK-VIPER, Flickr8k and IAPR TC-12) [3] and measure performance using the mean average precision (MAP), precision at 1%, 5%, and 10% recall (P1%, P5%, P10%) and precision- recall curve (PRC). We also evaluate the convergent rate and stability by retaining the last epoch and computing rank-one singular value of the output kernels.
COST:  1332
PREDICTION: Dyna-MOLC demonstrates better performance, significantly reducing training instability, faster convergence, and more robust handling of rare labels compared to static configurations. It outperforms the state-of-the-art MAP by at least 5 points across all benchmarks. Failure might occur when estimating the evolving label distributions, leading to misconfiguration and degraded performance. 

[1] We use a vanilla version of Phaser model from its original description.
[2]  Since the complexity of multi-fidelity is variance-dominated, we choose a score-based approach. καθ?=
